passages.title: Humility in prayer, turning from vain talk, zakah
passages.tafsir:
**The passage announces the verdict first and the evidence afterwards.** Ayah 1 declares that the believers have won — and then, instead of leaving "believer" as a label, ayat 2–4 begin listing the qualities that make the word real: stillness of heart in prayer, turning away from what is empty, and zakah. What holds these ayat together is that grammatical shape: one sweeping verdict, followed by a chain of relative clauses ("those who… and those who… and those who…"), each one a portrait of the person the verdict is about.

## Ayah 1: what *falāḥ* actually means

Ibn Kathir glosses قَدْ أَفْلَحَ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ simply: "they have attained victory and are blessed, for they have succeeded."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stops here to open the word up, because everything after it hangs on this promise. Quoting the lexicon *Qāmūs*, it defines **falāḥ** as "the attainment of all desires as well as protection from all misfortunes." Hold both halves in mind. It is not merely getting what you want; it is also never losing it, never dreading its loss. It is so comprehensive, Maʿārif says, that it may be regarded as the very summit of what a human being could wish for.

And that is precisely why it stings. Maʿārif presses the point honestly: total falāḥ in this sense — no desire left unfulfilled, complete immunity from the turns of fate — is granted to no one on earth. Not to great kings. Not even, in this worldly life, to the most revered prophets of Allah. There is always the fear of fortune declining, the apprehension of some disaster on the way; no living person can claim to be free of that.

So the conclusion is unavoidable: **complete falāḥ cannot be had in this world at all.** This is a place of pain and toil where nothing lasts and everything must perish. The commodity exists, but it is stocked elsewhere — in Paradise, where, as Allah says, *"They have all that they call for"* (36:57), and where the people of Paradise enter saying: *"Praise belongs to Allah who has put away all sorrow from us…"* (35:34–35). Maʿārif draws a quiet inference from that verse: the fact that they thank Allah for removing sorrow tells you that there is no one in this world who has not, at some point, been touched by grief.

**"But the wicked seem to prosper."** Maʿārif raises the obvious objection: in plain experience it is often the disbelievers and the corrupt who enjoy prosperity, while prophets and reformers have in every age suffered hardship. Its answer follows from what it has already established. Since total falāḥ belongs to the next world, it follows that *everyone* here — pious or wicked — necessarily tastes some measure of pain, and everyone likewise has some of his wishes granted. So worldly comfort cannot be the measuring stick at all; the question is settled only by "the fate which awaits them." Even so, Maʿārif adds, observation shows that the righteous who carry these qualities may face trials for a time but are soon released from distress and given what they sought; they command respect while they live, and their memory is cherished after they die.

So Allah's promise here covers both: the total falāḥ that only the Hereafter can deliver, plus whatever measure of relief and prosperity He grants His servants in this life. Maʿārif also draws in Sūrah al-Aʿlā, where the Qur'an says that falāḥ is obtained by purifying oneself from sin (*qad aflaḥa man tazakkā*) — and where it also makes clear that total falāḥ is achieved in the Hereafter only, so that one who aims at falāḥ must not succumb to the temptations of this world: *"Nay, but you prefer the present life; and the world to come is better, and more lasting."*

**One detail worth noticing:** Maʿārif points out that the call to prayer invites every Muslim toward falāḥ five times a day. The very next ayah tells you what to do when you arrive.

**The foundation before the qualities.** Maʿārif is careful about the order: the first and most fundamental attribute, on which everything else rests, is that a person be a true believer. The qualities that follow are the qualities *of* faith, not substitutes for it.

## Ayah 2: *khāshiʿūn* — the stillness that success is built on

الَّذِينَ هُمْ فِي صَلَاتِهِمْ خَاشِعُونَ — "those who humble themselves in their prayer."

**The word.** ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that *khāshiʿūn* means "those with fear and with tranquillity" — and Ibn Kathir notes the same was narrated from Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, and az-Zuhrī. Feel the pairing: awe and calm together. Not agitation, and not indifference — the settledness of someone who knows exactly Whom he is standing before. Maʿārif gives the literal sense of *khushūʿ* as "calmness," and in religious usage, "to bring about a state of perfect concentration in the heart," so that a person does not knowingly let any thought enter it other than the remembrance of Allah. Tafsīr Maẓharī traces that definition to ʿAmr Ibn Dīnār.

**Where it lives.** It was reported from ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him) that khushūʿ is the khushūʿ *of the heart* — and Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī held the same. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said, "Their khushūʿ was in their hearts" — and then, Ibn Kathir adds, the effect showed outwardly: they lowered their gaze and were humble toward others. That is the direction of travel. Khushūʿ starts inside and shows on the body; it is not a posture you adopt to manufacture a feeling.

Maʿārif gathers the early definitions and treats them as details of that same one thing — the serenity of heart *and* limbs:

- **Mujāhid**: casting down one's eyes and keeping the voice low.
- **ʿAlī** (may Allah be pleased with him): refraining from casting sideways glances.
- **ʿAṭāʾ**: "not toying with any part of the body."

Practically, Maʿārif notes, this means avoiding unnecessary movement of the body and limbs in prayer — especially the movements the Prophet ﷺ forbade, which the jurists have collected under the heading *makrūhāt*, things disliked in prayer.

**From the Sunnah.** Maʿārif reports (citing Maẓharī) from Abū Dharr that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah keeps His attention on His servant during prayer for as long as the servant keeps his attention on Allah; when he turns away and glances aside, Allah turns away from him. And it is reported that the Prophet ﷺ directed Anas to keep his eyes fixed on the spot where his forehead touches the ground in sajdah, and not to look right and left in prayer.

Abū Hurayrah relates that the Prophet ﷺ saw a man praying while fiddling with his beard and said: *"If this man had khushūʿ in his heart, his limbs would have been still."* One line, and the whole relationship between inside and outside is settled.

**Khushūʿ as delight, not strain.** Ibn Kathir's most striking sentence is that khushūʿ in prayer is only attained by one who has emptied his heart entirely for it, who pays attention to nothing else, and who prefers it above everything else — and at that point prayer "becomes a delight and a joy for the eyes." He cites the hadith recorded by Imam Aḥmad and an-Nasāʾī from Anas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Fragrance and women have been made dear to me, and prayer was made the joy of my eye."* Read that against ayah 1: the prayer of the successful is not an obligation grimly discharged but the place where the heart finally rests.

**Is khushūʿ obligatory? The scholars differ.** Maʿārif reports the disagreement plainly:

- **Imam Ghazzālī, Qurṭubī and others** held that khushūʿ in prayer is obligatory, and that a prayer offered without it is deemed not to have been performed.
- **Others** held that although khushūʿ is the essence of prayer, and its absence strips prayer of its true purpose, it is not an indispensable condition of validity — its absence does not make repeating the prayer necessary.
- **Ḥakīm ul-Ummah**, in *Bayān ul-Qurʼān*, takes a middle position: khushūʿ is not a condition for the prayer's *validity*, but it is essential for the prayer's *acceptance* by Allah — and from that angle it is obligatory.

That last framing is the one to carry away. A prayer's being *counted* and a prayer's being *accepted* are two different questions, and this ayah is speaking about the second.

**And it will get harder.** Ṭabarānī, in *al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr*, relates from Abū Dardāʾ that the Prophet ﷺ said that the first thing to be taken away from this Ummah is khushūʿ — until a time comes when no one is left practising it. Anyone who has struggled to keep his mind in his prayer should hear that as consolation and as warning at once: the difficulty is real and foretold, which is exactly why the effort is worth so much.

## Ayah 3: turning away from *al-laghw*

وَالَّذِينَ هُمْ عَنِ اللَّغْوِ مُعْرِضُونَ.

Ibn Kathir defines *al-laghw* broadly: falsehood — which takes in shirk and sin — and, beyond that, "any words or deeds that are of no benefit." He connects it to Allah's description of the servants of the Most Merciful: *"And if they pass by al-laghw, they pass by it with dignity"* (25:72). Note the verb in our ayah — *muʿriḍūn*, they *turn away*. Not that they never encounter it; the world is full of it. They decline to be drawn in.

Maʿārif maps the two levels:

- **Laghw at its extreme** shades into acts that are outright sinful and harmful — these must be avoided outright.
- **Laghw in its mild form** is neither useful nor harmful; it simply earns nothing. Giving up this habit, Maʿārif says, is highly desirable.

And it cites the hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said that part of a person's being a good Muslim is his leaving what does not concern him.

**What makes this possible.** Qatādah's comment, quoted by Ibn Kathir, is worth sitting with: *"By Allah, there came to them from Allah that which kept them away from that."* The turning away is not raw willpower. Something arrived from Allah — and it displaced the appetite for emptiness.

## Ayah 4: *lil-zakāti fāʿilūn*

وَالَّذِينَ هُمْ لِلزَّكَاةِ فَاعِلُونَ.

**The literal root, and the technical sense.** *Zakāh* literally means "to purify." In religious terminology it means giving a prescribed portion of one's wealth in charity under set conditions, and this is how the Qur'an generally uses the word. Ibn Kathir reports that most commentators take it that way here too.

**But there is a historical difficulty.** This sūrah was revealed in Makkah, and obligatory zakāh — with its thresholds and fixed rates — was ordained in Madīnah, in the year 2 AH. So how can Makkan believers be praised for it?

Ibn Kathir's answer: what was instituted in Madīnah was zakāh *as a defined system* — the *nuṣub* (the thresholds of wealth) and the specific amounts. The underlying principle of giving a due out of one's wealth was already enjoined in Makkah. He cites Sūrat al-Anʿām, also Makkan: *"but pay the due thereof on the day of its harvest"* (6:141). Maʿārif reports the same answer from Ibn Kathir and other commentators, adducing Sūrah al-Muzzammil — by consensus Makkan — where *"and pay zakāh"* appears alongside *"establish the prayer."* On this reading, zakāh was obligated in Makkah and its administrative details — collection, and the determination of the wealth liable to it (*niṣāb*) — were settled after the Hijrah.

**The other reading: purification of the self.** Ibn Kathir offers a second possibility — that what is meant here is the purification of the soul from shirk and filth, as in *"Indeed he succeeds who purifies himself; and indeed he fails who corrupts himself"* (91:9–10). Notice that this verse uses the same verb of success, *aflaḥa*, as our ayah 1.

**A grammatical argument you can see with your own eyes.** Maʿārif reports that scholars who hold that obligatory zakāh was legislated only in Madīnah take the word here in its literal sense — and it points to a clue inside the ayah itself. Wherever the Qur'an speaks of the obligatory charity, the wording refers to the *payment* of zakāh: *yuʾtūn az-zakāh*, *ātū az-zakāh*. Here the wording is *lil-zakāti fāʿilūn* — "**performers** of zakāh" — which, Maʿārif says, clearly indicates the word is not being used in its technical sense here. And *fāʿilūn* derives from *fiʿl*, performance; but technically zakāh is not an act at all — it is a portion of wealth, so using "performers" of it needs suitable explanation.

**Both, most likely.** Ibn Kathir's own conclusion is generous: it may be that both meanings are intended — purification of the soul and of one's wealth — "because that is part of the purification of the soul, and the true believer is one who pays attention to both matters. And Allah knows best."

Maʿārif closes the same way by noting that on either reading nothing is lost. If the technical meaning is taken, zakāh's obligation on Muslims is undisputed. If the literal meaning is taken, that too is obligatory: cleansing the soul of shirk, hypocrisy, vanity, jealousy, hatred, greed and miserliness is what is called *tazkiyah*, and these things are forbidden and are major sins that one is obliged to purify oneself from.

## Holding the four together

Read as one unit, the passage draws a single line. Ayah 1 names a prize no one on earth fully possesses. Ayat 2–4 then describe the person who will be given it — and the description moves outward in widening circles: first the heart, standing still before Allah in prayer; then the tongue and the hours of the day, turned away from what is empty; then the hand and the wealth, giving out a due and letting go of greed. The purifying is the thread — the soul in ayah 2, the habits in ayah 3, the wealth and the self in ayah 4.

And the word that opens it all, Maʿārif reminds us, is the word the call to prayer sounds toward five times a day. You are summoned toward exactly what ayah 1 promises — and the first thing asked of you when you answer is the khushūʿ of ayah 2.

passages.title: Guarding chastity, and the bounds not to be crossed
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These three ayat describe one quality of the successful believer — chastity — but they describe it in three movements: the habit of guarding (ayah 5), the one place where that guard is lawfully lowered (ayah 6), and the verdict on anyone who reaches past that place (ayah 7). Read alone, ayah 5 could sound like a call to suppress desire. Read as a unit, the passage does something more balanced: it fences a powerful human appetite, opens one lawful door inside the fence, declares the one who enters by that door free of any blame at all, and then names everyone who climbs the fence for what they are — transgressors.

## Where these ayat sit in the surah

Surah al-Mu'minun opens with the declaration *qad aflaḥa al-mu'minūn* — "Successful indeed are the believers" — and then lists the qualities of those who attain that success. Ibn Kathir explains the opening to mean "they have attained victory and are blessed, for they have succeeded," and reads everything that follows as the description of *these* believers, the ones who actually have these characteristics.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word *falāḥ* — success — from the lexicon *Qāmūs*: it signifies "the attainment of all desires as well as protection from all misfortunes." That is the promise the whole list is attached to.

Maʿārif then sets out the qualities as *attributes* of the believer to whom that promise is made. Its heading reads "The seven attributes of a perfect Believer," while the discussion immediately beneath it names true faith as "the first and most important attribute which is fundamental and basic to everything else," and then turns to "the other seven attributes mentioned in the verse." The text as we have it is not consistent about the final count, and it is better to leave that as it stands than to tidy it. What is clear is the shape: true faith underneath, and these named qualities built on it. Guarding chastity is what Maʿārif labels the "Forth Attribute" — the fourth. Before it come *khushūʿ* (concentration and calm) in prayer, abstaining from *laghw* (useless talk and action), and *zakāh*. After it, in the ayat that follow, come faithfulness to trusts and covenants, and strict guarding of the prayers — of which Ibn Kathir notes that Allah "begins and ends this list of praiseworthy qualities with Salah, which is indicative of its virtue."

That placement is worth pausing on. Chastity is not filed away as a private matter of personal purity, off to one side of religion. It stands in the same list as prayer, charity and keeping one's word — one continuous portrait of a believing life. And it sits directly beside *zakāh*, about which Ibn Kathir says that most commentators take it as the zakah paid on wealth, though it could also mean purification of the soul "from Shirk and filth." He does not close the question: "It could be that both meanings are intended, purification of the soul and of one's wealth... and the true believer is one who pays attention to both matters. And Allah knows best."

## Ayah 5: guarding

*Wa'lladhīna hum li-furūjihim ḥāfiẓūn* — "and those who guard their chastity."

Ibn Kathir's gloss is direct: these are "those who protect their private parts from unlawful actions and do not do that which Allah has forbidden" — he names fornication and homosexuality — "and do not approach anyone except the wives whom Allah has made permissible for them or their right hand possessions."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this, like the other items on the list, as an *attribute* — a standing trait of the believer's character rather than an isolated act. Its summary of the fourth attribute is exactly that: such people "satisfy their needs with their wives and their legal bondmaids according to the prescribed laws and avoid unlawful liaison."

A reflection, offered as reflection: the ayah's image is of a guard. A guard is not someone who has no enemy; he is someone who has an enemy and stays awake. The ayah does not praise a man for having no desire. It praises him for keeping watch over a desire he certainly has.

## Ayah 6: the lawful door, and the freedom from blame

*Illā ʿalā azwājihim aw mā malakat aymānuhum fa-innahum ghayru malūmīn* — "except with their wives or those in their possession, for then they are free from blame."

Three things deserve attention here.

**First, the exception is a genuine permission, not a grudging tolerance.** Ibn Kathir writes: "One who seeks what Allah has made permissible for him is not to be blamed and there is no sin on him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase "because they are not liable to blame." Allah could have said simply "except with their wives" and moved on; instead He adds that within that bond a believer stands clear of reproach. Marriage is not presented as a permitted lapse from a purer ideal. The believer who fulfils his desire where Allah has opened the way has done nothing that stains him.

**Second, on "those whom their right hands possess."** Ibn Kathir explains this as "their right hand possessions from the captives." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān speaks of "legal bondmaids" and says that needs are satisfied with them "according to the prescribed laws"; elsewhere it uses the phrase *lawfully acquired*. Both commentaries are describing a form of servitude that existed in the society the Qur'an first addressed, and Maʿārif is explicit that it was bounded by law rather than being a general licence over anyone in one's power. The operative point of the ayah for a reader today is the structure it establishes: lawful intimacy runs through relationships that Allah Himself has defined and regulated, and through no others. Everything else in the passage turns on that principle.

**Third — and this is Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own reading of *ghayru malūmīn*** — being "free from blame" does not mean being free from all restraint. Maʿārif says the phrase "also means that the sexual desire must be kept under strict control and must not be allowed to become a means of gratification of one's passions." The lawful door is not an invitation to make appetite the organising principle of a life. Even inside the permission, the believer is still someone who governs the desire rather than being governed by it.

## Ayah 7: the boundary, and the word for those who cross it

*Fa-mani'btaghā warā'a dhālika fa-ulā'ika humu'l-ʿādūn* — "but whoever seeks beyond that, those are the transgressors."

**"Beyond that."** Ibn Kathir defines the phrase in a single line: "meaning, other than a wife or slave girl." The exception in ayah 6 is the *whole* of the exception. Once the lawful ground is named, everything outside it falls under "beyond that."

**"The transgressors."** The Arabic is *al-ʿādūn*, and Ibn Kathir glosses it in one word: "aggressors." That is a striking choice. He does not gloss it as "the weak" or "the tempted," which is how such a person usually thinks of himself. To cross this line is not merely to slip; it is to push past a limit that Allah set.

**What falls under "beyond that."** Ibn Kathir names fornication and homosexuality. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a fuller list drawn from the jurists, citing *Tafsīr Bayān ul-Qurʼān*, Qurtubi and *al-Baḥr ul-Muḥīṭ*. Satisfying one's desire with someone other than one's own wife or a lawfully acquired bondmaid is strictly forbidden, and the ban includes:

- adultery — and Maʿārif adds in the same breath that marrying a woman whom one is not allowed to marry under the religious code is also adultery;
- intercourse with one's wife or bondmaid when she is menstruating or is confined;
- unnatural intercourse with them;
- homosexuality;
- bestiality;
- and, as most jurists hold, masturbation.

Two features of that list are worth naming. A marriage performed over a union the religious code forbids does not change what the act is; Maʿārif still calls it adultery. And "beyond that" reaches even inside marriage: there are acts with one's own spouse that the list still counts as forbidden. That fits the point Maʿārif drew out of *ghayru malūmīn* — the desire stays under command.

Where the scholars are not unanimous, the source says so: Maʿārif reports masturbation as the position of *most* jurists, not of all, and an honest reader should hold it that way rather than flattening the difference.

## Living it

**Keep the guard posted.** Chastity here is named as an attribute of the believer, not as an emergency response. The one who only begins guarding when temptation is already in the room has misread what the ayah is describing.

**Do not feel ashamed of the lawful.** A believer who fulfils his desire where Allah has permitted is, in Ibn Kathir's words, "not to be blamed and there is no sin on him." Scrupulosity that treats marital intimacy as somehow low is not piety; the ayah explicitly clears it of blame.

**Do not treat permission as licence.** Maʿārif's reading is the corrective on the other side: the desire must be kept under strict control and not allowed to become a means of gratifying one's passions. The guarding continues inside the marriage, not only outside it.

**Recognise the name the Qur'an gives.** When a person is drawn "beyond that," the word the ayah uses for him is not *the weak* but *al-ʿādūn* — and Ibn Kathir's gloss for that is *aggressors*. Naming the act accurately is itself a defence.

## A closing thought

Taken together, these three ayat do not describe a man at war with himself. They describe a door that Allah opened and clearly marked, a believer who enters by it and stands free of blame, and a line he does not push past. And the whole list in which they sit is attached to a single promise: *falāḥ* — in Maʿārif's rendering from *Qāmūs*, "the attainment of all desires as well as protection from all misfortunes." A believer who keeps this guard is not being denied. He is being counted among those to whom that success is promised.

passages.title: Trusts, covenants, prayers — and the inheritance of Firdaws
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat bring to a close the portrait of the successful believer that opened this sūrah. Ayah 8 and ayah 9 supply the last two of the qualities in the list — being faithful to trusts and covenants, and guarding the prayers — and then ayat 10 and 11 name the reward the whole passage has been building toward: these people are *the heirs*, and what they inherit is Firdaws, forever.

What holds the four ayat together is that movement from description to destination. Everything before ayah 10 is a portrait of character; ayah 10 turns the portrait into a title deed.

## Ayah 8: two words that hold a life together

**"Those who are faithfully true to their Amānāt and to their covenants are Rāʿūn."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is plain and practical: when they are entrusted with something, they do not betray that trust, but they fulfill it, and when they make a promise or make a pledge, they are true to their word.

**Why "trusts" is plural.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the form of the word. *Amānah* — a trust — covers "everything which a person has undertaken to perform or which have been placed under his care as trust." Since it may be of many kinds, the word is used in the plural, so that it may include all sorts of trusts "whether they may relate to the rights of Allah or to the rights of human beings."

That two-sided division is worth pausing on, because it quietly widens the ayah far beyond what an English reader first hears in the word "trust":

- **Trusts owed to Allah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that to perform scrupulously all the injunctions and duties made obligatory by religious laws, and to abstain from things which have been forbidden or declared undesirable, is to look after the trust that relates to the rights of Allah. Your own religion, on this reading, is a deposit left in your hands.
- **Trusts owed to people.** These, it says, "take numerous forms." The most well-known is that a person must promptly return to the owner on demand any goods which have been in his custody as trust. But it goes further: **information received in confidence is a trust**, and to reveal it to anybody else without the permission of the person who gave it is a breach of trust. And the mutual settlement between an employer and an employee of the terms of employment — the work to be done, the time to be spent in performing it, and the wages to be paid — is a trust binding on *both* parties, so that a violation of this agreement by either party would constitute a breach of trust.

Notice how even-handed that last example is. The employee who does not give the hours, and the employer who does not give the wage, are described by the same word. "Hence," Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, "discharge of trust is an all-encompassing word."

**Why "covenant" is a separate quality.** The commentary treats trust (ayah 8's first half) and covenant (its second half) as two distinct attributes — the fifth and the sixth in its counting of this list. The word *ʿahd* has two connotations:

1. **A covenant between two parties**, specifying the duties and obligations of either party and binding on both. A breach of this covenant by either party, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, "is a fraud and deceit and therefore forbidden in Islam."
2. **A one-sided promise** — where a person voluntarily promises to give something to someone, or undertakes to do some job. This is *waʿdah*, a promise, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that its fulfilment too is obligatory under the dictates of the Sharīʿah.

On this second kind it says there is a hadith which means **"a promise is like a debt."** (No collection is named for it there, so none is named here.) Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the comparison with real precision: a promise must be fulfilled in the same manner as a debt must be discharged, the difference being that whereas the repayment of a debt can be enforced through a court of law, a voluntary promise is not enforceable in the same way. The person making the promise is nevertheless morally bound to abide by it, and failure to do so would be a sin unless there is a religious ground for his inability to fulfil it. So the ayah is describing exactly the area of life where nobody can compel you — and saying that this is where the believer is most reliable.

**The mirror image.** Ibn Kathir sets these believers against their opposite. This, he says, is not like the hypocrites, about whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"The signs of the hypocrite are three: when he speaks he lies, when he makes a promise he breaks it, and when he is entrusted with something he betrays that trust."** (Ibn Kathir quotes this without naming a collection here, so none is named here either.) Read the two side by side and ayah 8 sharpens: what separates the believer from the hypocrite in these words is not belief professed but words kept and deposits returned. Faith is being tested at the point where it touches other people's property, secrets and expectations.

## Ayah 9: the prayers, in the plural

**"And those who strictly guard their Ṣalawāt."** Ibn Kathir explains this — they guard, they keep watch over — as meaning that **they persistently offer their prayers at their appointed times**. Qatādah adds the outward dimension: "At the fixed times, with the proper bowing and prostration." So guarding a prayer means guarding both its clock and its shape.

**A grammatical detail with a lesson in it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that to observe one's prayers here means to offer them regularly at the appointed time, and that the word *ṣalawāt*, "prayers," has been used in the plural form to include all five of the daily prayers. In an earlier ayah of the sūrah the word was used in the singular, because there the emphasis was on khushūʿ — the humble stillness that is the essence of *all* prayers, whether farḍ (obligatory), wājib (necessary), sunnah or nafl (voluntary). The singular speaks of the inner state that every prayer must have; the plural speaks of the schedule that must not be missed. The sūrah asks for both.

**How beloved this is to Allah.** Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, 'O Messenger of Allah, which deed is most beloved to Allah?' He said, **'Prayer at the appointed time.'** I said, 'Then what?' He said, **'Kindness to one's parents.'** I said, 'Then what?' He said, **'Jihad in the way of Allah.'**" Ibn Kathir notes that it was recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs.

**The list is book-ended by prayer.** Both commentaries notice the same structural fact, and both draw meaning from it. Ibn Kathir observes that Allah *begins* and *ends* this list of praiseworthy qualities with Ṣalāh, which is indicative of its virtue — quoting the Prophet ﷺ: "Adhere to righteousness, you will never be able encompass it all. Know that the best of your deeds is Salah. None will preserve his Wuddu' except the believer." (Again, no collection is named for this at this point in the tafsir. "Wuḍūʼ" is the ritual washing performed before prayer.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same observation and adds a conclusion: a careful study of these seven attributes would show that they encompass all the duties which man owes to Allah and to fellow men, and all the laws governing those duties; a person who possesses these attributes and adheres to them is a complete muʼmin (believer), deserving of *falāḥ* in this world and in the Hereafter. And because the list begins and ends with a reference to prayers, this suggests that **if prayers are offered in the prescribed manner with all their requirements, the other attributes will appear automatically.** Prayer is not simply one item among seven; the commentary presents it as the thing from which the other six follow.

## Ayat 10–11: heirs, not merely entrants

**"These are indeed the heirs. Who shall inherit Firdaws. They shall dwell therein forever."** Ibn Kathir introduces these two ayat by saying that having described them with these praiseworthy characteristics and righteous deeds, Allah then says this — the reward is attached directly to the character just described.

**Why the language of inheritance?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān finds a suggestion in the very word: just as the assets of a deceased person must devolve on his heirs, similarly the possessors of these attributes will, without doubt, enter Paradise. Inheritance is not a favour granted at someone's discretion on the day; it is a transfer that the law itself guarantees. That is the confidence the word is carrying.

Ibn Kathir gathers several strands on what exactly is inherited.

- **Each person's two homes.** Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Abu Hurayrah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"There is not one among you who does not have two homes, a home in Paradise and a home in Hell. If he dies and enters Hell, the people of Paradise will inherit his home"** — and this, the narration says, is what Allah said in *These are indeed the heirs.*
- **Mujāhid's explanation.** Ibn Jurayj narrated from Layth from Mujāhid that the believers will inherit the homes of the disbelievers, because they were created to worship Allah alone with no partner or associate. So when these believers did what was enjoined on them of worship, and the disbelievers neglected to do that which they were commanded to do and for which they had been created, the believers gained the share that they would have been given if they had obeyed their Lord — "Indeed, they will be given more than that as well."
- Ibn Kathir supports this with what was reported in **Sahih Muslim** from Abu Burdah, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Some of the Muslims will come on the Day of Resurrection with sins like mountains, but Allah will forgive them and put (their burden of sin) on the Jews and Christians." According to another version, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will appoint for every Muslim a Jew or Christian, and it will be said, 'This is your ransom from the Fire.'" Ibn Kathir records that ʿUmar bin ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz asked Abu Burdah to swear by Allah, three times, that his father had told him that from the Prophet ﷺ, and he swore that oath — a small window into how carefully this report was handled.

Ibn Kathir then places the ayah alongside two others that use the same verb: "Such is the Paradise which We shall give as an inheritance to those of Our servants who have had Taqwa" (19:63), and "This is the Paradise which you have been made to inherit because of your deeds which you used to do" (43:72). Inheritance in the Qurʼān's usage is not a windfall detached from conduct — the second ayah ties it explicitly to deeds.

**Firdaws — ask for the top.** Ayah 11 names the specific place. Ibn Kathir records from the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"If you ask Allah for Paradise, then ask him for Al-Firdaws, for it is the highest part of Paradise, in the middle of Paradise, and from it spring the rivers of Paradise, and above it is the (Mighty) Throne of the Most Merciful."** What the hadith gives the reader is a practical instruction: when you make duʿāʼ, do not ask small. The sūrah has just set a demanding standard of character; the Sunnah answers by telling you to aim your request at the summit.

**"They shall dwell therein forever."** The passage ends on permanence — *khālidūn*. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the circle here in a way worth carrying away. The possessors of these seven qualities were mentioned at the beginning of the sūrah as those who attain *falāḥ*, success; then, after describing those qualities, this last sentence says that they will inherit Paradise. This, it concludes, indicates that **the total falāḥ (success) may be achieved in Paradise only.** Whatever a believer receives of falāḥ here is real but partial; the complete version is the inheritance, and it is not handed over in this life.

## Living it

The two attributes in ayat 8 and 9 are strikingly ordinary, and that is the point of placing them where they are — between guarding one's chastity and inheriting the highest Paradise.

- **Return what was left with you, on demand.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names this as the most well-known form of the human trust.
- **Keep confidences.** Something received in confidence is, in the language of this ayah, an *amānah*; revealing it without the permission of the person who gave it is named a breach of trust — not gossip, a breach of trust.
- **Honour work agreements from both sides** — the work and the hours from the employee, the wages from the employer. The commentary puts a violation by either party under the same word.
- **Treat a promise as a debt.** No court will make you keep it, which is exactly why keeping it is the measure of faith rather than of law. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān allows only a religious ground as an excuse.
- **Pray at the time, not merely at some point.** Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 9 is about persistently offering the prayers at their appointed times; Qatādah's addition is about the proper bowing and prostration. And by the Ibn Masʿūd narration, this is the deed most beloved to Allah.
- **Ask for Firdaws by name.**

Read as one unit, ayat 8 to 11 make a single claim: the person who can be trusted with other people's property, words and secrets, and who keeps an appointment with Allah five times a day, is the person whose name is already on the deed to the highest part of Paradise.

passages.title: From clay to the womb to resurrection
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat trace one unbroken arc: a handful of earth, a drop placed in the womb, the hidden stages of the unborn child, the soul breathed in — then death, then rising again on the Day of Judgment. Nothing in the sequence is left to itself; every step is "We". And that is the argument holding the passage together: the same power that carried you through all of that is the power that raises you again.

## Why this comes here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places the passage against what has just been said. The surah has been describing how a person achieves *falāḥ* — success in this world and in the Hereafter — by spending his time in assiduous worship of Allah, by keeping his body and soul pure at all times, and by discharging the claims and duties he owes to fellow human beings. Now the verses give an account of the universal and supreme power of Allah, shown in the process leading to the creation of the human race. The point is not information but decision: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that a person whom Allah has given wisdom and intelligence, if he ponders these verses seriously, must necessarily choose the path that leads him to *falāḥ* in this world and the next. The evidence being placed before the reader is his own body.

## Ayah 12 — "an extract of clay"

Two words carry the ayah. **سُلَالَة (sulālah)** means an *extract* — something drawn out of a larger mass. **طِين (ṭīn)** is wet earth, clay. So the verse means that man was created from some special elements extracted from earth (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). Not from earth crudely, but from earth selected.

Who is the "man" of this ayah? Ibn Kathir holds that this is Adam, peace be upon him, whom Allah created from sounding clay of altered black smooth mud. He cites Ibn Jarir — "Adam was called Ṭīn because he was created from it" — and Qatadah — "Adam was created from Ṭīn." Ibn Kathir judges this the more apparent meaning and the one closer to the context: Adam was created from a sticky ṭīn, which is a sounding clay of altered black smooth mud, and that in turn is created from dust, as Allah says: "And among His signs is this that He created you from dust, and then — behold you are human beings scattered!" (30:20).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same as the explanation of the majority of commentators: the creation of mankind began with Sayyidnā Ādam, peace be upon him, who was himself created from this essence of earth, and it continued further with the seed, which is a refined element of that same earth. It also mentions a second view — that "an extract of clay" may mean the human seed itself, because the seed is produced from the food a man takes, and that food grows out of the earth. On either reading the conclusion is the same: you are earth, refined.

**Where our differences come from.** Ibn Kathir cites here a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Abu Musa, in which the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah created Adam from a handful which He picked up from throughout the earth, so the sons of Adam came forth accordingly — red and white and black and in between, evil and good and in between. Abu Dawud and At-Tirmidhi recorded something similar; At-Tirmidhi said, "It is Sahih Hasan." Human variety, of colour and of character, is traced back to the variety of the earth itself. There is no lineage in it for anyone to boast of.

## Ayah 13 — a weak drop in a secure lodging

Ibn Kathir notes that in "then We made him a nuṭfah," the pronoun refers back to humankind — the species — rather than to Adam. Adam came from clay; his descendants come by a different route. He supports this with 32:7–8: "and He began the creation of man from clay. Then He made his offspring from semen of despised water" — meaning, Ibn Kathir explains, *weak*.

Now hold the two halves of ayah 13 together, because the contrast is the whole force of it. The material is weak and lowly; the place is secure. Ibn Kathir reads it through 77:20–21: "Did We not create you from a despised water? Then We placed it in a place of safety" — and he explains that this place of safety is the womb, "which is prepared and readily equipped for that." Then 77:22–23: "For a known period. So We did measure; and We are the Best to measure" — meaning, for a known period of time, until it is established and moves from one stage to the next. Before you existed as anything a person could see, shelter had already been arranged for you, and a term measured out.

## Ayah 14 — the stages, told from the inside

Ibn Kathir walks through the ayah phrase by phrase.

**The nuṭfah** is the water gushing forth that comes from the loins of the man — that is, his back — and the ribs of the woman, that is, the bones of her chest between the clavicle and the breast.

**ʿAlaqah** — then it becomes a red clot, like an elongated clot. ʿIkrimah said, "This is blood."

**Muḍghah** — "which is like a piece of flesh with no shape or features." Nothing recognisable yet, nothing you could call a person to look at.

**Bones** — and here everything changes: "We gave it shape, with a head, two arms and two legs, with its bones, nerves and veins." The shapeless lump is given an architecture.

**Clothing the bones with flesh** — Ibn Kathir: "We gave it something to cover it and strengthen it." Flesh is described not as bulk but as a covering over the frame — covering and strengthening at once.

Read the whole ayah again and notice what is missing: at no point does the embryo do anything. It does not develop, does not progress, does not become. Every verb belongs to Allah: We made, We made, We gave shape, We clothed.

## The particle that tells the time

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something a translation cannot easily show. The seven stages are not all described in the same manner. In describing the change of the human foetus from one stage to the next, the word **ثُمَّ (thumma)**, "afterwards," is used in some places, which suggests some delay in the process; in other places the particle **فَ (fa)** is prefixed, which indicates uninterrupted succession. Some of the changes take a long time; others occur in relatively shorter periods.

Map it onto the passage and the pattern is exact:

- *thumma* from the extract of clay to the sperm-drop — because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, the production of food from the earth and the body's absorption of the special element which changes into the seed is a long drawn-out process;
- *thumma* again for the next transformation — a change that takes a long time to materialise;
- then **fa … fa … fa** — clot to lump, lump to bones, bones clothed with flesh — three changes occurring in short periods, run together without a pause;
- then *thumma* once more for the final stage, because by human reckoning putting life and soul into a lifeless mass must necessarily take a long time.

The rhythm of the sentence follows the rhythm of the pregnancy. That is what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān has in view when it calls this the supreme beauty and eloquence of the Qur'anic language.

## Seven stages — and a boy's answer to ʿUmar

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts seven stages of the creation of man in this verse: (1) an extract of clay, (2) the sperm-drop, (3) the clot, (4) the foetus-lump, (5) bones, (6) the clothing of bones with flesh, and (7) the completion of the process by the blowing of the spirit into the child.

It then relates a story which Qurtubi records in his commentary, and which is reproduced at length in the Musnad of Ibn Abi Shaibah. Sayyidnā ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, sitting in the company of some eminent Companions, asked them on what date of Ramadan the Night of Majesty (Laylat al-Qadr) would fall. None of them was able to mention a specific date; they all said that only Allah knew the answer. He then turned to Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās, the youngest among them, who said: "O Amir ul-Mu'minin! Allah created seven skies and seven earths. He created man in seven stages and provided him sustenance from seven sources. Therefore in my opinion the Night of Majesty will surely fall on the twenty-seventh night of the month of Ramadan." Hearing this reasoning, ʿUmar said to the others, "See, this lad has given an answer which none of you could give."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that when Ibn ʿAbbās mentioned the seven stages of man's creation, he was obviously alluding to this very verse; and that the seven sources of sustenance refer to the verse in Surah ʿAbasa (80:27–31), which mentions eight items, of which the first seven are food for human beings and the eighth provides fodder for animals.

## "Then We brought it forth as another creation"

This is the hinge of ayah 14. Ibn Kathir explains: "then We breathed the soul into it, and it moved and became a new creature, one that could hear, see, understand and move." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the Qur'an calls it *khalqan ākhar*, "another creation": the first six stages in the creation of man are related to the world of elements and substances, whereas this final stage relates to the transfer of soul from the world of spirits into the body, and is therefore described as a special or distinct creation.

Al-ʿAwfi reported a further meaning from Ibn ʿAbbas, that "another creation" also covers the changing that does not stop: "We change it from one stage to another until it emerges as an infant, then it grows up through the stages of being a child, adolescent, youth, mature man, old man and senile man." On this reading the ayah does not close at birth. The same hand that moved you from drop to clot is moving you still, through every age you will pass through.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir cites here the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud, recorded by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad and recorded by Al-Bukhari and Muslim, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — the Truthful One — told them that the creation of any one of us is gathered for forty days in his mother's stomach as a nuṭfah, then he becomes a clot for a similar period of time, then a little lump of flesh for a similar length of time. Then the angel is sent to him and breathes the soul into it, and four things are decreed: his provision, his life-span, his deeds, and whether he will be wretched or blessed.

The Prophet ﷺ then swore an oath — by the One besides Whom there is no other god — that one of you may do the deeds of the people of Paradise until there is no more than a forearm's length between him and it, then the decree will overtake him and he will do the deeds of the people of Hell and thus enter Hell; and a man may do the deeds of the people of Hell until there is no more than a forearm's length between him and it, then the decree will overtake him and he will finally do the deeds of the people of Paradise and thus enter Paradise.

Two things are set down together here. Your provision and your life-span were decreed while you were still being formed. And no one — however far along — may feel secure about his ending, or write anyone else off as beyond hope.

## Biological spirit and Real Spirit

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that "We developed it into another creature" was interpreted by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Shaʿbī, ʿIkrimah, Ḍaḥḥāk and Abul-ʿĀliyah, may Allah be pleased with them, to mean the blowing of the spirit into the body. It then reports from Tafsir Mazhari that this most probably refers to the *biological spirit*. On that explanation, spirits are of two kinds. The biological spirit is a subtle substance embedded in every part of the body of a human being or an animal — the spirit recognised by medical scientists and philosophers — and it is created after the organs are created. That, Tafsir Mazhari says, is why its creation is mentioned in this verse with the word *thumma*, "thereafter."

The other kind is the *Real Spirit*, which belongs to the spiritual universe. It was created long before the creation of human beings, and these are the spirits which Allah assembled when He asked them, "Am I not your Lord?" and they answered, "Why not?" This Real Spirit, having been created long before, is connected by Allah with the biological spirit in a manner not known to anyone. The life of a man depends on this connection, and when the biological spirit of a person is disconnected from the Real Spirit, he dies. Tafsir Mazhari therefore says it is also possible that it is this connection which the verse refers to by the words "another creation."

What the authorities named above state plainly is the sense the passage turns on: at this stage the spirit is breathed into the body, and what was flesh becomes, in Ibn Kathir's words, "a new creature, one that could hear, see, understand and move."

## "So Blessed is Allah, the Best of creators"

Ibn Kathir places this exclamation exactly where it belongs: when Allah mentions His ability and His subtlety in creating this nuṭfah and taking it from stage to stage until it takes the shape of a perfectly formed human being, He says, *fa-tabāraka'llāhu aḥsanu'l-khāliqīn*.

Why the plural, "creators", when creating belongs to Allah alone? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers with a point of language. *Khalq* and *takhlīq* mean "to create something from nothing", which is a very special and exclusive attribute of Allah: Allah alone is the Creator and none else, and neither an angel nor a man can create anything. But sometimes these two words are used in the sense of *manufacturing*, which is no more than the reshaping and assembly by man of substances created by Allah — and the man who does this is also called the creator of the article he makes. The Qur'an uses the verb in this borrowed way: "you invent a lie" (29:17), and of Sayyidnā ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, "I create for you from clay something in the shape of a bird" (3:49) — metaphorical in both places. So the plural takes in everyone who may be called a maker in that metaphorical sense, and declares Allah the best among all of them. Every human maker begins with material he did not make.

## Ayat 15 and 16 — death, then rising

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān marks the turn: the preceding three verses were about the creation of man, while this verse and the one which follows are about the life to come. After his creation, man will spend a period of time in this world and then meet his death, from which there is no escape. Ibn Kathir puts it in one line: "after first being created from nothing, you will eventually die."

Then ayah 16 — "then on the Day of Judgment you will be resurrected" — which Ibn Kathir explains simply as: you will be created anew. He connects it with "and then Allah will bring forth the creation of the Hereafter" (29:20), meaning the Day of Return, when the souls will be restored to their bodies and all of creation will be brought to account; everyone will be rewarded or punished according to his deeds — if they are good he will be rewarded, and if they are bad he will be punished. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: man is raised again so that his deeds and actions in this world may be weighed, and he may be sent to Paradise or Hell as he deserves.

Notice that ayat 15 and 16 both open with *thumma*. Between the clay and the grave there is an interval; between the grave and the rising there is another. The passage compresses an entire human existence into five ayat — and the One who took you from stage to stage until you were a perfectly formed human being is the One who says, in the same breath, that He will create you anew.

## Living it

**The proof is your own body.** These ayat point at the reader. Whoever moved you from a shapeless lump to a hearing, seeing, understanding creature can create you anew after death.

**Nobody's origin is grander than anyone else's.** A handful taken from throughout the earth produced red and white and black and everything in between. Racial pride has no ground to stand on in the light of that hadith.

**You were cared for before you could ask.** The *qarār makīn* of ayah 13 — the womb, "prepared and readily equipped for that" — was arranged for you when you were a weak drop, for a period already measured out.

**Fear your ending and hope in it.** The hadith of Ibn Masʿud closes off both arrogance and despair.

**Live toward the scales.** The passage opens where the surah opened — with those who worship and keep themselves pure — and ends at the weighing of deeds. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that from here the surah goes on to mention briefly the events of the period between this life and the life to come, and the gifts and blessings Allah will bestow — prefaced by a reference to the creation of the skies. The same power, on a larger canvas.

passages.title: Signs in the heavens, rain, crops and cattle
passages.tafsir:
This passage turns the reader's eyes outward. Ibn Kathir observes that after mentioning the creation of man, Allah goes on to mention the creation of the seven heavens — and here He shows the enormous world prepared to receive that human being: seven levels overhead, rain measured out with exact care, gardens and olive groves, and animals that feed, clothe and carry us. What holds ayat 17–22 together is one unbroken chain of provision — sky, then water, then soil, then crops, then cattle, then travel — every link of it evidence that the Creator who made you did not then forget you.

## Where this comes in the surah

Ibn Kathir notes that Allah often places the creation of the heavens and earth alongside the creation of man. Elsewhere He says, **"The creation of the heavens and the earth is indeed greater than the creation of mankind"** (40:57). Ibn Kathir points to the same pattern at the opening of Sūrat as-Sajdah — which, he says, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite on Friday mornings — where the creation of the heavens and earth is mentioned, then how man was created from a fluid drop from clay, and where the resurrection, reward and punishment are also discussed. The pattern is worth noticing: the Lord who built all of that, and who watches over it, is the same Lord who will raise the dead and settle every account.

## Ayah 17: "seven levels above you"

The word is **ṭarāʾiq** (طرائق), the plural of **ṭarīqah**. Mujahid said it means the seven heavens, and Ibn Kathir lines the ayah up with several parallels: "The seven heavens and the earth and all that is therein, glorify Him" (17:44); "See you not how Allah has created the seven heavens one above another?" (71:15); and "It is Allah Who has created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof. His command descends between them, that you may know that Allah has power over all things, and that Allah surrounds all things in knowledge" (65:12).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up further. **Ṭarīqah** can be used as a synonym for **ṭabaqah** — a tier, a layer — in which case the ayah means Allah created seven skies overhead, ranged row upon row in tiers. But the more common meaning of *ṭarīqah* is a road or a passage; on that reading the ayah means these skies provide a path for the angels who bring Allah's commands down to the earth. Both meanings serve the passage: a structure of astonishing scale, and a structure that is not inert — Allah's commands are travelling through it, and what they govern is your world.

## "And We were never unaware of the creation"

This closing clause of ayah 17 is the hinge of the whole passage. Ibn Kathir explains it as the sweep of Allah's knowledge: He knows what goes into the earth and what comes out of it, what comes down from heaven and what goes up into it; He is with you wherever you are, and Allah sees what you do. **No heaven is hidden from Him by another and no earth is hidden from Him by another.** There is no mountain whose features He does not know, and no sea but He knows what is in its depths; He knows the numbers of what is in the mountains, the hills, the sands, the seas, the landscapes and the trees — as He says, "And not a leaf falls, but He knows it. There is not a grain in the darkness of the earth nor anything fresh or dry, but is written in a Clear Record" (6:59).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the practical edge of the same words: Allah did not simply abandon man after creating him, but was ever mindful of his needs and provided the means for his sustenance and growth. To this end He first created the skies, and from the skies He sent rains down upon the earth, which then produced food for man's nourishment. That single sentence is the outline of everything that follows in ayat 18–22. Divine knowledge here is not a cold fact about Allah; it is the reason there is water in your tap and food on your plate.

## Ayah 18: water sent down "in due measure"

**"We sent down water from the sky bi-qadar"** — in due measure. Ibn Kathir explains: according to what is needed, not so much that it damages the lands and buildings, and not so little as to be insufficient for crops and fruits, but whatever is needed for irrigation, drinking and other benefits.

He then gives a striking illustration of how finely calibrated this is. If there is a land that needs a great deal of water for irrigation, but whose fertile soil would be carried away if rain fell on it, Allah sends water to it from another land — as in the case of Egypt, which is said to be a barren land, most of it sand. Allah sends it the water of the Nile, which brings red soil from Ethiopia when it rains there; the water irrigates the land, and whatever soil is deposited is used for agriculture. Ibn Kathir's response to this is not analysis but praise: *Glory be to the Subtle One, the All-Knowing, the Most Merciful, the Forgiving.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads **bi-qadar** as a standing exposure of how feeble and utterly powerless man really is: the very things without which no life can exist become the cause of death and destruction the moment they exceed a certain limit. Water is the case in point — no living thing, man or beast, can survive without it, yet torrential rains coming down from the sky cause a deluge that becomes a source of misery. But Allah is kind and merciful, and He sends rains which meet man's needs without turning into flood, except at those places where it is His will that they should be engulfed in water.

The same commentary presses the point with a thought experiment. Suppose man had to obtain his daily requirement of water through daily rainfall — that too would cause extreme discomfort and suffering, since we are not by nature adapted to live in an environment where rain falls every day, and the conduct of business would become impossible. Suppose instead that a whole year's water, or six months', or even three months', came down in a single downpour and people were told to store their quota: that would be an impossible task, both for lack of adequate storage capacity and because the water would become foul and unfit for consumption.

## "Then We lodged it in the earth"

So Allah regulated the supply another way, and the Qur'an compresses the whole design into one short phrase: **fa-askannāhu fi'l-arḍ** — "then We lodged it in the earth." Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: when the water comes down from the clouds, He causes it to settle in the earth, and causes the earth to absorb it and the seeds in the earth to be nourished by it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks what that lodging involves. The rain saturates the earth and the plants, then flows into lakes, ponds and natural depressions where men and animals use it according to their needs — but water stored that way lasts only a limited time, and people in different regions need a continuous supply of fresh water. So Allah designed a system by which very large quantities of water are converted into oceans of ice and snow and placed on top of mountains, where the atmosphere is pure and free from pollution. Slowly and gradually the snow melts; the water seeps through the pores in the mountains into a network of underground channels, which carry it to all parts as springs and flow on the surface as streams, watercourses and rivers — drinking water for men and animals, and irrigation for the fields that yield food and fodder for all living things. Another part of the water percolates deep into the ground, becomes sub-soil water, and is drawn up from wells.

Read the phrase again with that in view. *We lodged it in the earth* — one verb, and beneath it an entire order of water.

## "And We are surely able to take it away"

Ibn Kathir turns the closing clause of ayah 18 into a list of everything Allah could have done and did not: if He wanted to cause it not to rain, He could do so; if He wanted to divert it towards the wilderness and wastelands, He could do so; if He wanted to make it salty so that you could not benefit from it for drinking or irrigation, He could do so; if He wanted to cause it not to be absorbed by the earth but to remain on the surface, He could do so; if He wanted to make it go deep underground where you would never reach it or benefit from it, He could do so.

**But by His grace and mercy** He causes sweet, fresh water to fall on you from the clouds, then it settles in the earth and forms springs and rivers, and you use it to irrigate your crops and fruits, and you drink it and give it to your livestock and cattle, and you bathe and purify yourselves with it. "To Him is due the praise and thanks," says Ibn Kathir — the only sane conclusion.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān finds one more mercy hidden in the same clause: the sub-soil water drawn from wells has been placed by merciful Allah at a depth from which it can be drawn easily, because by its nature water flows downwards and could have gone down to a depth from which it would have been impossible to draw it out. That it did not is not luck; it is restraint on the part of the One who is able to take it away.

## Ayah 19: gardens of date palms and grapes

"Then We brought forth for you therewith gardens of date palms and grapes." Ibn Kathir: from that which We send down from the sky, We bring forth for you gardens and orchards *which look beautiful* — the beauty is part of the blessing, not incidental to it.

Why dates and grapes in particular? Because these were the kinds of gardens that were known to the people of the Ḥijāz. Ibn Kathir makes an important point here: there is no difference between a thing and its counterpart. The people of each region have fruits which are the blessing of Allah given to them, and for which they cannot properly thank Allah enough. The specific fruits named are a sample, not a limit; whatever grows in your own region falls under the same blessing.

"Wherein is much fruit for you" means fruit of all kinds, as Allah says elsewhere: "With it He causes to grow for you the crops, the olives, the date palms, the grapes, and every kind of fruit" (16:11).

And "and whereof you eat" — Ibn Kathir draws out something quietly beautiful in the sequence: this implies that you look at its beauty, wait for it to ripen, then eat from it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes in the same phrase that people eat these fruits for their taste and flavour and also preserve some of them for future use as articles of food.

## Ayah 20: the tree of Ṭūr Saynāʾ

"And a tree that springs forth from Ṭūr Sinai." This, Ibn Kathir says, means the olive tree. **Ṭūr** means a mountain — and some of the scholars said it is called *ṭūr* if there are trees on it, and if it is bare it is called *jabal*, not *ṭūr*. Ibn Kathir adds, "and Allah knows best." Mount Sinai is the same as Ṭūr Sinīn: the mountain on which Allah spoke to Mūsā ibn ʿImrān, peace be upon him, and in the surrounding mountains there are olive trees. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Sinai is the name of the area where the mountain of Ṭūr is located, and that since Mount Sinai produces an abundant crop of olives, a reference has been made to it here. It also relates from Mazhari that the olive is associated with the Ṭūr mountain because this tree first grew on that mountain — and that some have said it was the first tree to grow on earth after the great Deluge in the days of Sayyidnā Nūḥ, peace be upon him.

So one tree carries a memory: the place where Allah spoke to a prophet, and the olives growing in the mountains around it for anyone's table.

**"That grows oil."** The Arabic is *tanbutu bi'd-duhn*, and Ibn Kathir reports two views among the scholars of language: some think it means the tree *brings forth* oil, others that it *comes forth with* oil. Either way the point stands — the fruit arrives already carrying its own oil.

**"And a relish"** — *ṣibgh*, which Ibn Kathir reports, according to Qatadah, means a condiment. "For the eaters" means, as Ibn Kathir puts it, that it contains a beneficial oil and condiment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists the uses: olive oil can be used to massage the body, in lamps to provide light, and in food as a curry or dressing — several needs met by one fruit.

**From the Sunnah:** ʿAbd bin Humayd recorded in his *Musnad* and *Tafsir* from ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Eat olive oil as a condiment and apply it as oil, for it comes from a blessed tree."* Ibn Kathir notes that it was also recorded by At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah.

## Ayat 21–22: the cattle are a lesson

"And verily, in the cattle there is indeed a lesson for you." The word rendered "lesson" is **ʿibrah**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the whole run of blessings this way: Allah mentions the gifts He has provided for the benefit of mankind *so that they may ponder and worship Him*. The animal is placed in front of you as something to think from.

And the ayah tells you where to look for the lesson. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the lesson referred to is described further in the very next words: **"We give you a drink from that which lies in their bellies."** Ibn Kathir's comment on this is arresting — they drink their milk, which comes out from between dung and blood. That is the *ʿibrah*.

Then the benefits are stacked up. Ibn Kathir: they eat their meat and clothe themselves with their wool and hair, they ride on their backs and carry heavy burdens on them to far away lands — as Allah says, "And they carry your loads to a land that you could not reach except with great trouble to yourselves. Truly, your Lord is full of kindness, Most Merciful" (16:7). And he cites the passage that ends with exactly the question this whole section is driving at: "Do they not see that We have created for them of what Our Hands have created, the cattle, so that they are their owners. And We have subdued them unto them so that some of them they have for riding and some they eat. And in them there are benefits for them, and drink. **Will they not then be grateful?**" (36:71–73).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān expands the same list in everyday terms: they provide milk, which is a very clear and nourishing food; every part of their body is put to some use — wool, hides, intestines and the rest — utilised in industries which support a country's economy; and the meat of the ḥalāl animals is a favourite food for people everywhere. And finally they are used, together with ships, as mounts and as a means of transporting goods from one place to another.

Ayah 22 closes the arc: **"And on them, and on ships, you are carried."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that ships and boats are included in this last benefit because they too are used in transportation — and adds that all types of mounts which run on wheels may also be added to *fulk* (boats), because they render the same service. Living animals, ships, and by that reasoning the wheeled transport of our own day, all fall under one heading in the ayah: things that carry you, which you did not make carriable.

## Living it

The passage never argues abstractly. It hands you a set of ordinary things — the sky over your head, the rain, the well, the fruit bowl, the bottle of olive oil, the animal and the vehicle — and asks you to see each one as a deliberate act of a Lord who was "never unaware."

Three things follow directly from what the commentators say. **First, gratitude as a habit of attention.** Ibn Kathir's response to the Nile and to the sweet rain is *to Him is due the praise and thanks*; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading of the cattle is that these gifts are given so that people *may ponder and worship Him*. The blessing is already in your hand; what is asked is that you notice whose hand it came from. **Second, humility.** *Bi-qadar*, on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, is a reminder of how powerless man is — the very things life depends on turn destructive the moment they pass their limit, so you live inside a margin that Someone else maintains. **Third, hope in that same power.** The Lord who is able to take the water away and does not, who could have sunk it beyond reach and did not, is the Lord you are asking for provision now.

And Ibn Kathir's note about dates and grapes leaves a gentle closing thought: the people of each region have fruits which are the blessing of Allah given to them, *and for which they cannot properly thank Allah enough*. The right response is not to settle the debt but to keep acknowledging it.

passages.title: Noah, his people's mockery, and the Ark
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat tell one complete story: a Messenger is sent, he is mocked and dismissed, he turns to his Lord, and Allah answers by commanding a ship that will carry the believers over the ruin of the deniers. What holds them together is a single movement — **from a rejected call, to a prayer, to a rescue** — and the closing line in ayah 30 tells us why it is being retold: it is a sign, and a pattern, because Allah is always testing.

Notice, too, where the passage sits. Just before it, in ayah 22, Allah reminded people of a favour: *"And on them and on the boats you are transported."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the *fulk* — boats and ships — belong to that list of Allah's provisions for travel, and that by the same logic every wheeled mount people ride today can be added to it, since they render the same service. Then the surah moves straight to a ship of another order altogether: the one Allah Himself commanded, to save His servants. The everyday gift of a boat and the once-in-history gift of the Ark are the same mercy at different scales.

## Ayah 23 — the whole message in one sentence

Ibn Kathir opens simply: Allah sent Nūḥ, peace be upon him, to his people "to warn them of the severe punishment of Allah and His severe vengeance on those who associated partners with Him, defied His commands and disbelieved His Messengers."

And Nūḥ's message is four short clauses: *Worship Allah — you have no other god but Him — will you not then have taqwā?* Ibn Kathir glosses that last question: **"Do you not fear Allah when you associate others in worship with Him?"** *Taqwā* is that protective mindfulness, the awareness of Allah that makes a person guard himself from what displeases Him.

Two things are worth pausing on. First, that this is the message of worship of Allah alone, nothing beside Him. Second, the form of address: **"O my people"** (*yā qawmi*). He does not open by calling them strangers or enemies. He calls them his own.

## Ayat 24–25 — three ways to dismiss a prophet

The reply does not come from the people at large. It comes from **al-malaʼ** — what Ibn Kathir calls "the chiefs or leaders of his people." These are the men with standing, and the Qur'an is careful to name them. And note who they are speaking to: the ayah has them addressing the masses. The dismissal is managed from the top down.

Their argument has three moves.

**1. "He is no more than a human being like you."** Ibn Kathir explains their reasoning: *he is a human being like you, so how can he receive revelation when you do not?* The very thing that makes a Messenger reachable — that he is one of us — is turned into the objection against him.

**2. "He seeks to make himself superior to you."** They read his mission as ambition. Ibn Kathir: "he is putting himself above you and trying to make himself great by claiming to be a Prophet." Sincerity is recast as a bid for status, so that nobody has to weigh what he actually said.

**3. "Had Allah willed, He surely could have sent down angels."** Ibn Kathir renders their meaning: *if Allah had wanted to send a Prophet, He would have sent an angel from Him, not a human being.* They have decided in advance what Allah's method must be, and then rejected the reality for failing to match their theory. And they buttress it with custom: **"Never did we hear such a thing among our fathers of old"** — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, that no man was ever sent to "our forefathers, their predecessors in times past." Inherited habit is offered as if it were evidence.

Then, in ayah 25, the sneer sharpens: **"He is only a man in whom is *jinnah*"** — madness. Ibn Kathir spells out the accusation precisely: "he is crazy in his claim that Allah has sent him and chosen him from among you to receive revelation." Note what they are calling insane. Not his morals, not his conduct — only his claim that Allah has sent him. The charge does the work of an argument without being one.

And their strategy? **"So wait for him a while."** Ibn Kathir: "wait until he dies, put up with him until you are rid of him." They are not going to refute him; they are going to outlast him. They plan to let time do their work, treating a man's death as the solution to a message they cannot answer.

There is quiet instruction here for every believer who meets the same reception — *he's just a man, he wants status, he's mad, ignore him till he goes away.* The objections are recorded in the Qur'an, and so is how the story ended.

## Ayah 26 — the prayer of a man who has run out of people

**"My Lord! Help me, because they have denied me."** *Rabbi anṣurnī bimā kadhdhabūn.*

He does not curse them in this wording; he lays the fact before his Lord. Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: Nūḥ "invoked his Lord to help him against his people." The reason given is not his own hurt but their *takdhīb* — their calling the message a lie. What was rejected was Allah's word, and so it is Allah he asks to vindicate it.

Ibn Kathir sets this alongside another verse where the same moment is recorded: **"Then he invoked his Lord (saying): 'I have been overcome, so help me!'"** (54:10). *I have been overcome* — a Prophet is permitted to say plainly that he has been overmatched. That is not weakness in faith; it is the honesty that faith makes possible.

Read ayat 25 and 26 together and you see two ways of waiting. They said, *wait for him a while* — waiting on time. He said, *my Lord, help me* — waiting on Allah. Only one of those waits was answered.

## Ayah 27 — the command: build

Ibn Kathir marks the turn exactly: **"At that point, Allah commanded him to build a boat."** The prayer is answered with an instruction and a job of work. Rescue, in this passage, is something Nūḥ has to build.

**"Under Our Eyes and under Our revelation."** What this gives Nūḥ is unmistakable: he is not working unseen and not working unaided. Allah is watching over the building, and *wa-waḥyinā* — "and under Our revelation" — means the instruction itself comes from Allah. Ibn Kathir notes the substance of it: to build the boat "strong and firm." Nūḥ supplies the hands; the command and the watchful care are Allah's.

**"When Our command comes, and the oven gushes forth."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *tannūr*: the word means the oven used for making flat, round bread, and it is also used in the sense of the whole earth. On its location the scholars differed — some said it was a particular oven in the Kufah mosque, others that it was somewhere in Syria. What matters is reported by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from Mazharī: Allah informed Nūḥ that **when water began boiling forth from the oven, that would be the sign that the Deluge had come.** The signal for a world-ending flood is water rising in an ordinary bread oven. Nothing in creation is too small for Allah to make it a sign.

**"Take on board of each kind two."** Ibn Kathir: "a male and a female of every species of animals, plants and fruits etc." The Ark is not only a lifeboat; it carries the seed of a world to come.

**"And your family, except those thereof against whom the Word has already gone forth."** Ibn Kathir explains: "those whom Allah had already decreed were to be destroyed. These were the members of his family who did not believe in him, such as his son and his wife. And Allah knows best." The exception is stated before the flood, so that Nūḥ would know, in advance, that blood is not a boarding pass. Faith is.

**"And address Me not in favour of those who have done wrong. Verily, they are to be drowned."** Ibn Kathir opens this up with great tenderness toward Nūḥ: it means, *when you witness the heavy rain falling, do not let yourself be overcome with compassion and pity for your people, or hope for more time for them so that they may believe, for I have decreed that they will be drowned and will die in their state of disbelief and wrongdoing.*

Read that again. Allah is pre-empting the mercy of the man they called mad. The danger Allah guards against is that Nūḥ will start pleading for them when he sees the water — for the very people who dismissed him. That is who Allah's Messengers are. And the reason the door is closed is stated: the decree has issued, and they will die in that state of disbelief and wrongdoing.

(Ibn Kathir adds that "the story has already been told in detail in Sūrah Hūd, and there is no need to repeat it here" — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise refers the reader back to the fuller account in earlier surahs. Sūrat al-Muʼminūn is not retelling the flood; it is drawing out its lesson.)

## Ayat 28–29 — two prayers, one at each end of the journey

Now come the words Allah puts on Nūḥ's tongue — not left to his choice, but taught.

**On boarding (ayah 28):** *"All praise be to Allah, Who has saved us from the people who are wrongdoers."* Ibn Kathir places this beside the traveller's remembrance in 43:12–14 — that Allah "appointed for you ships and cattle on which you ride: in order that you may mount on their backs, and then may remember the favour of your Lord when you mount thereon, and say: 'Glory to Him Who has subjected this to us, and we could never have it by our efforts. And verily, to our Lord we indeed are to return.'" The same verb of settling firmly onto a mount runs through both passages (*istawayta* here, *listawū… idhā istawaytum* there).
