The point is a habit of the heart: **the moment you are safely seated is the moment to remember who seated you.** Nūḥ's ship and your wheeled transport are on the same list.

Note also what the praise is *for* — not "who saved us from the water," but *"who has saved us from the people who are wrongdoers."* The flood was the instrument; the deliverance named is deliverance from a wrongdoing people.

**On landing (ayah 29):** *"My Lord! Cause me to land at a blessed landing place, for You are the Best of those who bring to land."* Having been saved, he does not assume the rest. He asks for the arrival itself to be *mubārak* — blessed. And he seals the request with praise of Allah: *You are the Best of those who bring to land.*

Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion out of the pair: **"So Nūḥ mentioned Allah at the beginning of his journey and at the end."** He cites the words recorded elsewhere: *"Embark therein: in the Name of Allah will be its moving course and its resting anchorage"* (11:41) — Allah's name over the sailing and Allah's name over the anchoring. And Ibn Kathir affirms that "certainly, Nūḥ adhered to what he was commanded."

That pattern is worth borrowing. Whatever you set out on — a journey, a marriage, a project, a treatment — begin it in Allah's name, and when it delivers you safely, praise Him, and ask that where you have landed be blessed.

## Ayah 30 — why we are told all this

**"Surely in this are signs — and We are ever putting people to the test."**

Ibn Kathir explains *"in this"* as this whole event: **the saving of the believers and the destruction of the disbelievers.** In it, he says, are "clear evidence and proof that the Prophets speak the truth in the Message they bring from Allah, may He be exalted, and that Allah does what He wills, and He is able to do all things and knows all things." Three certainties, then, in one story: the Messengers are truthful; Allah's will is effective; Allah's power and knowledge are complete.

And the closing clause — *wa in kunnā la-mubtalīn* — Ibn Kathir renders: **"We try Our servants by means of sending the Messengers."** This is the key that unlocks the passage. The sending of a Messenger is itself the test. The mockers of ayah 24 were not merely being rude; they were sitting an examination and did not know it.

## Living it

- **Test the message, not the messenger.** Every objection in ayat 24–25 is about Nūḥ — his species, his motives, his sanity, his novelty — and not one is about whether what he said is true. When you feel the pull to dismiss someone rather than weigh what they said, remember whose argument you are borrowing.
- **When you have exhausted people, do not exhaust hope.** Ayah 26 is a Prophet's honest *"help me."* Say it plainly.
- **Answers often arrive as assignments.** Nūḥ asked for help and was told to build. Expect the rescue to require your hands.
- **Work as one watched over.** *Under Our Eyes* is the antidote to both despair and carelessness in long, unglamorous obedience.
- **Bracket every journey with Allah.** His name over the setting out, praise on arriving, and a prayer that the place you land in be blessed.
- **Keep the tenderness even when the door closes.** Nūḥ had to be told not to plead for the very people who called him mad. Judgement belongs to Allah, and the decree in ayah 27 is His alone — mercy toward people is still ours to carry until He says otherwise.

passages.title: A later generation destroyed for denying resurrection
passages.tafsir:
## The story told again

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān sets the scene for us: in the earlier ayat, the story of Sayyidnā Nūḥ (peace be upon him) was told — a prophet sent to his people to guide them along the path of righteousness. What follows, Maʿārif says, is "a brief account of some other prophets without mentioning their names and the people for whose guidance they were sent."

That namelessness is worth noticing before anything else. Ayat 31–41 give us a messenger, a nation, an objection and an ending — and withhold the labels. What is put before us is not a piece of tribal history but a shape.

And the shape has a single fault line running through it: **the denial of resurrection**. Everything the chiefs say, and everything that happens to them, turns on that.

## Who were "another generation"?

Ayah 31 says only: *"Then We raised another generation after them."*

Ibn Kathir reports two identifications. It was said that this was **ʿĀd**, because they were the successors of the people of Nūḥ. Or it was said that they were **Thamūd**, because Allah says: *"So, the Sayhah overtook them in truth"* (ayah 41).

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān sets out the reasoning behind that second view and its consequence. From certain references and allusions, the commentators concluded that these ayat refer to Sayyidnā **Hūd** or Sayyidnā **Ṣāliḥ** (peace be upon them), sent for the guidance of the tribes of ʿĀd and Thamūd respectively. In this passage both tribes are reported to have perished as a result of the **Ṣayḥah** — the Cry — from an unseen source; but in other ayat it has been specifically mentioned that it was the tribe of Thamūd which perished from the Ṣayḥah. That, Maʿārif explains, is what led some scholars to hold that *qarnan ākharīn*, "another generation," refers to Thamūd.

Maʿārif then offers an alternative: the word **ṣayḥah** may have been used here in the general sense of *a punishment from Allah*, in which case the tribe of ʿĀd would be included too.

This is a genuine difference among the scholars, and it is worth leaving where they left it. The Qurʾān itself does not settle it — and that silence is part of the lesson.

## The message that never changes (ayah 32)

*"And We sent to them a Messenger from among themselves: Worship Allah! You have no other god but Him. Will you not then have Taqwa?"*

Two things are packed into this ayah.

**"From among themselves."** He was one of them — their own kin, their own tongue. In ayah 33 they will turn that very likeness into their main accusation against him.

**The message itself.** Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: Allah sent to them a Messenger from among themselves, and he called them to worship Allah Alone with no partner or associate. One demand, nothing else. And notice the form the ayah ends in — not a threat but a question put to them: *"Will you not then have Taqwa?"*

## The chiefs, and what they had been given (ayah 33)

The Qurʾān is precise about who leads the rejection: *al-malaʾ*, **the chiefs** of his people. Three things are said of them in a single breath:

1. they disbelieved,
2. they **denied the meeting in the Hereafter**, and
3. they were those **"whom We had given the luxuries and comforts of worldly life."**

The third clause sits deliberately beside the second. The Qurʾān names their comfortable share of this world in the same sentence in which it names their denial of the next.

## "He eats what you eat" (ayat 33–34)

Their argument is not an argument about Allah at all. It is an objection to the messenger's ordinariness: *"He is no more than a human being like you, he eats of that which you eat, and drinks of what you drink."*

Ibn Kathir's summary is exact: they belied him, opposed him and refused to follow him **because he was a human being like them**; they refused to follow a human Messenger.

Then ayah 34 pushes it further: *"If you were to obey a human being like yourselves, then verily, you indeed would be losers."* They have a theory of loss. Following a man like themselves, they say, is the losing move. Hold that word "losers" in mind until ayah 41, and see whose account actually came out empty.

## The heart of it: dust and bones (ayat 35–38)

Now the real objection surfaces, and it is the one that governs the passage.

**Ayah 35** — *"Does he promise you that when you have died and have become dust and bones, you shall come out alive?"* Ibn Kathir states precisely what they were rejecting: they did not believe in the meeting with Allah on the Day of Resurrection, and **they denied the idea of physical resurrection**. Not a vague afterlife of the spirit — the bodily raising of what has crumbled into dust and bone. That is exactly what they found ridiculous.

**Ayah 36** — *hayhāt, hayhāt li-mā tūʿadūn*. Ibn Kathir renders it: *"Far, very far is that which you are promised!"* — and glosses it in three words: **very unlikely**. That is the whole of their reply. Not a case against resurrection, but a word of dismissal, and they say it twice.

**Ayah 37** — *"There is nothing but our life of this world! We die and we live! And we are not going to be resurrected!"* Their creed, stated flat: existence is bounded by birth and death, and that is all there is.

**Ayah 38** — having ruled out the message, they rule on the man: *"He is only a man who has invented a lie against Allah, and we are not going to believe in him."* Ibn Kathir specifies what the alleged lie was: *"in the Message he has brought to you, and his warnings and promise of resurrection."* The fabrication they charge him with is precisely the Hereafter.

## Maʿārif ul Qurʾān's warning — and it is aimed at us

Commenting on ayah 37, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān makes the sharpest practical point in this passage. This, it says, is the argument the unbelievers advance when denying belief in the Day of Judgment. Those who deny it publicly are confirmed infidels. **But** — and here the commentary turns towards the Muslim reader — it is very unfortunate that many Muslims also act in a manner that the same denial can be felt from their deeds and actions. They seem to be totally oblivious of the coming in of the Hereafter. Maʿārif closes not with a rebuke but with a prayer: may Allah Taʿālā grant them faith to release themselves from the clutches of this belief of theirs.

That deserves to be sat with. The chiefs of ayah 37 said it out loud. Maʿārif's warning is that a life can say it without ever saying it.

## The messenger's prayer (ayah 39)

*"He said: O my Lord! Help me because they deny me."*

Ibn Kathir: the Messenger prayed against his people and asked his Lord to help him against them.

Look at the grounds he gives: *bimā kadhdhabūn* — **"because they deny me."** After everything in ayat 33–38 — the objection to how he eats and drinks, the charge that he is a liar — the reason he lays before his Lord is the denial of the message he was sent with.

## Allah's answer (ayah 40)

*"(Allah) said: In a little while, they are sure to be regretful."*

Ibn Kathir says simply: **His Lord answered his prayer** — and explains what the regret would be for: *"their opposition towards you and their stubborn rejection of the Message you brought to them."*

Set ayah 40 beside ayah 36 and the passage's finest stroke appears. They said *hayhāt, hayhāt* — far, very far is the thing you promise us. Allah replies: *ʿammā qalīl* — **in a little while**. What they had pushed away as remote was not remote at all.

## The end (ayah 41)

*"So, the Sayhah overtook them in truth, and We made them as rubbish of dead plants. So, away with the people who are wrongdoers."*

**The Ṣayḥah** — the Cry, which Maʿārif describes as coming from an unseen source. Ibn Kathir adds that the apparent meaning is that the Ṣayḥah was combined with the furious cold wind, and cites Allah's words: *"Destroying everything by the command of its Lord! So they became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings!"* (46:25). The dwellings remained; the people did not.

**"In truth"** — *bi'l-ḥaqq*. Ibn Kathir: they deserved that from Allah because of their disbelief and wrongdoing. The word forbids reading this as raw force. It was deserved; it was justice.

**"Rubbish of dead plants"** — *ghuthāʾ*. Ibn Kathir explains: they are dead and destroyed, like the scum and rubbish left by a flood — *something insignificant and useless that is of no benefit to anyone*. Return to ayah 33: these were the people to whom Allah had given "the luxuries and comforts of worldly life," the chiefs whose word set the tone for a nation. The last image the Qurʾān gives of them is debris left on a waterline. And in ayah 34 it was they who had warned that following the messenger would make you *losers*.

**"Away with the wrongdoers"** — Ibn Kathir reads *ẓālimīn* here through Allah's words *"We wronged them not, but they were the wrongdoers"* (43:76): they are wrongdoers because of their disbelief and stubborn opposition to the Messenger of Allah. The wrong began in them; the punishment answered it.

Ibn Kathir ends his comment on this passage with the lesson he wants the reader to carry away, and it is the right place to stop: **so let those who hear this beware of disbelieving in their Messengers.**

## Living with these ayat

- **Hold to the raising of the body.** What the chiefs dismissed in ayah 35 — dust and bones brought out alive — is exactly the physical resurrection Ibn Kathir says they denied.
- **Do not judge a messenger by his ordinariness.** Their whole case in ayat 33–34 was that he ate and drank as they did. Ibn Kathir names this as the reason they refused to follow a human Messenger.
- **Notice the company that comfort keeps.** Ayah 33 names the luxuries and comforts they had been given in the same breath as their denial of the meeting in the Hereafter.
- **Let your deeds not say what your tongue denies.** This is Maʿārif ul Qurʾān's warning on ayah 37, and it is the passage's most searching question for a believing reader.
- **Take "in a little while" seriously.** They stretched the promise out to *hayhāt, hayhāt*; Allah called it *ʿammā qalīl*.

passages.title: No nation can outrun its appointed term
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat compress a long stretch of human history into a single movement of cause and effect: Allah raises up nation after nation, each with a fixed term it cannot move by a moment, and into each He sends a messenger — and when the messenger is denied, the nation itself becomes nothing but a story people tell.

Twice the passage opens with "Then" (ثُمَّ). **Then** We created other generations (ayah 42) — **then** We sent Our Messengers in succession (ayah 44) — and between them, in ayah 43, the law that governs the whole sequence: no nation gets ahead of its term or lags behind it. Ibn Kathir treats the three ayat as one connected statement, heading his comment on them "Mention of Other Nations."

## Ayah 42 — "Then, after them, We created other generations"

The word translated "generations" is قُرُونًا (*qurūnan*). Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: **"meaning, nations and peoples."** So this is not merely one age-group succeeding another. It is peoples — whole communities — coming into existence.

Notice the verb: **أَنشَأْنَا** (*ansha'nā*), rendered here "We created" and also translated "We raised." Nations do not simply *appear*. They are brought into being, and it is Allah who brings them into being. A community looks to itself like the achievement of its own founders; the Qur'an describes it as something Allah originated.

And "after them" (مِن بَعْدِهِم) quietly does something devastating: it tells you the previous ones are gone. The verse takes the passing of a whole people and makes it a subordinate phrase — the backdrop to the next act.

## Ayah 43 — the term that cannot be moved

**"No nation can advance their term, nor can they delay it."**

This is the hinge of the passage, and it is worth sitting with. Ibn Kathir explains it as meaning **"they are taken at the appropriate time, as decreed by Allah in His Book that is preserved with Him, before they were created, nation after nation, century after century, generation after generation, successors after predecessors."**

Two things in that sentence deserve unpacking.

**First: it was written before they existed.** Ibn Kathir is explicit — the time is decreed by Allah in His Book preserved with Him, "before they were created." The end of every nation was recorded before that nation had drawn a single breath. And his phrasing — "nation after nation, century after century, generation after generation, successors after predecessors" — makes the point that this is not an occasional intervention but the steady pattern of how peoples come and go.

**Second: the two directions.** The ayah does not only say a nation cannot *delay* its end — it says it cannot **advance** it either (مَا تَسْبِقُ). That is not the fear anyone actually has. So why mention it? Because the point is not merely that you cannot escape; it is that **the timing is entirely out of your hands in both directions.** A people cannot hurry the appointed moment and cannot postpone it. This cuts against the arrogant, who assume their power buys them time — and against the impatient believer who wonders why a tyranny is still standing. On the reading Ibn Kathir gives, it is standing because its appointed time has not come, and every people is taken "at the appropriate time."

Note also that the term belongs to an **أُمَّة** (*umma*) — a nation, a whole community. What we are used to thinking of as belonging to a person is here applied to an entire people.

## Ayah 44 — messengers in an unbroken line

**"Then We sent Our Messengers in succession."**

The key word is **تَتْرَا** (*tatrā*). Ibn Kathir reports that **Ibn 'Abbas** said it means **"following one another in succession"** — one after another, in an unbroken chain. Allah did not send a single warning and leave the rest of history to fend for itself. As each new nation was raised up, a messenger came with it.

Ibn Kathir connects this to Allah's words elsewhere:

> "And verily, We have sent among every Ummah a Messenger (proclaiming): 'Worship Allah, and avoid Taghut (all false deities).' Then of them were some whom Allah guided and of them were some upon whom the straying was justified." (16:36)

That cross-reference does three things at once. It confirms the *universality* — **every** community received a messenger, so no people can plead that they were left in the dark. It tells you the *message*: worship Allah alone, and avoid *Taghut*, which the translation itself explains as all false deities — every false object of devotion. And it shows the *outcome* was never uniform — some Allah guided, and against others the straying was justified.

**"Every time there came to a nation their Messenger, they denied him."**

The wording is "every time" — no exceptions are carved out. But Ibn Kathir adds a precise and merciful qualification: this denial means **"the greater majority of them."** It was never literally everyone. The verse describes the dominant response of a people, not the fate of every soul within it. That is an important corrective for anyone reading these verses and despairing of their own society.

And note the phrase "**their** Messenger" — رَسُولُهَا. He was theirs. The verse Ibn Kathir cites says Allah sent a messenger *among* every community (16:36). They rejected not a stranger but one sent among them. Ibn Kathir places alongside it:

> "Alas for mankind! There never came a Messenger to them but they used to mock at him." (36:30)

Mockery, not merely disagreement. The exclamation "Alas for mankind" (يَا حَسْرَةً عَلَى الْعِبَادِ) carries a note of grief over what people do to themselves.

**"So, We made them follow one another."**

Here the Arabic is quietly terrible. فَأَتْبَعْنَا بَعْضَهُم بَعْضًا. Ibn Kathir states the meaning bluntly: **"We destroyed them."** The same language of succession that described the messengers now describes the ruins. Prophets came one after another; nations fell one after another. He cites:

> "And how many generations have We destroyed after Nuh!" (17:17)

**"And We made them as Ahadith."**

This is the last and sharpest stroke. Ibn Kathir explains أَحَادِيث (*aḥādīth*) here as **"stories and lessons for mankind,"** and quotes:

> "So, We made them as tales (in the land), and We dispersed them all totally." (34:19)

Think about what that means as a fate. A nation that once had its own life and pride is reduced to *something people mention* — a tale, a lesson, a name in a lesson like this one. The people who denied their messenger did not merely lose; on Ibn Kathir's reading they became instruction for the nations that came after them. And the surah is saying, to the first listeners and to us: you are reading about them — take care that no one ends up reading about you.

**"So, away with a people who believe not."**

The passage closes on that note. And notice the grounds the words themselves give: not poverty, not weakness, not defeat, but that **they did not believe**. That is the single thread running through the collapses these ayat describe.

## What this asks of us

**Stop reading history as a series of accidents.** These ayat give you a lens: peoples are brought into being by Allah, are taken at the time decreed for them, and in this passage are spoken of in terms of how they answered the messenger sent to them. Ayah 43 removes both panic and complacency at once.

**Take the fixed term seriously.** If a whole nation cannot move its appointed end forward or back, that is a reason to work now rather than assume there is time — and a reason not to be terrified of what you cannot control.

**Read the ruins as they were meant to be read.** Ibn Kathir says the destroyed peoples were made "stories and lessons for mankind." The lesson is only received if you actually take it: the fallen nations were not a different species. They had messengers sent among them, and the greater majority turned away — often with mockery rather than argument, as 36:30 describes.

**Be among those who believed.** Ibn Kathir's careful note that denial was "the greater majority of them" implies its opposite: it was not all of them. When the dominant current of a society runs against the truth, being few is not evidence of being wrong. And 16:36 says plainly that of every community "were some whom Allah guided" — in every generation Allah has raised up.

passages.title: Moses, Aaron, Pharaoh, and Jesus as a sign
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath:** two brothers are sent to Fir'awn and his court with decisive proof, are refused on the flimsiest of grounds, and the refusers are drowned — and then, in the very next breath, a mother and her son are shown to us not as a warning but as a *sign*, given refuge by Allah on high ground, fertile, with water running through it.

What holds these six ayat together is a single movement — from **arrogance destroyed** (45–48) to **guidance given** (49) to **mercy sheltered** (50).

## "With Our Ayat and manifest authority" (ayah 45)

Allah says He sent Musa **and his brother Harun** — the brotherhood is named, not assumed.

They came, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "with decisive evidence and definitive proof." Ibn Kathir's rendering of the ayah pairs two things: *Ayat* — signs — and **manifest authority**. The point matters for what follows: Fir'awn's court did not turn Musa away because the evidence was thin. Ibn Kathir calls it decisive. They turned him away for another reason entirely.

## Arrogance at the top (ayah 46)

They were sent "to Fir'awn **and his chiefs**" — the ruler and the ruling class together. Rejection here is not a private failure of one man; the chiefs are named alongside him.

Ibn Kathir's translation of the ayah gives us two descriptions of what went wrong. First, "they behaved insolently" — they made themselves big. Then, "they were people self-exalting," and Ibn Kathir's rendering adds the crucial gloss: *by disobeying their Lord*. Notice the shape of that second phrase: it does not describe something they *did* on one occasion but something they **were**. Arrogance had become their settled character.

This is the diagnosis the whole passage rests on. Ibn Kathir does not say they were confused. He says they "were too arrogant to follow them and obey their commands."

## "Shall we believe in two men like ourselves?" (ayah 47)

Now the objection itself, and it is worth sitting with how weak it is:

> "Shall we believe in two men like ourselves, and their people are obedient to us with humility!"

Two complaints, neither of them about truth.

**First: the messengers are human.** Ibn Kathir points out that Fir'awn's people "were too arrogant to follow them and obey their commands **because they were human beings**, just as previous nations had denied the Message of the human Messengers. They were of a similar mentality." The objection is not that a sign failed; it is that the men carrying the signs were men.

**Second: the messengers come from the wrong side of the social order.** "And their people are obedient to us with humility" — the people Musa and Harun belonged to were, in the court's eyes, subject to them. So the argument, stripped bare, is about rank rather than evidence. Nothing in it engages a single sign that Musa brought.

## Denial, then destruction (ayah 48)

"So, they denied them both and became of those who were destroyed."

The Arabic moves in two quick steps — *fa-kadhdhabūhumā fa-kānū* — denial, and then consequence, with nothing in between. Ibn Kathir states the outcome plainly: "so Allah destroyed Fir'awn and his chiefs, **drowning them all in one day**." The court that would not believe in two men "like ourselves" was finished inside a single day.

And notice the phrasing: they *became of those who were destroyed*. They did not merely die; they joined a category. Ibn Kathir has just told us that previous nations denied the human Messengers in exactly the same way, and the ayah he cites next speaks of "the generations of old" whom Allah had destroyed. The point of such a category is that anyone can be added to it.

## The Book after the drowning — and a turn in history (ayah 49)

"And indeed We gave Musa the Scripture, that they may be guided."

Ibn Kathir is careful about the sequence, and it is the same sequence the ayat follow: Allah "revealed the Book to Musa, i.e., the Tawrah, in which were rulings, commands and prohibitions, **after** He had destroyed Fir'awn and the Egyptians and seized them with a punishment of the All-Mighty, All-Capable to carry out what He wills." The judgment came first; the law came after. Destruction was never the end in itself — guidance was.

Then Ibn Kathir draws out a genuinely striking observation about the shape of sacred history:

> "After Allah revealed the Tawrah, Allah did not destroy any nation with an overwhelming calamity; instead, He commanded the believers to fight the disbelievers."

In other words, the era of whole peoples being erased by an overwhelming calamity closed with the giving of the Tawrah. He supports it from the Qur'an itself:

> **"And indeed We gave Musa — after We had destroyed the generations of old — the Scripture as an enlightenment for mankind, and a guidance and a mercy, that they might remember."** (28:43)

"After We had destroyed the generations of old" is the hinge Ibn Kathir leans on: the Book arrives at the close of that age.

## The son of Maryam and his mother: made into a sign (ayah 50)

Now the passage turns, without transition, from a drowned court to a sheltered household.

"And We made the son of Maryam and his mother as a sign." Ibn Kathir: Allah "tells us about His servant and Messenger 'Isa bin Maryam, peace be upon them both, and that He made them as a sign for mankind, i.e., **definitive proof of His ability to do what He wills**."

Two people, but the word "sign" is singular — mother and son together form one piece of evidence.

Then Ibn Kathir gives the argument in four moves that between them exhaust every possibility of human origin:

- **Adam** — created without a father or a mother.
- **Hawwa'** — created from a male without a female.
- **'Isa** — created from a female without a male.
- **Everyone else** — created from both male and female.

Laid out like that, you can see what the birth of 'Isa demonstrates. It fills in the one remaining corner of the possible, so that no one could imagine Allah's creating is bound to a single channel — which is exactly how Ibn Kathir reads it: "definitive proof of His ability to do what He wills." And notice the order of these ayat: the court that exalted itself was drowned, while a mother and her son were given refuge and made into the standing proof of who actually holds power.

Note also what the ayah does **not** say. It calls him *the son of Maryam* — his mother named, and he named by her — and Ibn Kathir calls him "His **servant** and Messenger." A miraculous birth makes him a sign of Allah's power, never a sharer in it.

## "A Rabwah, Dhat Qarar and Ma'in" — the refuge

"And We gave them refuge on a *Rabwah*, *Dhat Qarar*, and *Ma'in*." Three words, and the early scholars unpacked each:

- **Rabwah** — "a raised portion of land, which is the best place for vegetation to grow," said Ibn 'Abbas as reported by Ad-Dahhak; this was also the view of Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id bin Jubayr and Qatadah. Mujahid also described it as "a level hill" — high ground, but flat enough to live on.
- **Dhat Qarar** — Ibn 'Abbas: "a fertile place."
- **Ma'in** — Ibn 'Abbas: "water running on the surface," and likewise Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id bin Jubayr and Qatadah. Mujahid and Qatadah: "running water." Sa'id bin Jubayr said the pairing *Dhat Qarar and Ma'in* means "water was flowing gently through it."

Put together: elevation, fertility, and open water. Ibn Kathir's rendering of the phrase gathers it up as "high ground, a place of rest, security and flowing streams." Allah did not merely spare them; He settled them somewhere good.

**Where was it?** The early authorities differed, and Ibn Kathir reports the range honestly:

- **Damascus** — recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim from Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib, who added that "something similar was also narrated from 'Abdullah bin Salam, Al-Hasan, Zayd bin Aslam and Khalid bin Ma'dan." Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded from 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas that the ayah referred to the rivers of Damascus, and Layth bin Abi Sulaym narrated from Mujahid that it meant 'Isa and his mother sought refuge in Damascus and the flatlands around it.
- **Ramlah in Palestine** — 'Abdur-Razzaq recorded this from Abu Hurayrah.
- **Jerusalem** — the view of Ad-Dahhak and Qatadah.

Ibn Kathir weighs them. He says the most correct opinion on the matter is the one Al-'Awfi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas: that *Ma'in* is running water, and is the river Allah mentions elsewhere to Maryam — **"your Lord has provided a water stream under you"** (19:24). On that basis he calls Jerusalem "the most apparent meaning, and Allah knows best."

His reason for preferring it is a lesson in method, and worth carrying beyond this ayah:

> "because it is mentioned in the other Ayah, and **parts of the Qur'an explain other parts**, so it is more appropriate to interpret it by another Ayah, then the Sahih Hadiths, then other reports."

That is the order of authority in tafsir: Qur'an first, then authenticated hadith, then other reports. Where the early scholars differ on a detail like a place-name, a believer is not obliged to pick a side — and the meaning of the ayah does not hang on it.

## Why they needed a refuge

Ma'ariful-Qur'an, quoting Bayan-ul-Qur'an, supplies the human situation behind the word "refuge": a tyrant was resolved to kill 'Isa and his mother, peace be upon them both, right from his childhood. They escaped him and, by Allah's grace, found a place on a height where they lived a peaceful life until 'Isa reached maturity and was entrusted with prophethood.

Read the passage again with that in view and its architecture is complete. Ayat 45–48: a tyrant who denied Allah's messengers and was drowned with his chiefs. Ayah 50: another tyrant set on killing Allah's servants — and Allah lifted them out of his reach and settled them on high ground with running water until the time of prophethood came. The same power that drowns a court also shelters a mother and a child.

## Living it

**Check the shape of your objections.** By Ibn Kathir's reading, Fir'awn's court refused the messengers "because they were human beings" and because of where their people stood socially — not because a sign had failed. That should make anyone pause who has ever dismissed a reminder because of who delivered it.

**Arrogance is the disease, not ignorance.** The ayah does not say they lacked evidence; it says they were "people self-exalting" — and Ibn Kathir adds, *by disobeying their Lord*. Whatever makes a person unable to accept correction from someone he considers beneath him is the same thing named here.

**Allah's help does not have one shape.** With Musa it came as the destruction of the tyrant and then the Book, "that they may be guided." With Maryam and her son it came as a quiet height with water. And when He shelters someone, ayah 50 shows He tends to shelter them well: rest, fertile ground, and flowing water, until the purpose He made them for is ready.

passages.title: One religion, one Lord, and the sects
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat move from the private discipline of a prophet's own body to the public fracture of whole nations. Allah addresses every messenger He ever sent with a single instruction — eat what is pure, act righteously (ayah 51) — then tells them that the religion they all carried was one religion under one Lord (ayah 52), then reports what their followers did with it: they tore it into pieces, each faction delighted with its own scrap (ayah 53). The passage closes with a command to the Prophet ﷺ that is really a sentence of judgement: leave them in it, for a time (ayah 54).

What holds the four together is one idea seen from two angles — **purity**. Pure intake and pure action in the individual; pure, undivided creed in the community. The passage shows both, and shows what it looks like when the second is lost.

## Ayah 51 — an address to all the messengers at once

"O messengers! Eat from what is good and lawful, and act righteously." Ibn Kathir notes that Allah here commands His servants and His messengers, peace be upon them all, to eat lawful food and to do righteous deeds — and that the two commands being placed side by side "indicates that eating what is lawful helps one to do righteous deeds." That is the hinge of the ayah. These are not two unrelated pieces of advice; the first is the ground of the second.

**Ṭayyibāt.** The word translated "good things" is *ṭayyibāt*. Sa'id bin Jubayr and Ad-Dahhak said plainly: this means *lawful*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word further — *ṭayyib* means pure and good, and since what the Sharīʿah forbids is neither pure nor desirable to anyone gifted with common sense, the word points to exactly what the Sharīʿah permits: things that are "not only good in appearance, but also pure in their intrinsic nature." So *ṭayyib* is not a compliment about taste or quality. It is a word about what a thing *is*: pure in itself.

**Why address the prophets?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the force of the address: these two injunctions are given to prophets, who are impeccable in any case. If men who never sinned are told to watch what enters their mouths and to act righteously, then "it is necessary that their followers should strive hard to mould their lives according to these injunctions. This in fact is the real meaning of this verse." The command is aimed high precisely so that it lands on everyone below.

Ibn Kathir adds that the prophets fulfilled it in the most perfect manner, doing every kind of good deed "in words, actions, guidance and advice" — and he pauses to pray that Allah reward them with good on behalf of the people.

**"Verily, I am Well-Acquainted with what you do."** The ayah does not end with the two commands. It ends with Allah's knowledge closing over them. Nothing in the food, the earning, or the deed lies outside it.

## Prophets who earned with their hands

Under this ayah Ibn Kathir cites two reports about what lawful eating looked like in prophetic lives. In the Ṣaḥīḥ: "There is no Prophet who was not a shepherd." They asked, "And you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said, "Yes, I used to tend the sheep of the people of Makkah for a few Qirats." And again in the Ṣaḥīḥ: "Dawud, upon him be peace, used to eat from the earnings of his own hand."

Set beside the command in ayah 51, these are not incidental biography. They show the messengers themselves living on income they had earned with their own labour.

## "Allah is Ṭayyib and only accepts what is ṭayyib"

Ibn Kathir then brings the central hadith on this ayah. It was recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Jāmiʿ at-Tirmidhī and Musnad al-Imām Aḥmad — the wording he gives is Aḥmad's — that Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "O people, Allah is Ṭayyib and only accepts that which is Ṭayyib, and Allah commands the believers as He had commanded the Messengers."

He then recited this very ayah, 23:51, and alongside it "O you who believe! Eat of the Ṭayyibāt that We have provided you with" (2:172). Notice what the hadith does: it takes the address that seemed reserved for prophets in ayah 51 and hands it straight to the believers. The two verses are quoted back to back to make exactly that point.

Then the Prophet ﷺ mentioned how a man may travel on a long journey, dusty and unkempt — "and his food, drink and clothing are unlawful, and he has nourished himself with what is unlawful, and he extends his hands towards the sky, saying, 'O Lord, O Lord!' — how can his prayer be answered." At-Tirmidhī said that it is *ḥasan gharīb*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same hadith (through Qurṭubī) and states the conclusion without softening it: a person who hopes his worship will win Allah's pleasure, or that his prayers will be granted, "must pay scrupulous attention to what he eats and must, at all times, avoid eating unlawful things." Scholars, it adds, have read the pairing of the two commands to mean that lawful food has a very important bearing on human actions: with lawful intake, a divine guidance takes a person's actions along the path of righteousness; with unlawful intake, "serious obstacles will prevent the accomplishment of good deeds in spite of his best intentions." Sincerity of intention, on this reading, is not enough on its own if what feeds the body is corrupt.

## Ayah 52 — one creed, one Lord

"Surely this religion of yours is only one, and I am your Lord."

**The word *ummah*.** We usually hear *ummah* as "community" — a group, or the followers of a prophet — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān confirms that is one of its uses. But it is also used in the sense of "faith", "creed", or "way of life", as in the words "We found our fathers upon a creed (*ummah*)" (43:22). In this verse, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, it is used in that second sense. So the statement is not primarily "you prophets are one community" but "the creed you all carry is one creed."

Ibn Kathir gives both dimensions: "your religion, O Prophets, is one religion and one group, which is the call to worship Allah Alone with no partner or associate." That is the content of the oneness — the worship of Allah alone. Grammatically, Ibn Kathir notes, the phrase "one nation" here is descriptive: it tells you what this creed *is*, rather than introducing something new.

**"And I am your Lord, so have taqwā."** The oneness of the religion is anchored in the One who is Lord over all the messengers who carried it. On this closing phrase Ibn Kathir says simply that he has already discussed it in Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ.

## Ayah 53 — what the nations did with it

"Yet the people have divided it into different sects, each rejoicing in what it has."

Ibn Kathir identifies who "they" are: **the nations to whom prophets were sent.** The fracture is not the prophets' doing. It is what came after them, to the message they had left behind.

**The word *zubur*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two readings. It may be the plural of *zabūr*, meaning a book: Allah had commanded all the prophets and their followers to adhere to the one and only faith He revealed in all matters of basic principle and belief, but the followers of the different prophets "split up into groups and sects and each one of them chose a different way of life and adopted a different book in which the beliefs of each group and sect were recorded." Or *zubur* may be the plural of *zubrah*, meaning "fragment" or "group". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges this second meaning "more appropriate here": these people were divided into sects even in the matter of the *fundamental* beliefs of their religion.

**"Each group rejoicing in what is with it."** This is the most piercing phrase in the passage. Ibn Kathir explains: "they rejoice in their misguidance because they think that they are rightly-guided." The tragedy is not that the factions are miserable — it is that they are *happy*. Each one looks at the fragment in its hands and celebrates. Error that knows itself can be corrected; error that feels like victory is much harder to reach.

**An important limit.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to fence this verse off from misuse: the difference of opinion among the *mujtahidīn* — competent scholars of the Sharīʿah — on some minor issues is **not** included in the division condemned here, "because these differences do not cause a division of the religion, nor do the people maintaining these differences become separate sects." And it goes further: "Giving these interpretative and subsidiary differences a sectarian colour is the height of ignorance and no religious scholar would support it." The ayah condemns splitting over foundations; it does not license turning branches into banners.

## Ayah 54 — "So leave them in their heedlessness for a while"

Ibn Kathir glosses *ghamrah*, the word rendered "heedlessness", simply as "their misguidance." And "for a time" he explains as: "until the appointed time of their destruction comes."

Read carefully, this is not permission to relax. Ibn Kathir introduces the ayah with the words: "Allah says, threatening and warning." The command to *leave them* is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and what it announces is that a clock is running. Ibn Kathir links it to "So give a respite to the disbelievers; deal gently with them for a while" (86:17) and to "Leave them to eat and enjoy, and let them be preoccupied with false hope. They will come to know!" (15:3).

## Ibn Kathir's closing hadith — and the way it returns to ayah 51

Ibn Kathir closes this stretch of commentary with a hadith recorded by Imam Aḥmad from ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Allah has distributed your behavior to you just as He has distributed your provision. Allah gives the things of this world to those whom He loves and those whom He does not love, but He only gives religious commitment to those whom He loves. Whoever is given religious commitment by Allah is loved by Him."

The same hadith continues: "By the One in Whose Hand is my soul, no servant truly submits until his heart and his tongue submit, and he does not truly believe until his neighbor is safe from his harm" — and when they asked what that harm was, he said, "His wrongdoing and misbehavior." Then, returning us precisely to ayah 51: "No person who earns unlawful wealth and spends it will be blessed in that; if he gives it in charity, it will not be accepted from him and if he leaves it behind (when he dies), it will be his provision in the Fire. Allah does not wash away an evil deed with another, but he washes away evil deeds with good deeds, for impurity cannot wash away with another impurity."

That last line is the passage's logic in a sentence. Impurity cannot clean impurity — which is why the command to the messengers began where it did: at the mouth.

## Living it

- **Watch what enters, not only what is intended.** Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 51 is that lawful intake *helps* righteous action; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's is that unlawful intake raises "serious obstacles" to good deeds "in spite of his best intentions."
- **Treat unanswered prayer as a question about intake, not only about sincerity.** The image of the dusty traveller with raised hands is placed in this hadith exactly there — right after "Allah is Ṭayyib and only accepts that which is Ṭayyib."
- **Honest work is prophetic work.** Shepherding for a few Qirats; Dawud eating from his own hands' earnings. There is no version of piety in these sources that floats above earning a lawful living.
- **How wealth is earned matters, not only what is bought with it.** The closing hadith says unlawful earnings carry no blessing when spent, are not accepted as charity, and become "his provision in the Fire" when left behind.
- **Guard the foundations; do not manufacture sects out of branches.** Ayah 53 condemns tearing up the creed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explicitly refuses to let it be turned against the disagreements of qualified scholars on minor issues.
- **Do not read prosperity as approval.** In that same hadith: Allah gives the things of this world to those He loves and to those He does not love, but He gives religious commitment only to those He loves.

passages.title: Wealth is no proof of Allah's favour
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat take apart one of the oldest illusions of the human heart: that if Allah is giving you wealth and children, He must be pleased with you. Ayat 55–56 name the illusion and demolish it; ayat 57–61 then answer the question the illusion was really asking — *who are the people Allah is actually rushing good towards?* — and the answer turns out to be almost the opposite of what the wealthy scoffers assumed.

The unity of the passage is held together by a single phrase repeated twice. In ayah 56 the disbelievers imagine that Allah is "hastening to them all kinds of good" — نُسَارِعُ لَهُمْ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ. In ayah 61, the same verb and the same word return, but with the subject changed: أُولَٰئِكَ يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ — "it is *these* who hasten in the good things." The illusion is that good things race towards you. The truth is that the people of faith race towards the good things. Reading 55–61 as one unit is the only way to feel that reversal land.

## What comes just before

The passage does not begin cold. In the preceding ayat Allah addresses the Messengers — eat of the lawful, do righteous deeds — and declares that their religion is one religion and He is their one Lord (23:51–52). Ibn Kathir explains that this means: your religion, O Prophets, is one religion and one group, which is the call to worship Allah alone with no partner or associate. Then the nations to whom the Prophets were sent "broke their religion among them into sects, each group rejoicing in what is with it" (23:53) — rejoicing, Ibn Kathir says, in their own misguidance, because they think they are the rightly guided ones.

On that word for "sects" — زُبُر — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes two possibilities. It may be the plural of زُبُور, a book, meaning that the followers of the different prophets split into groups and each adopted a different book in which its own beliefs were recorded. Or it may be the plural of زُبْرَة, a fragment or group, and Maʿārif considers this the more fitting sense here: these people were divided into sects even in the matter of the fundamental beliefs of their religion. Maʿārif adds an important guard-rail: the difference of opinion among the *mujtahidīn* — competent scholars of Sharīʿah — on some minor issues is not part of the division this ayah condemns, because such differences neither divide the religion nor make those who hold them separate sects; giving these interpretative and subsidiary differences a sectarian colour, it says, is the height of ignorance, and no religious scholar would support it.

Then comes 23:54 — "So leave them in their error for a time" — which Ibn Kathir reads as: leave them in their misguidance until the appointed time of their destruction comes. He places it alongside *"So give a respite to the disbelievers; deal gently with them for a while"* (86:17) and *"Leave them to eat and enjoy, and let them be preoccupied with false hope. They will come to know!"* (15:3). This is a threat, not an indulgence. And it is precisely the "time" they are being left in that ayat 55–56 now explain.

## Ayat 55–56: reading prosperity backwards

"Do they think, since We provide them with wealth and children, that We hasten to honour them with all kinds of good? No!"

Ibn Kathir puts the question in plain terms: do these deceived people think that what We give them of wealth and children is because they are honoured and precious in Our sight? He then reaches for their own words as the Qur'an records them elsewhere: *"We are more in wealth and in children, and we are not going to be punished"* (34:35). That is the whole creed of the affluent sceptic in one line — success now, safety later.

"But this thinking is wrong," Ibn Kathir writes, "and their hopes will be dashed. We only give those things to them in order to make them go further in sin and to give them more time." He gathers the verses that state this openly: *"So let not their wealth nor their children amaze you; in reality Allah's plan is to punish them with these things in the life of this world"* (9:55); *"We postpone the punishment only so that they may increase in sinfulness"* (3:178); *"We shall punish them gradually from directions they perceive not. And I will grant them a respite"* (68:44–45); and the passage beginning *"Leave Me alone to deal with whom I created lonely"* (74:11–16). Read together, these describe being drawn in by degrees — every fresh gift is another rung down a ladder the person thinks is going up.

Notice how ayah 55 comes into English two ways in our sources. The translation before us reads "since We provide them with wealth and children"; the version Ibn Kathir's text uses reads "wealth and children with which We prolong them." Either way, the ayah does not dispute that the giving is real or that Allah is the one giving it — Ibn Kathir's own paraphrase says plainly, *what We give them of wealth and children*. What the ayah rejects is the conclusion drawn from the gift.

And the verdict of ayah 56 is devastatingly short: **بَل لَّا يَشْعُرُونَ** — "Nay, but they perceive not." They are not merely mistaken in an argument; they cannot feel what is happening to them. The ladder is going down and the sensation is of climbing.

The counter-principle is given in the verse Ibn Kathir cites next: *"And it is not your wealth, nor your children that bring you nearer to Us, but only he who believes and does righteous deeds"* (34:37). Wealth and children are not disqualifications either — the ayah does not say the rich are far. It says the currency of nearness is faith and righteous action, and that money is simply not that currency.

## The hadith that settles it

Ibn Kathir supports this with a narration recorded by **Imam Ahmad** from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Allah has distributed your behaviour to you just as He has distributed your provision. Allah gives the things of this world to those whom He loves and those whom He does not love, but He only gives religious commitment to those whom He loves. Whoever is given religious commitment by Allah is loved by Him."

This is the key that unlocks ayat 55–56. Worldly provision is distributed across both sides of the line — the beloved and the not-beloved both receive it — so it can carry no information about which side you are on. *Dīn*, religious commitment, is given only to the beloved. So the honest question is never "how much has Allah given me?" but "what has Allah given me?"

The same hadith continues past the point of wealth into the point of character: no servant truly submits until his heart and his tongue submit, and he does not truly believe until his neighbour is safe from his harm — and when the Companions asked what that harm was, the Prophet ﷺ said, "His wrongdoing and misbehaviour." He then added that no person who earns unlawful wealth and spends it will be blessed in it; if he gives it in charity it will not be accepted from him, and if he leaves it behind when he dies it will be his provision in the Fire — for Allah does not wash away an evil deed with another evil deed, but washes away evil deeds with good deeds; impurity cannot be washed away with another impurity.

That last clause reaches back to ayah 51 and its command to the Messengers to eat of the *ṭayyibāt*, the wholesome. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk explained *ṭayyibāt* simply as "lawful," and Ibn Kathir observes that Allah commanding lawful food alongside righteous deeds indicates that eating what is lawful helps one to do righteous deeds. He cites the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, recorded in **Sahih Muslim, Jāmiʿ At-Tirmidhī and Musnad Al-Imām Aḥmad** — the version Ibn Kathir gives coming from the last of these — in which the Prophet ﷺ said: "O people, Allah is Ṭayyib and only accepts that which is Ṭayyib, and Allah commands the believers as He had commanded the Messengers" — quoting this very surah's ayah 51 alongside 2:172. He then mentioned a man travelling on a long journey, dusty and unkempt, extending his hands towards the sky, saying "O Lord, O Lord!" — while his food, his drink and his clothing are unlawful, and he has nourished himself with what is unlawful — "how can his prayer be answered?" (At-Tirmidhī said that it is *ḥasan gharīb*.)

So the passage's teaching on wealth has two edges. Ayat 55–56: having wealth proves nothing about Allah's love. The supporting hadiths: *how* you got it decides whether anything you do with it counts.

## Ayat 57–61: the portrait of the real hasteners

Having emptied the scoffers' self-image, Allah now fills the frame with the people who genuinely have what the scoffers imagined they had. Ibn Kathir titles this section "Description of the People of Good Deeds." Four qualities, then the verdict.

**Ayah 57 — they tremble.** *"Surely those who tremble in awe of their Lord"* — or, in the rendering Ibn Kathir's text carries, *"those who live in awe for fear of their Lord."* Ibn Kathir's comment is striking: even though these people have reached the level of *Iḥsān* and have faith and do righteous deeds, they are still in awe of Allah and fear Him and His hidden plans for them. (The sources here use the word *Iḥsān* without stopping to define it; what they show us is the picture the ayah draws — people who already have faith and righteous deeds, and who are still not comfortable.) He quotes Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī: **"The believer combines Iḥsān with awe, while the disbelievers combine evil deeds with a sense of security."** Set that beside ayat 55–56 and the two halves of the passage lock together: the man in ayah 55 feels safe because he is rich; the believer in ayah 57 does not feel safe, because he knows Whom he stands before. Their inner states are exactly inverted — and so is their standing with Allah.

**Ayah 58 — they believe in their Lord's signs.** Ibn Kathir explains *āyāt* here as His universal and His legislative signs — that is, both what He *does* in creation and what He *reveals* as command. He illustrates with what Allah says of Maryam, peace be upon her: *"and she testified to the truth of the Words of her Lord, and His Scriptures"* (66:12), meaning that she believed that whatever existed was by the will and decree of Allah, and that whatever Allah decreed — if it was a command, it was something He liked and accepted; if a prohibition, something He disliked and rejected; and if it was good, it would be true. Faith in the signs is therefore not only assenting to revelation but reading events as His.

**Ayah 59 — they associate nothing with their Lord.** They do not worship anyone or anything besides Him, Ibn Kathir writes, but worship Him alone and know that there is no god except Allah alone, the One, the Self-Sufficient Master, who does not take a wife or have any offspring, and there is none comparable or equal unto Him. This is placed deliberately: a person can tremble and can believe in signs, yet direct some part of worship elsewhere. What Ibn Kathir's own heading calls *Tawhid* — that "call to worship Allah alone with no partner or associate" which he says was the one religion of all the Prophets — is what makes the rest genuine.

**Ayah 60 — they give, and their hearts shake as they give.** *"And who do whatever good they do with their hearts fearful, because they are sure to return to their Lord."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the verb يُؤْتُونَ is derived from إيتاء, "to give, to spend," and is used in the commentaries in the sense of *ṣadaqāt*, alms to the poor. It also records another reading of the verse reported from Sayyidah ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her — "they do whatever they do" — which covers all good deeds: charity, prayers, fasting and the rest. Maʿārif adds that even on the generally accepted reading, which mentions alms only, all good deeds would be included, as is borne out by a hadith.

What are they afraid of? Ibn Kathir: they give in charity fearing that it may not be accepted from them because of some shortcoming or failure to meet the required conditions of giving. This, he says, has to do with fear and taking precautions.

The hadith that settles the meaning is ʿĀ'ishah's own question. **Imam Ahmad** records that she asked, "O Messenger of Allah — *those who give that which they give with their hearts full of fear* — are these the ones who steal and commit *zinā* and drink alcohol while fearing Allah?" He ﷺ replied:

> "No, O daughter of Abu Bakr, O daughter of aṣ-Ṣiddīq — rather it is the one who prays and fasts and gives in charity, fearing Allah."

Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by **At-Tirmidhī**, and that **Ibn Abī Ḥātim** recorded something similar in which the Prophet ﷺ said, "No, O daughter of aṣ-Ṣiddīq — they are the ones who pray and fast and give in charity while fearing that it will not be accepted from them," and then recited: *"It is these who hasten in the good deeds."* Ibn Kathir adds that this is also how Ibn ʿAbbās, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb Al-Quraẓī and Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī interpreted the ayah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same exchange — in its wording, that these are people who fast, pray and give alms, yet are apprehensive lest their good deeds not be accepted by Allah — citing Aḥmad, Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah and Mazharī.

Feel the size of that correction. ʿĀ'ishah's reading was the humane one — surely the trembling heart belongs to the sinner. The answer is that the trembling heart belongs to the *worshipper*. The person praying, fasting and giving is the one who cannot relax about whether it was good enough. Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī said that he knew people who did virtuous deeds yet were more fearful than people who committed evil deeds (cited via Qurṭubī in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān).

**Ayah 61 — the verdict.** *"It is they who race to do good deeds, always taking the lead."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the image inside *musāraʿah fi'l-khayrāt*: just as ordinary human beings run after worldly gains and try to leave other competitors behind, these good and virtuous people strive to gain spiritual reward and try to excel others in their efforts to fulfil their religious obligations. The same competitive energy — redirected.

And this is where ayah 61 answers ayah 56 directly. The rich mockers thought Allah was hastening the good things *to* them. In truth, the good things are being hastened *by* these trembling, believing, undivided, anxiously generous servants — and they are the foremost to attain them.

## Living it

**Stop reading your bank balance as a report card.** Provision reaches the loved and the unloved alike; only *dīn* is the sign of love. If you want a reading of your standing with Allah, look at what He has given you of faith, prayer, and steadiness — not at what He has given you of money.

**Check the source, not just the destination.** Ayah 51 is upstream of this whole passage: unlawful earnings poison what is built on them. Charity from forbidden wealth is not accepted; the prayer of the man nourished by the unlawful is not answered.

**Give, and don't award yourself the medal.** The mark of the people in ayah 60 is that they act *and* worry. Not paralysing anxiety — they still pray, fast and give — but the refusal to sign off their own deeds as accepted. Do the deed; leave the verdict to Allah.

**Let your fear be of the right kind.** Ayah 57 places awe inside worship, not instead of it. Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī's contrast is the diagnostic: *Iḥsān* combined with awe on one side, evil deeds combined with a sense of security on the other. If your religious life has become entirely comfortable, that is worth noticing.

**Compete — upward.** Ayah 61 does not ask you to stop racing. It asks you to change the finish line.

passages.title: Hearts oblivious until the torment seizes them
passages.tafsir:
This passage moves from a statement about Allah's justice to a portrait of hearts that cannot receive the Qur'an, to the moment punishment seizes the comfortable, to the charge sheet that explains it. Ibn Kathir titles his treatment of these ayat "The Justice of Allah and the Frivolity of the Idolators" — those two things, side by side, are the passage.

The order runs: **justice → obliviousness → seizure → the door shut → the reason**. Ayah 62 settles the fairness of the arrangement; ayat 63–67 then trace the disbelievers and idolaters of Quraysh from their covered hearts, through the moment the punishment grips them and they scream, to the sins that Ibn Kathir calls the greatest of their sins — turning back on their heels from the recited revelation, proud over the sanctuary, spending their nights in tales and foul talk.

## Ayah 62 — the ground rules before the verdict

Ibn Kathir reads this ayah as Allah telling us of **His justice towards His servants in this world**: He does not task any person except according to his capacity — that is, He does not burden any soul with more than it can bear. Before a single accusation is made, the fairness of the arrangement is settled. Nobody in this passage is condemned for failing at something beyond them.

Then the reckoning: on the Day of Resurrection He will call them to account for their deeds, which He has recorded in **a written Book from which nothing is omitted**. The phrase *kitābun yanṭiqu bi'l-ḥaqq* — "a Record which speaks the truth" — Ibn Kathir explains simply as the Book of deeds. Notice the verb: the record does not merely exist, it *speaks*.

And *wa hum lā yuẓlamūn* — "and they will not be wronged." Ibn Kathir draws out something easy to skim past. It means **nothing will be omitted from their record of good deeds**; as for evil deeds, "He will forgive and overlook many of them in the case of His believing servants." So the exactness cuts one way only. Every good is preserved in full; the evil of a believing servant meets pardon and overlooking. Justice with no wrong done — and generosity layered on top of it.

## Ayah 63 — *bal*: hearts under water

Then comes the turn. *Bal* — "Nay, but…" — and Ibn Kathir names precisely who is now in view: Allah speaks here "denouncing the disbelievers and idolators of the Quraysh."

**The key word is *ghamrah*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the root: lexically *ghamrah* means **deep water where a person may drown or be overwhelmed**, and for that reason the word is also used for a covering, something that conceals an object. In this ayah, Maʿārif says, it means "the ignorance in which the hearts of the infidels are submerged and hidden so that no light can reach them."

Sit with that image. The Qur'an is not describing people who heard the message and weighed it. It is describing a heart at the bottom of deep water, where no light arrives. Ibn Kathir gives the same sense from another angle: their hearts are covered "because of negligence and misguidance." Negligence (*ghaflah*) is the water; nothing dramatic is required to drown, only enough distraction, deep enough.

And covered from *what*? Ibn Kathir: **"from this" means the Qur'an which Allah revealed to His Messenger ﷺ.** The very thing that would have saved them is the one thing that cannot get through.

## "And they have other deeds besides that"

The second half of ayah 63 is read in two ways in the sources, and both are worth carrying.

**First reading — more sin on top of the sin.** Al-Ḥakam bin Abān narrated from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that "they have other deeds" means **evil deeds apart from that, i.e. Shirk** (associating partners with Allah), and *hum lahā ʿāmilūn*, "which they are doing," means which they will inevitably do. Ibn Kathir notes this was also narrated from Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and others. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same sense: in addition to their rejection of the Oneness of Allah and their denial of the true faith, they engage themselves in other sinful deeds. A submerged heart does not stay still; it keeps producing.

**Second reading — the decree runs its course.** Others said the meaning is that it was decreed that they would do evil deeds, and they will inevitably do them before they die, "so that the word of punishment may be justified against them." Ibn Kathir reports a similar view from Muqātil bin Ḥayyān, as-Suddī and ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam, and comments: **"This is a clear and appropriate meaning."**

In support of it he recalls the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, in the wording Ibn Kathir quotes: *"By Him besides Whom there is no other deity, a man may do the deeds of the people of Paradise until there is no more than a forearm's length between him and it, then the decree will overtake him and he will do the deeds of the people of Hell, then he will enter Hell…"*

Note that the ayah still speaks of these people as the ones acting — *hum lahā ʿāmilūn*, "which they are doing." And the sober note the hadith leaves is worth carrying home: a forearm's length is not a safe distance.

## Ayah 64 — *until* the comfortable are seized

*Ḥattā idhā* — "until when." The sentence has been waiting since *bal*, and now the clock runs out.

**Who gets seized: *mutrafīhim*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces *mutraf* to *taraf*, meaning **comfort and prosperity** — "their affluent ones." The punishment described here, Maʿārif explains, descends upon the unbelievers **whether rich or poor**; the rich are specially mentioned **because they are the ones who make adequate arrangements to protect themselves against disasters and misfortunes** — and when retribution comes from Allah, they find themselves totally helpless. The people with the most insulation are named precisely because their insulation is the illusion being punctured.

**What the punishment refers to.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that according to Sayyidunā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) it is an allusion to **the crushing defeat which the infidels of Makkah suffered at the hands of the Muslims in the Battle of Badr**. Some others say the reference is to **the severe famine which afflicted the people of Makkah**, when they were forced to eat dead animals and cats and dogs — a famine which Maʿārif describes as the result of the curse laid on them by the Prophet ﷺ.

Maʿārif gives the background: although the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions used to remain patient in the face of ill-treatment from the idolaters and never complained, when their suffering and torment became unbearable he ﷺ invoked divine punishment upon them in these words, which Maʿārif cites to al-Bukhārī and Muslim (through Qurṭubī and Maẓharī):

> "O Lord! Let thy punishment descend hard on the tribe of Mudar and make their land barren like the land of Yusuf."

This is the ayah's warning made concrete: within their own lifetimes, men who thought themselves untouchable were reduced to eating carrion.

**The sound they make: *yajʾarūn*.** Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase — **they scream their calls for help.** The contrast is the point. These are the *mutrafūn*, the people of soft living, and the ayah leaves them screaming.

Ibn Kathir sets two other ayat alongside it. From Sūrat al-Muzzammil: *"And leave Me Alone (to deal) with the beliers, those who are in possession of good things of life. And give them respite for a little while. Verily, with Us are fetters, and a raging Fire"* (73:11–12) — the same pairing of luxury now and shackles later. And from Ṣād: *"How many a generation have We destroyed before them! And they cried out when there was no longer time for escape"* (38:3).

## Ayah 65 — the door closes

*"Invoke not loudly this day! Certainly you shall not be helped by Us."*

Ibn Kathir's comment is stark: **no one is going to save you from what has happened to you, whether you scream aloud or remain silent. There is no escape and no way out. It is inevitable: the punishment will surely come to you.**

Screaming and silence become the same thing. Whatever the noise was meant to accomplish, it accomplishes nothing at that point — and the reader hearing this ayah is, mercifully, still on the near side of that moment.

## Ayat 66–67 — the charge sheet

Ibn Kathir introduces these two ayat with a phrase worth pausing over: "Then Allah mentions **the greatest of their sins**." What follows is their conduct towards revelation itself.

**"Indeed My Ayat used to be recited to you, but you used to turn back on your heels."** Ibn Kathir: "when you were called, you refused and resisted." Picture the gesture the Arabic describes — *tankiṣūn ʿalā aʿqābikum*, retreating backwards, heels first. Not a rejection after examination; a refusal to face the thing at all. Ibn Kathir pairs it with Sūrah Ghāfir: *"This is because, when Allah Alone was invoked, you disbelieved, but when partners were joined to Him, you believed! So the judgment is only with Allah, the Most High, the Most Great!"* (40:12). Tawḥīd — the affirmation that Allah alone is worshipped — was the specific trigger for the retreat.

Ayah 67 then names three causes of that aversion. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays them out as three, and it is the clearest map of the ayah. (Maʿārif notes that its explanation rests on a second possible rendering of the ayah: "but you used to turn back on your heels, being over-proud of it (the Ḥaram being looked after by you), indulging in tales at night, talking nonsense.")

**1. Pride — *mustakbirīna bihi*.** According to many commentators, Maʿārif notes, "it" refers to the Ḥaram, the sanctuary of Makkah; the Ḥaram is not specifically mentioned in the ayah, but the very close association of the Quraysh of Makkah with it, and their great pride in that association, renders a specific mention unnecessary. The first factor, then, was their pride in being the neighbours and care-takers of the Ḥaram. Ibn Kathir says the same: this is the arrogant pride the Quraysh felt because **they believed themselves to be the guardians of the Kaʿbah — "when in fact this was not the case."** That last clause is the sharpest line in the passage: they held the association and had, in Ibn Kathir's judgement, no real claim to the office.

**2. Frivolity — *sāmiran*.** Maʿārif opens this word beautifully. *Sāmir* derives from *samar*, meaning **"moonlit night"**. It was a favourite pastime with the Arabs to assemble on moonlit nights and tell stories; from that, *samar* came to be used for stories and anecdotes, and *sāmir* for a raconteur. The word is singular in form but, Maʿārif notes, is often used as a plural, as here — a whole company of them. This is the second reason for their repudiation of the divine communications: **preoccupation with petty and frivolous matters such as story-telling, and a lack of interest in the divine messages.** The revelation did not lose an argument. It lost an evening, repeatedly.

**3. Foul talk — *tahjurūn*.** Maʿārif derives it from *hujr* (with a ḍammah on the *hāʾ*), meaning **"to speak nonsense, to use foul language"** — and gives the third reason: they used to indulge in foolish talk and pass unseemly remarks about the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir renders the phrase "In pride, talking evil about it by night."

**The night gatherings at the Kaʿbah.** An-Nasāʾī, in his Tafsīr of this ayah in his *Sunan*, brings a narration from Ibn ʿAbbās (Aḥmad bin Sulaymān ← ʿUbaydullāh ← Isrāʾīl ← ʿAbd al-Aʿlā ← Saʿīd bin Jubayr ← Ibn ʿAbbās) in which Ibn ʿAbbās said that **talking by late night became disapproved of when this ayah was revealed**. He described the scene: they boasted about the Kaʿbah and said, *"We are its people who stay up talking at night."* They used to boast and stay up and talk at night around the Kaʿbah — "they did not use it for the proper purpose, and so in effect they had abandoned it."

That is the verdict in one sentence: they were beside the sanctuary and had, in effect, abandoned it.

## Living it

**Night hours have weight.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this under the heading "Ban on story-telling after ʿIshāʾ prayers." Story-telling was a favourite pastime among the Arabs and the Persians since ancient times — not only time-wasting but the cause of certain evils. With a view to discouraging the practice, Maʿārif states, the Prophet ﷺ **enjoined upon the Muslims not to sleep before the ʿIshāʾ prayer**. The reasoning Maʿārif gives: all daily human activity ended with the ʿIshāʾ prayer, which should arguably be a person's last action of the day and which might even atone for his lapses during it. But if after ʿIshāʾ he sits down to while away his time on silly and frivolous tales, he makes himself guilty of encouraging falsehood, backbiting and other sins — and he goes to bed late, rises late, and misses his early morning prayers. Maʿārif adds, citing Qurṭubī, that Sayyidunā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) used to admonish people he found listening to stories after ʿIshāʾ, and advised them to go early to bed so that by Allah's grace they might be enabled to pray in the middle of the night.

**Audit what you are proud of.** The Quraysh had the closest association in Arabia with the Sacred House, and ayah 67 turns that association into the first item on the indictment. Ibn Kathir's "when in fact this was not the case," and Ibn ʿAbbās's "they did not use it for the proper purpose," both say the same thing: proximity to a sacred place is not a shield when the recited ayat are being backed away from.

**Watch for water, not for walls.** *Ghamrah* is not opposition; it is submersion — deep water where the light cannot reach. The heart in this passage is not lost because it fought the Qur'an, but because it was too far under to receive it. The remedy runs the other way: come up towards the recitation, deliberately, before the negligence gets any deeper. Ayah 62 has already settled the terms — the standard is your capacity, and nothing will be omitted from your record of good deeds.

passages.title: Why they reject: a chain of rhetorical questions
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is doing

After a long stretch of the sūrah describing the signs of Allah in creation and the fate of earlier nations, the address turns and becomes a cross-examination. Allah puts to the Quraysh a chain of questions, each beginning with "or…", that walks through the excuses a person could offer for rejecting this message — and closes each door in turn. What holds ayat 68–74 together is that structure: a list of possible reasons for disbelief, every one of them ruled out, until nothing is left standing except the real reason, which is not an argument at all but a distaste for the truth.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayat 68, 69 and 70 as setting out five possible causes that might have kept the unbelievers from accepting the faith brought by the Prophet ﷺ, and as rebutting each one. On one side every argument the deniers advanced is demolished; on the other side compelling grounds and irrefutable evidence are laid out, enough to convince any right-minded person. Their persistence, therefore, cannot be explained by reasoning. It is, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the result of unreasoning hatred and blind prejudice against the Prophet ﷺ — rooted, in the end, in a love of undisputed power and a reluctance to share it with anyone else.

## Every excuse, closed in turn (68–70)

The first question is aimed at how they *read*: **afalam yaddabbarū al-qawl** — "Have they not pondered over the Word?" **Al-qawl**, "the Word", is the Qur'an, and **yaddabbarū** is to ponder it, to contemplate its meaning. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is here denouncing the idolaters for not understanding the Qur'an or contemplating its meaning, and for turning away from it — and this despite the fact that they were the ones addressed specifically in a Book which Allah did not reveal to any Messenger more perfect and noble.

Qatadah's comment on this ayah is one of the sharpest lines in the whole passage: "Because, by Allah, if the people had pondered the meaning and understood it properly, they would have found in the Qur'an a deterrent to disobeying Allah. But they only paid attention to the Ayat which are not entirely clear, and so they were destroyed because of that."

Notice the failure he identifies. It is not that they never touched the Qur'an. It is that they went at it in the wrong way — paying attention to the verses that are not entirely clear, the places where an objection could be lodged, instead of sitting with the meaning until it became a deterrent against disobedience. Reading the Qur'an as material for argument rather than as a summons ruined them.

The second half of ayah 68 turns to a different objection: **has something come to them that never came to their forefathers?** Ibn Kathir takes this as an argument from the other direction. No Book and no warner had come to their forefathers, who had died during the Jahiliyyah, the age of ignorance before Islam. So this revelation is not an intrusion; it is a blessing bestowed on this particular people. What those upon whom the blessing had been bestowed *should* have done, Ibn Kathir says, is accept it, give thanks for it, and try to understand it and act in accordance with it night and day — as was done by the wise ones among them who became Muslim and followed the Messenger ﷺ, may Allah be pleased with them.

So the novelty of the message is no defect, and the fact that some of their own people saw this and submitted shows the excuse to be hollow: the same evidence was in front of everyone.

Then the next question — **"Or is it that they did not recognize their Messenger, so they deny him?"** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out how much force this carries. A genuine ground for hesitation would exist if the message had been brought by an outsider, a stranger with whose character and antecedents they were unfamiliar. That plea was simply not available here. He ﷺ belonged to the noble family of Quraysh, was born in Makkah, grew up among them, and his whole life was like an open book before them. Before prophethood was bestowed on him, the unbelievers of Makkah themselves knew him as **Amīn** (trustworthy) and **Sādiq** (truthful), and nobody had ever raised an accusing finger against his character or general behaviour. They could not plead ignorance of the man or of his family connections.

Ibn Kathir presses the same point — do they not recognize Muhammad ﷺ and the honesty, trustworthiness and good character with which he grew up among them? Can they deny that or argue against it? — and then recalls three occasions on which that reputation was stated before a foreign court and stood unchallenged.

Ja'far bin Abi Talib said to An-Najashi, the king of Ethiopia: "O King, Allah has sent to us a Messenger whose lineage, honesty and trustworthiness are known to us."
