The credential offered to a foreign king was not a marvel but a reputation. Al-Mughirah bin Shu'bah said something similar to the deputy of Kisra when he wanted to challenge him. And when the Byzantine ruler Heraclius asked Abu Sufyan Sakhr bin Harb and his companions about the characteristics, lineage, honesty and trustworthiness of the Prophet ﷺ — men who, as Ibn Kathir notes, were still disbelievers and had not yet become Muslim — they could only tell the truth and admit that he was indeed noble and truthful.

That is the weight of ayah 69. The testimony that clears him comes from the mouths of those who had not accepted him. A person whom you yourself named "the trustworthy" does not suddenly become a liar about the one subject on which lying would cost him everything.

The next question quotes them: **am yaqūlūna bihī jinnah** — "or do they say there is madness in him?" Ibn Kathir notes that this is a narration of what the Quraysh actually said about the Prophet ﷺ. They said he was making up the Qur'an by himself, or that he was crazy and did not know what he was saying. The two charges do not sit together: a man cannot both be the deliberate author of the Qur'an and be unaware of what he is uttering.

And Ibn Kathir tells us something further about what lay beneath the words: their hearts did not believe what their tongues said. They knew that what they were saying about the Qur'an was falsehood, for it had come to them from the Words of Allah and could not be resisted or rejected. So Allah challenged them — and all the people of the world — to produce something like it if they could. They could not, and would never be able to do so.

## Aversion, not evidence (70–71)

Then comes the verdict, and it is the hinge of the whole passage: **"Nay, but he brought them Al-Haqq, but most of them are averse to the truth."** After the chain of excuses, the diagnosis. The obstacle was never a missing proof. The word the ayah uses of them is **kārihūn** — those who find a thing distasteful, who are averse to it. They did not lack evidence; they disliked where the evidence led.

This is the passage's most searching question for anyone who reads it. When we resist something we know to be true, is the resistance really about the argument, or is the argument a service we are performing for a dislike we already had?

Ayah 71 takes that dislike and holds it up against the universe: **"And if Al-Haqq had followed their desires, verily, the heavens and the earth, and whosoever is therein would have been corrupted!"** Mujahid, Abu Salih and As-Suddi said that **Al-Haqq** here is Allah, may He be glorified. Ibn Kathir explains the sense: if Allah had responded to the desires in their hearts and prescribed things accordingly, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted — because their desires are themselves corrupt, and because they are inconsistent with one another.

He then draws in what Allah says about them elsewhere to show how badly human wanting would govern a world. They complained, "Why is not this Qur'an sent down to some great man of the two towns?" (43:31) — they wanted prophethood awarded by social rank — and were answered, "Is it they who would portion out the mercy of your Lord?" (43:32). Elsewhere: "Say: If you possessed the treasure of the mercy of my Lord, then you would surely hold back for fear of spending it" (17:100). And: "Or have they a share in the dominion? Then in that case they would not give mankind even a Naqīr" (4:53) — a naqīr being a thing of almost no value at all. All of this, Ibn Kathir concludes, goes to show how incapable mankind is and how divergent and inconsistent their ideas and desires are. Only Allah, may He be glorified, is Perfect in all His attributes, words, actions, laws, power and control of His creation. There is no true deity but He, and no Lord besides Him.

So the ayah is not floating a live possibility. It holds up something that will not be, in order to show its absurdity: a creation run on our preferences would tear itself apart, because our preferences do not even agree with each other.

And then the ayah answers the whole chain of excuses at once: **"Nay, We have brought them their reminder, but they turn away from their reminder."** The *dhikr*, Ibn Kathir says, is the Qur'an. And it is called *theirs* — their own reminder. They are not turning away from a stranger's property. They are turning away from what belonged to them.

## Nothing to gain, and a straight road (72–74)

One excuse remains, the most worldly and in some ways the most common: perhaps he is in it for the money. **"Or is it that you ask them for some kharj?"** Al-Hasan glossed *kharj* as "a reward"; Qatadah as "some payment". Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: you are not asking them for any wages or payment or anything at all for calling them to right guidance — rather you are hoping for a great reward from Allah.

He gathers the Qur'an's other statements of the same principle: "Say: Whatever wage I might have asked of you is yours. My wage is from Allah only" (34:47); "Say: No wage do I ask of you for this, nor am I one of the pretenders" (38:86); "Say: No reward do I ask of you for this except to be kind to me for my kinship with you" (42:23). And the man who came running from the farthest part of the town, calling to his people: "O my people! Obey the Messengers. Obey those who ask no wages of you, and who are rightly guided" (36:20–21). That man, with no elaborate argument to offer, reasoned from exactly the sign this ayah points to — a caller who wants nothing from you is a caller worth hearing.

The ayah's own answer is beautiful in its economy: **"But the recompense of your Lord is better, and He is the Best of those who give sustenance."** The very thing they might imagine him chasing is turned around: yes, there is a payment, but it is with Allah, and it is better — and the One who pays it is **khayr ar-rāziqīn**, the Best of those who provide. A believer's provision is not at risk because he refuses to sell the truth.

With the excuses dismantled, Allah states the conclusion in two clean lines. **"And certainly, you call them to the straight path"** (73). The Arabic carries a double emphasis — *wa innaka la-tadʿūhum* — as if to settle beyond dispute that the direction of the call is not in question. **"And verily, those who believe not in the Hereafter are indeed deviating far astray from the path"** (74); which means, Ibn Kathir says, that they have gone astray and deviated.

Set the two ayat side by side and the geometry is complete: the road he ﷺ calls to is straight, and those who reject the Hereafter are the ones who have veered off it. Ayah 74 also names what the swerve is tied to — disbelief in the Hereafter. Deny the reckoning and there is little to hold a person to a straight line, because there is no destination that makes the direction matter.

## Living it

**Read the Qur'an the way Qatadah describes.** The failure of ayah 68 is a reading failure. If we go to the Qur'an to find leverage for opinions we already hold — dwelling on the less clear verses while the plain commands go unread — we can spend a lifetime with the Book and be untouched by it. Following Qatadah, the aim of pondering is to stay with a passage until it becomes a deterrent between us and disobedience.

**Test the source of your resistance.** Ayah 70 says the problem was aversion, not evidence. When a ruling or a truth grates on us, the honest question is not only "what is the counter-argument?" but "would I prefer this to be false?"

**Stop asking the truth to bend.** Ayah 71 puts human desires on the throne for a moment and shows the result: a corrupted heavens and earth. Our wants are inconsistent even with each other. The peace of submission comes precisely from the fact that the law we live under is Allah's — Perfect in His attributes, words, actions, laws, power and control of His creation — and not the shifting average of what human beings happen to want.

**Carry the message without a price tag.** Ayah 72 makes wanting nothing the credential of a true caller. Whoever invites others to Allah while looking to them for money, standing, loyalty or applause has taken part of his wage in advance — and the recompense of your Lord is better, from the Best of those who give sustenance.

passages.title: Mercy and affliction fail to humble them
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close Allah's long indictment of the Makkan idolaters with a hard truth about the human heart: neither kindness nor hardship will move a heart that has decided not to be moved. Ayah 75 says that if Allah lifted their suffering they would go straight back to their blind defiance; ayah 76 reports that He had in fact already gripped them with hardship and they still did not humble themselves; ayah 77 shows where that road ends — a gate of severe punishment opened upon them, and all hope draining away. Mercy is tried, affliction is tried, and both are refused. That is what holds the passage together.

## Where the passage sits in the sūrah

The ayat immediately before this have been dismantling the excuses of the Quraysh one by one. Ibn Kathir summarises the thrust of them: Allah denounces the idolaters for not pondering the Qur'an and for turning away from it, though they were the ones specifically addressed in it; they could not honestly claim not to recognise their Messenger ﷺ, whose honesty, trustworthiness and good character they had watched him grow up with; and he was asking them for no payment at all. So by the time we reach ayah 75, every external reason for their rejection has been stripped away. What remains is the will itself.

## Ayah 75 — the mercy that would change nothing

"And though We had mercy on them and removed the distress which is on them, still they would obstinately persist in their transgression, wandering blindly."

Ibn Kathir reads this as a statement about their sheer stubbornness in disbelief: even if Allah had removed the calamity from them and made them understand the Qur'an, they still would not have followed it — they would still have persisted in their disbelief and stubborn transgression.

Ibn Kathir sets two other ayat beside this one. "Had Allah known of any good in them, He would indeed have made them listen; and even if He had made them listen, they would but have turned away with aversion" (8:23). And the scene at the Fire, where they cry, "Would that we were but sent back! Then we would not deny the Ayat of our Lord, and we would be of the believers!" — to which the answer comes, "But if they were returned, they would certainly revert to that which they were forbidden" (6:27–29). The pattern is identical: the missing ingredient was never information, or relief, or even a second chance. It was willingness.

**A point of ʿaqīdah in the word "if."** Ibn Kathir pauses here on something worth understanding carefully. "This has to do with the knowledge of Allah. He knows about something that will not happen, but if it were to happen, He knows how it would be." And Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Everything that is implied in the word *law* (if) is something that will never happen." So the ayah is not describing an experiment Allah ran; it is telling us what Allah knows about a possibility that never came to pass. That is a real teaching about His knowledge: it encompasses not only what is and what will be, but how things would have turned out had they been otherwise. Nothing is hidden from Him, not even the unrealised.

## Ayah 76 — and the famine that actually happened

Then ayah 76 moves from the hypothetical to the historical: "And indeed We seized them with punishment, but they humbled not themselves to their Lord, nor did they invoke with submission to Him."

Ibn Kathir explains "We seized them with punishment" as: *We tried and tested them with difficulties and calamities.* This is affliction as a summons — hardship sent so that a person turns back. And Ibn Kathir's comment on the rest of the ayah is that it did not deter them from their disbelief and resistance; rather they persisted in their sin and misguidance. On "nor did they invoke with submission to Him," his gloss is simply: *they did not call on Him.*

Here the sources give us the episode behind the ayah, and it is the single most illuminating thing in this passage.

Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, 'O Muhammad, I ask you by Allah and by the ties of kinship between us, we have been reduced to eating camel hair and blood.' Then Allah revealed, *And indeed We seized them with punishment, but they humbled not themselves.*" This was also recorded by An-Nasā'ī. And Ibn Kathir adds that the basis of this hadith is in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, where it says that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when he could not make any headway with the Quraysh, prayed against them and said: **"O Allah, help me against them by sending on them seven years (of famine) like the seven (years of drought) of Yūsuf."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazharī, fills in the scene. The famine came, and the people of Makkah were reduced to such straits that they were forced to eat dead animals. At last Abū Sufyān presented himself before the Prophet ﷺ in Madīnah and said: "I appeal you in the name of Allah, did you not say that you had been sent by Him as mercy for the whole world?" The Prophet ﷺ replied, "Yes I did, and what I said is true also." Then Abū Sufyān said: "You killed the leaders of your clan with sword at the battle of Badr and now you are killing those who still survive with starvation. Pray to Allah, I beseech you, to remove this curse from over our heads." The Prophet ﷺ then prayed to Allah to forgive the people of Makkah and deliver them from the agony of hunger, and his prayer was granted forthwith. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this ayah was revealed on that occasion and refers to that incident.

Sit with what that means. The man who came pleading was the man who had met him in arms at Badr — as his own words admit. When hunger broke them, they came not to their idols but to him ﷺ, and they came invoking the very mercy they had denied: that he was sent as a mercy for the whole world. He did not bargain. He prayed for them, and the prayer was answered at once. And then, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, once they had been delivered from their sufferings through the Prophet's ﷺ intercession on their behalf, they still did not humble themselves before Allah but persisted in idolatry and unbelief. That is exactly the behaviour ayah 75 had described in advance: relieve their distress and they will return to their blindness. Ayah 76 records that it happened.

**Two things they refused to do.** The ayah denies them both an inward humbling before their Lord and any calling upon Him — as Ibn Kathir puts it, "they did not call on Him." They begged a man for relief while refusing to beg their Lord. Ibn Kathir places alongside it the reproach in Sūrat al-Anʿām: "When Our torment reached them, why then did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hardened" (6:43). Hardship is meant to soften; on a hard heart, it only sets the shape more firmly.

## The gate that opens (ayah 77)

"Until, when We open for them the gate of severe punishment, then lo! they will be plunged in despair."

Ibn Kathir: when the command of Allah reaches them and the Hour comes to them suddenly, and they are overtaken by the punishment of Allah which they were not expecting, "then they will despair of any ease and goodness, and all their hopes will disappear."

Feel the contrast the passage builds. The famine was painful but survivable, and it ended — a prayer was made and it was lifted. What ayah 77 describes has no such exit: Ibn Kathir's words are that every hope disappears. Every earlier hardship was mercy in the shape of a warning. This one is not a warning; it is the thing the warnings were about.

## Living it

**Read your hardships as summons, not just misfortune.** Ibn Kathir's gloss on ayah 76 — that being "seized with punishment" means being tried and tested with difficulties and calamities — turns the ayah into a mirror. The question the passage puts to a believer in hardship is not "why me" but: *has this humbled me before my Lord, and has it made me call on Him?* The Quraysh failed at exactly those two points, and the ayah names both.

**Beware of a faith that lives only in the crisis.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the pattern precisely: when the unbelievers are chastised for their sins they plead to Allah and to the Prophet ﷺ for mercy, and when Allah, who is Merciful, relieves their suffering, they return to their evil practices and wicked deeds. The test of the famine was not whether they would ask — hunger makes everyone ask. It was what they would do afterwards.

**Do not measure a person's guidance by their circumstances.** Ayah 75 warns that comfort restored is not repentance, and ayah 76 warns that suffering imposed is not repentance either. A soul is not guided by its conditions but by its response to them — and only Allah, whose knowledge reaches even to how the never-happened would have gone, knows those hearts fully.

**And notice the Prophet ﷺ in the middle of it.** The man who came asking him for relief was, by his own admission, from the side that had fought him at Badr. He prayed for them anyway, and his prayer was granted forthwith. That is what "sent as a mercy for the whole world" looked like in practice, on the day it was put to him to his face.

passages.title: Hearing, sight and hearts — yet little thanks
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are a short, concentrated reminder of what Allah has given us and what He alone controls — the faculties inside us, the earth we are spread across, and the life, death and turning of night and day around us. They hold together as one argument: the evidence a person needs is either lodged in his own body or passing over his head every twenty-four hours, and the passage closes by asking why that evidence is not being used.

## The hardness this reminder is addressed to

Just before these ayat, Allah says, *"And indeed We seized them with punishment, but they humbled not themselves to their Lord, nor did they invoke with submission to Him"* (76). Ibn Kathir explains that being seized with punishment here means that Allah tried and tested them with difficulties and calamities — and that this did not deter them from their disbelief and resistance; rather they persisted in their sin and misguidance. They did not humble themselves, and they did not call on Him. He sets beside it Allah's words about an earlier people: *"When Our torment reached them, why then did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hardened"* (6:43).

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said that Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "O Muhammad, I ask you by Allah and by the ties of kinship between us, we have been reduced to eating camel hair and blood," and that Allah then revealed this ayah. Ibn Kathir notes that this was also recorded by An-Nasa'i, and that the basis of the hadith is in the Two Sahihs, where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, unable to make any headway with the Quraysh, prayed against them: *"O Allah, help me against them sending on them seven years (of famine) like the seven (years of drought) of Yusuf."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, citing Mazhari, that when Abu Sufyan came to the Prophet ﷺ at Madinah and begged him to pray for relief, he ﷺ prayed for the people of Makkah to be forgiven and delivered from the agony of hunger — and his prayer was granted at once. And still, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, they did not humble themselves before Allah but persisted in idolatry and unbelief.

Hunger did not soften them; deliverance did not soften them. So in ayah 78 the argument moves inward — away from famine and rescue, to the equipment they are using at that very moment to reject the message.

## Ayah 78: the three faculties

*"He is the One Who created for you hearing, sight, and intellect."*

The commentary here falls under the heading "A Reminder of the Blessings of Allah and His Immense Power," and Ibn Kathir's reading is precise: Allah mentions His blessings to His servants, in that He has given them hearing, sight and understanding **through which they come to know things and draw lessons from them** — the signs which attest to the Oneness of Allah and indicate that He is the One Who does what He wills and chooses what He wants.

Two things are worth pausing on there.

**First, these faculties are described as gifts.** The ayah does not say we have hearing and sight; it says He *created* them — and created them **for you**. Nobody arranged for his own ears or his own eyes. They arrived, fully working, before we were capable of asking for them, and they were put at our disposal.

**Second, they are given for a purpose, and the purpose is knowledge.** On Ibn Kathir's reading these three are not merely channels of pleasure or convenience; they are the means by which a person comes to know things and *draws lessons* from them. Hearing is how the message reaches you. Sight is how the signs of creation reach you. And the third faculty — rendered in the translation as "intellect," and by Ibn Kathir as "hearts" and as "understanding" — is where what you heard and saw is weighed and turned into conviction. Take away any one of the three and the chain from evidence to faith is broken. That is exactly the tragedy of the people being described: the equipment was fully intact; the chain was broken by choice.

**"Little thanks you give."** Ibn Kathir glosses this simply: how little you thank Allah for the blessings He has given you. He puts alongside it Allah's words in Surah Yusuf, *"And most of mankind will not believe even if you desire it eagerly"* (12:103) — a striking pairing, because it sets ingratitude and disbelief side by side as one condition. To be given hearing and not listen to the truth, to be given eyes and not read the signs, to be given a heart and not use it to conclude anything — that is the ingratitude, whatever the tongue happens to be saying.

## Ayah 79: scattered across the earth, gathered back to Him

*"And He is the One Who has dispersed you all over the earth, and to Him you shall be gathered back."*

Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah telling us about His great power and overwhelming authority: He is the One Who originated creation and put people in all parts of the earth, **with their different nations, languages and characteristics.**

Then comes the counter-movement in the second half of the ayah: **to Him you shall be gathered back.** Ibn Kathir spells out what the gathering means — on the Day of Resurrection He will gather them all together, the first of them and the last, at a fixed time on a day appointed, and none will be left out, young or old, male or female, noble or insignificant, but all will be brought back as they were originally created.

The two halves of the ayah are the whole argument in miniature. The same power that placed humanity across every part of the earth, in all its variety of nation and language, is not going to be defeated by the task of collecting it again. And note the last phrase of Ibn Kathir's gloss — *brought back as they were originally created*. The resurrection is not an unheard-of act; it is a repetition of one already performed on every person listening.

## Ayah 80: life, death, and the turning of the days

*"And He is the One Who gives life and causes death, and His is the alternation of night and day. Will you not then understand?"*

**"He gives life and causes death."** Ibn Kathir gives this an unmistakably eschatological reading: it means He will bring the scattered bones back to life, and cause the death of the nations. So this is not only a statement about individual birth and dying — it is about whole peoples raised and whole peoples ended, on a scale no human agency touches.

**"And His is the alternation of night and day."** Ibn Kathir explains: by His command night and day are subjugated, each of them following the other and never departing from that pattern. He cites Allah's words, *"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day"* (36:40).

There is deep comfort and deep warning in that. The alternation is the most ordinary thing in a human life — it happens whether we notice it or not — and it is precisely its unfailing regularity that makes it a sign. Night has never once jumped its turn. A person who can watch that happen every day of his life and conclude nothing from it has a faculty of understanding lying unused.

**"Will you not then understand?"** Ibn Kathir turns the question into its full force: do you not have minds that tell you of the Almighty, the All-Knowing, to Whom all things are subjugated, Who has power over all things and to Whom all things submit?

This is where the passage lands, and it is why ayah 78 had to come first. Ayah 78 named the faculty of understanding as a gift. Ayah 80 asks whether you are going to use it. The gift and the demand are two ends of the same rope: *little thanks you give* in ayah 78 is answered by *will you not then understand?* in ayah 80 — the thanks being asked for here is not primarily a word on the tongue but the honest working of the faculties He installed.

## What was said in reply

The ayat that follow show what this appeal was up against. Ibn Kathir tells us that Allah then speaks of those who denied the resurrection, who were like the disbelievers before them: *"Nay, but they say the like of what the men of old said. They said: 'When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we be resurrected indeed?'"* They thought it very unlikely, Ibn Kathir says, that this could happen after they had disintegrated into nothing. He sets beside this Allah's words in Surah Ya-Sin: *"And he puts forth for Us a parable, and forgets his own creation. He says: 'Who will give life to these bones after they are rotten and have become dust?' Say: 'He will give life to them Who created them for the first time! And He is the All-Knower of every creation!'"* (36:77–79).

**And forgets his own creation** — that is the exact hinge our three ayat turn on. The man arguing that resurrection is impossible is arguing with ears, eyes and a mind he did not make, standing on an earth he was placed upon, under a sky whose turning he cannot delay by a moment.

## Living it

**Use the faculties for what they were given for.** Ibn Kathir defines hearing, sight and heart as the means by which we come to know things and draw lessons from them. So the honest question at the end of a day is not only *what did I see and hear* but *what did I draw from it*. Faculties employed only for consumption, never for reflection, are being used below their design.

**Understand what gratitude means here.** "Little thanks you give" is not, in Ibn Kathir's reading, a complaint about missing pleasantries; it is about how little we thank Allah for what He has given. Gratitude for hearing is listening to the truth. Gratitude for sight is looking at the signs. Gratitude for the heart is letting the conclusion land. And the ayah is bracing precisely because even the believer, measuring his thanks against three faculties working freely every waking second, will find the phrase fits him more closely than he would like.

**Let the ordinary be evidence.** The night that follows the day, the day that follows the night — Ibn Kathir says they never depart from that pattern, by Allah's command. The passage asks us to treat the utterly routine as the loudest sign rather than the most invisible one.

**Remember that hardship alone does not soften anyone.** The people in ayah 76 were seized with difficulties and were not humbled. What Allah names as missing is not the experience but the turning: humbling oneself to the Lord, and calling upon Him. When difficulty comes, that is the response the Qur'an is asking for.

passages.title: The old denial of resurrection, repeated
passages.tafsir:
Allah has just laid out an argument that ought to have settled the matter: He gave you hearing, eyes and hearts; He created you on the earth and to Him you shall be gathered back; He gives life and causes death, and His is the alternation of night and day — *"Will you not then understand?"* Ayat 81–83 give their answer. It is not an argument at all. It is a quotation. They repeat what those before them had already said: dust and bones cannot be raised, and the whole thing is only tales of the ancients.

What holds these three ayat together is that single point. Ibn Kathir introduces them by saying that Allah "tells us about those who denied the resurrection, who were like the disbelievers who came before them" — and he adds, of their closing sneer, that "this was said by those who learned it from the books and disputes of the ancients." The denial is presented as something received rather than something reasoned.

## The run-up: an argument they refused to answer

To feel the force of ayah 81 you have to hear what comes immediately before it.

Ibn Kathir explains ayah 76, "And indeed We seized them with punishment," to mean: *We tried and tested them with difficulties and calamities.* And the response? "But they humbled not themselves to their Lord, nor did they invoke with submission to Him" — which, he says, means the hardship "did not deter them from their disbelief and resistance, rather they persisted in their sin and misguidance." They did not call on Him. Ibn Kathir places this alongside another ayah: *"When Our torment reached them, why then did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hardened"* (6:43).

Then ayah 77 warns of the gate that will one day be opened on them — "then lo! they will be plunged in despair." Ibn Kathir describes that moment: when the command of Allah reaches them and the Hour comes to them suddenly, and they are overtaken by a punishment they were not expecting, "then they will despair of any ease and goodness, and all their hopes will disappear."

Ayat 78–80 then change register completely, from warning to kindness. Ibn Kathir titles this section *A Reminder of the Blessings of Allah and His Immense Power*. Allah mentions that He has given them hearing, sight and understanding — the faculties, Ibn Kathir says, "through which they come to know things and draw lessons from them, the signs which attest to the Oneness of Allah and indicate that He is the One Who does what He wills and chooses what He wants." The instruments of denial were themselves gifts. "Little thanks you give," ayah 78 closes — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, how little you thank Allah for the blessings He has given you.

Ayah 79 widens the frame. Ibn Kathir describes Allah's great power and overwhelming authority: He originated creation and put people in all parts of the earth, "with their different nations, languages and characteristics," and on the Day of Resurrection He will gather them all together, "the first of them and the last, at a fixed time on a day appointed, and none will be left out, young or old, male or female, noble or insignificant, but all will be brought back as they were originally created." Ayah 80 seals it: He gives life and causes death — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, "He will bring the scattered bones back to life and cause the death of the nations" — and His is the alternation of night and day, by His command subjugated, "each of them following the other and never departing from that pattern," as in *"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day"* (36:40).

The question that ends ayah 80, *"Will you not then understand?"*, Ibn Kathir unpacks as: do you not have minds that tell you of the Almighty, the All-Knowing, to Whom all things are subjugated, Who has power over all things and to Whom all things submit?

That is the question ayah 81 answers.

## What the famine of Makkah shows about a hardened heart

Ibn Kathir preserves a report that grounds ayah 76 in a specific episode. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said: "Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, 'O Muhammad, I ask you by Allah and by the ties of kinship between us, we have been reduced to eating camel hair and blood.'" Then Allah revealed, *"And indeed We seized them with punishment, but they humbled not themselves."* Ibn Kathir adds that this was also recorded by An-Nasa'i, and that the basis of this hadith is in the Two Sahihs, where it says that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed against the Quraysh when he could not make any headway with them, and said: *"O Allah, help me against them sending on them seven years (of famine) like the seven (years of drought) of Yusuf."*

Maarif ul Quran tells the encounter more fully, citing Mazhari. The Prophet ﷺ had prayed to Allah to punish the people of Makkah with famine, and as a result they were reduced to great straits and were forced to eat dead animals. At last Abu Sufyan presented himself before the Prophet ﷺ at Madinah and said, "I appeal you in the name of Allah, did you not say that you had been sent by Him as mercy for the whole world?" The Prophet ﷺ replied, "Yes I did, and what I said is true also." Then Abu Sufyan said, "You killed the leaders of your clan with sword at the battle of Badr and now you are killing those who still survive with starvation. Pray to Allah, I beseech you, to remove this curse from over our heads." The Prophet ﷺ then prayed to Allah to forgive the people of Makkah and deliver them from the agony of hunger, and his prayer was granted forthwith.

Maarif ul Quran draws out exactly why this belongs here. The pattern set in the preceding verse was that when the unbelievers are subjected to chastisement for their sins they plead to Allah and to the Prophet ﷺ for mercy, and when Allah, who is Merciful, relieves their suffering, they return to their evil practices and wicked deeds. This episode is that pattern in the flesh: they were delivered from their sufferings as a result of the intercession of the Prophet ﷺ on their behalf, and still "they did not humble themselves before Allah but persisted in idolatry and unbelief."

Hold that beside ayat 81–83 and the shape of the passage becomes clear. Hunger did not move them. Rescue did not move them. Hearing, sight and understanding did not move them. What, then, do they say when the Resurrection is put to them? Not a new thought. The old one.

## Ayah 81: "Nay, but they say the like of what the men of old said"

Ibn Kathir renders the opening of the ayah as "Nay, but they say the like of what the men of old said." The bundle's translation puts it just as plainly: *"But they ˹just˺ say what their predecessors said."*

The weight of the ayah falls on that likeness, and Ibn Kathir's own introduction to the passage places it there: Allah "tells us about those who denied the resurrection, who were like the disbelievers who came before them." What is being reported is not a fresh objection but a repeated one. Whatever the men of old said, these people are saying the like of it.

## Ayah 82: dust and bones

Now their actual words: *"When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we be resurrected indeed?"*

Ibn Kathir's comment is one line, and it carries the whole psychology of the verse: **"They thought it very unlikely that this would happen after they had disintegrated into nothing."**

That is the shape of their case. It is not a proof; it is an estimate of likelihood made from the graveside. They looked at *dust and bones* — تُرَابًا وَعِظَامًا — and judged that nothing could follow. Because it seemed impossible to them, they treated it as impossible.

Ibn Kathir shows that this is a settled habit of speech among the Qur'an's opponents by placing two other passages beside it. The first is from Surah An-Nazi'at: *"'Even after we are crumbled bones?' They say: 'It would in that case be a return with loss!' But it will be only a single Zajrah — when behold, they find themselves on the surface of the earth alive after their death"* (79:11–14). A *Zajrah* is a single shout or cry. They imagine an impossible reassembly; the reply is that it takes one shout, and they are standing on the surface of the earth, alive.

The second is from Surah Ya-Sin: *"Does not man see that We have created him from a Nutfah? Yet behold, he stands forth as an open opponent. And he puts forth for Us a parable, and forgets his own creation. He says: 'Who will give life to these bones after they are rotten and have become dust?' Say: 'He will give life to them Who created them for the first time! And He is the All-Knower of every creation!'"* (36:77–79). A *Nutfah* is the drop of fluid from which a human being is first formed.

That passage names the flaw exactly: **he forgets his own creation.** The one arguing that bones cannot live has already been brought into being once, from a drop. His own body is the answer to his own question. And this is why ayat 78–80 came first: hearing, sight and hearts, people spread across the earth in all their nations and languages, the giving of life and death, the unbroken turning of night into day. Every one of those, in Ibn Kathir's reading, is the same power, already at work, in plain view.

## Ayah 83: "This is only the tales of the ancients"

*"Verily, this we have been promised — we and our fathers before! This is only the tales of the ancients!"*

Ibn Kathir gives the sense of it plainly: **"It is impossible that we could be brought back."** Underneath the rhetoric, that is what the sentence amounts to. They mention that the promise had been made to them and to their fathers before them, and they conclude from it not that the message is consistent but that it is a story.

Ibn Kathir then adds a second observation about the speakers themselves: "This was said by those who learned it from the books and disputes of the ancients." Their dismissal, on this reading, was itself picked up from elsewhere — from older books and older arguments — which sits closely with ayah 81, where what they say is "the like of what the men of old said."

Ibn Kathir treats this denial as of a piece with the rejection recorded in Surah An-Nazi'at and Surah Ya-Sin, quoted above: the same refusal, in different mouths, met each time by the reminder that the One who created the first time can create again.

## Living it

**Ask where your objections came from.** What the ayah records about these people is not that they had a difficulty but that they repeated one — "the like of what the men of old said," learned, as Ibn Kathir notes, "from the books and disputes of the ancients." Whatever we believe or doubt about the Hereafter, it is worth asking honestly whether we arrived at it or simply received it — from a family, a culture, a mood of the age. A borrowed conviction is no safer than a borrowed denial.

**Do not let what you can imagine set the limits of what is possible.** Their whole case rested, in Ibn Kathir's words, on thinking it "very unlikely that this would happen after they had disintegrated into nothing." The reply he brings from Surah Ya-Sin does not argue about likelihood at all: *"He will give life to them Who created them for the first time."* What we cannot picture tells us something about ourselves, not about the power of Allah.

**Use the faculties for what they were given for.** Ayah 78 names hearing, eyes and hearts as blessings, and Ibn Kathir says they are how a person comes "to know things and draw lessons from them, the signs which attest to the Oneness of Allah" — and then the ayah adds: *little thanks you give.* The deepest ingratitude is not failing to say thank you; it is taking the instrument of understanding and turning it against the One who gave it.

**Notice that relief is a test too.** Maarif ul Quran's account of the famine describes people who begged, who were delivered through the intercession of the Prophet ﷺ, and who then "did not humble themselves before Allah but persisted in idolatry and unbelief." Hardship softens most hearts for a while. The real question is what we do in the week after the hardship lifts.

**Live toward an appointed day.** They dismissed the promise as an old tale. Ibn Kathir, explaining the very blessings they were ignoring, describes what is actually coming: on the Day of Resurrection Allah "will gather them all together, the first of them and the last, at a fixed time on a day appointed, and none will be left out, young or old, male or female, noble or insignificant, but all will be brought back as they were originally created." That is the appointment the passage asks us to keep in view.

passages.title: They concede the Lord of all — then invent His partners
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** Allah instructs His Prophet ﷺ to put three questions to the idolaters — questions whose answers they already know and will not deny — and each time their own answer is turned back on them as an argument against the others they worship. The unit runs as a single cross-examination: three questions (ayat 84, 86, 88), three admissions from their own mouths (85, 87, 89), three escalating rebukes, then a verdict (90) and a closing declaration of Allah's absolute oneness (91–92).

## The hidden fault line: they admitted His Lordship, yet worshipped others

Ibn Kathir heads this section with the whole point: *The Idolators Believe in Tawhid Ar-Rububiyyah, Which Requires Them to Believe in Tawhid Al-Uluhiyyah*. Two Arabic terms worth pausing over, glossed from what Ibn Kathir himself says here:

- ***Rububiyyah*** is Allah's **Lordship** — that He "is One and that He is independent in His creation, control, dominion."
- ***Uluhiyyah*** is His being the only true **object of worship**, so that, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "none should be worshipped except Him Alone, with no partner or associate."

The idolaters, Ibn Kathir explains, already held the first: they "admit His Lordship, that He has no partner in Lordship." But despite this, he says, "they still attributed partners in divinity to Him, and worshipped others besides Him even though they recognized the fact that those whom they worshipped could not create anything, did not own anything, nor do they have any control over anything." Their objects of worship were never rivals in creation.

So why worship them at all? Ibn Kathir gives their own stated reason from elsewhere in the Qur'an: they "believed that these creatures could bring them closer to Allah" — *"We worship them only that they may bring us near to Allah"* (39:3). They were middlemen: brokers of access, not creators.

That is exactly the fracture these ayat press on. If He alone made it, owns it, and runs it, then He alone deserves worship. Belief in the Lord that stops short of worshipping Him alone is not half a religion; it is a self-contradiction. Ibn Kathir states it directly: the fact that He is One and independent in His creation, control and dominion guides one to realize that there is no true deity except Him and that none should be worshipped except Him alone, with no partner or associate.

## Three questions, each one wider than the last

Notice the deliberate widening of the frame.

**Ayah 84 — the earth.** *"Whose is the earth and whosoever is therein? If you know!"* Ibn Kathir unpacks it as: "Who is the Owner Who has created it and whatever is in it of animals, plants, fruits and all other kinds of creation?" This is the question anyone can answer by looking down at the ground under their feet.

**Ayah 86 — the heavens and the Throne.** *"Who is Lord of the seven heavens, and Lord of the Great Throne?"* Ibn Kathir reads this as: "Who is the Creator of the higher realm with its planets, lights and angels who submit to Him in all regions and in all directions? Who is the Lord of the Great Throne, which is the highest of all created things?"

**Ayah 88 — sovereignty over everything, with no shelter from Him.** *"In Whose Hand is the sovereignty of everything? And He protects, while against Whom there is no protector, if you know?"* Now it is not ownership of a region but total, unopposable sovereignty.

The questions climb from the ground, to the heavens, to sovereignty itself — and at every level the answer they give is the same word: *Allah*.

**"They will say…"** Each answer in 85, 87 and 89 is introduced with *sa-yaqūlūn* — "they **will** say." The reply is stated before they give it. Ibn Kathir's comment on each is the same: "they will admit that this belongs to Allah Alone with no partner or associate." They are not being asked to learn something new; they are being made to hear what they already concede.

## The three rebukes escalate

The closing line of each round tightens the pressure:

1. **Ayah 85 — *"Will you not then remember?"*** (*a-fa-lā tadhakkarūn*). A call to the mind. Ibn Kathir supplies what is to be remembered: "that none should be worshipped except the Creator and Provider."
2. **Ayah 87 — *"Will you not then have Taqwa?"*** (*a-fa-lā tattaqūn*). Now a call to the heart. Ibn Kathir glosses it entirely in terms of fear of consequence: since you admit that He is the Lord of the heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne, "will you not fear His punishment for worshipping others besides Him and associating others with Him?"
3. **Ayah 89 — *"How then are you deceived and turn away from the truth?"*** Ibn Kathir turns the question on their own reasoning: "how can your minds accept the idea of worshipping others besides Him when you recognize and acknowledge that?"

Reminder, then fear, then bewilderment at the mind itself. When a person knows the truth, concedes it out loud, and still walks the other way, the question is no longer *what do you know* but *how can you possibly hold both*.

## "In Whose Hand is the sovereignty of everything" (ayah 88)

Two expressions here deserve unhurried attention.

**Sovereignty in His Hand.** The Arabic word rendered "sovereignty" here is *malakūt*; the ayah is also translated "In Whose Hands is the authority over all things." Ibn Kathir's comment is compact: "sovereignty is in His Hands." He then illustrates the kind of control meant with another ayah — *"There is not a moving creature but He has grasp of its forelock"* (11:56) — which he glosses simply: "He has control over it."

Rather than philosophising about the Hand, Ibn Kathir reaches for how the Prophet ﷺ spoke. He reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say, *"By the One in Whose hand is my soul,"* and that when he swore an oath he would say, *"By the One Who turns over (controls) the hearts."* (Ibn Kathir gives these words of the Prophet ﷺ here without naming a collection, so no collection is named for them.) Then Ibn Kathir sums up: "He, may He be glorified, is the Creator, the Sovereign, the Controller." The believer's response is awe: my very soul, and the turning of my own heart, are in His hand.

**"And He protects, while against Whom there is no protector."** Ibn Kathir opens this with a piece of Arabian social life that makes the phrase vivid: "Among the Arabs, if a leader announced his protection to a person, no one could go against him in that, yet no one could offer protection against that leader." Now scale that up without limit: Allah "is the greatest Master, and there is none greater than Him. His is the power to create and to command, and none can overturn or oppose His ruling. What He wills happens, and what He does not, will not happen."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, draws out the practical edge: "Allah alone can deliver a person from pain and suffering as He wills, but there is none who can save a person from divine punishment." This holds in this world, "because nobody can stop Allah from rewarding virtuous people nor can anyone protect someone whom He chooses to punish. And the same is true of the Hereafter also."

Ibn Kathir adds a further consequence of that unopposable sovereignty: *"He cannot be questioned about what He does, while they will be questioned"* (21:23). He cannot be asked about what He does, Ibn Kathir says, "because of His greatness, Pride, overwhelming power, wisdom and justice" — while all of His creation will be asked about what they did: *"So, by your Lord, We shall certainly call all of them to account. For all that they used to do"* (15:92–93).

## The Great Throne (ayah 86)

Ayah 86 names *al-ʿArsh al-ʿAẓīm*, which Ibn Kathir renders "the Mighty Throne" and describes as "the highest of all created things." He notices a companion phrase at the end of this very surah — *"the Lord of the Supreme Throne!"* (23:116) — "meaning splendid and magnificent." Read together, he says, "The Throne combines the features of height and vastness with splendor and magnificence." He then mentions, as something that has been said rather than as an assertion, that "it is made of red rubies," and quotes Ibn Masʿud: "There is no night or day with your Lord, and the light of the Throne is from the Light of His Face."

The point of naming the Throne in a cross-examination about false worship is scale. They were being invited to weigh their intermediaries against the Lord of the highest of all created things.

## The verdict: "Nay, but We have brought them the truth, and verily, they are liars" (ayah 90)

After three admissions, the questioning stops and the sentence is passed. The **truth** that has come to them, Ibn Kathir specifies, is "the declaration that there is no god worthy of worship besides Allah, and the establishment of clear, definitive and sound proof to that effect."

And **"they are liars"** — in what, exactly? Ibn Kathir: "in their worship of others alongside Allah when they have no evidence for doing so." He ties this to the surah's own closing warning: *"And whoever invokes, besides Allah, any other god, of whom he has no proof; then his reckoning is only with his Lord. Surely, the disbelievers will not be successful"* (23:117). Notice where the indictment falls: on the **absence of proof**. The truth arrived with "clear, definitive and sound proof"; the alternative arrived with none.

So what were they actually standing on? Ibn Kathir answers: "The idolators have no evidence for what they are doing, which has led them into lies and misguidance. Rather they are following their forefathers and predecessors who were confused and ignorant" — *"We found our fathers following a certain way and religion, and we will indeed follow their footsteps."* (43:23)

## Why there cannot be two (ayat 91–92)

Ayah 91 is the passage's theological climax, and it closes off two doors at once: *"No son (or offspring) did Allah beget, nor is there any god along with Him."* Ibn Kathir: Allah "declares Himself to be above having any child or partner in dominion, control and worship."

Then comes the reasoning, given in the ayah itself in two clauses:

**"Then each god would have taken away what he had created."** If a plurality of deities were decreed, Ibn Kathir explains, "each of them would have exclusive control over whatever he had created, so there would never be any order in the universe. But what we see is that the universe is ordered and cohesive, with the upper and lower realms connected to one another in the most perfect fashion." He supports this with *"you can see no fault in the creation of the Most Gracious"* (67:3). A seamless cosmos is the fingerprint of a single Maker.

**"And some would have tried to overcome others."** Rival deities would inevitably compete: "each of them would try to subdue the other with enmity, and one would prevail over the other." Ibn Kathir notes that this "has been mentioned by the scholars of ʿIlm-ul-Kalam" — the scholars of theological argument — "who discussed it using the evidence of mutual resistance or counteraction." The argument runs like this: suppose two or more creators, one willing a body to move and the other willing it to stay still. If neither could achieve what he wanted, both would be incapable — "but the One Whose existence is essential [i.e., Allah] cannot be incapable." Both wills cannot be fulfilled, "because of the conflict." And if one prevails and not the other, "the one who prevails will be the one whose existence is essential (i.e., the true deity) and the one who is prevailed over will be merely possible (i.e., he is not divine), because it is not befitting for the one to be defeated whose existence is essential." Every branch collapses back to One. The ayah is the proof; this is the scholars' unpacking of it, reported by Ibn Kathir as theirs.

**"Glorified be Allah above all that they attribute to Him!"** — Ibn Kathir: "high above all that the stubborn wrongdoers say when they claim that He has a son or partner."

**Ayah 92 — "All-Knower of the unseen and the seen! Exalted be He over all that they associate as partners to Him."** The passage began by asking them what they *know*; it ends by naming the One who knows absolutely — He "knows what is hidden from His creatures and what they see." Their knowledge was partial and they still buried it; His is total. And the final word of the unit is *fa-taʿālā*: "sanctified and glorified and exalted be He," says Ibn Kathir, "above all that the wrongdoers and liars say."

## Living it

**Test where your trust actually goes.** They failed not for lack of information but in what they attached themselves to: they admitted His Lordship and worshipped others anyway. Ask what you turn to first in fear or need, and whether the one you actually rely on is the One you say owns the earth and the heavens.

**Beware the middleman instinct.** Their whole rationale was that these would "bring us near to Allah" (39:3) — yet by their own admission those beings "could not create anything, did not own anything, nor do they have any control over anything," and there was no proof for turning to them at all.

**Demand evidence of yourself.** Ayat 90 and 117 both make the absence of proof the indictment. "This is what my family always did" is precisely the reasoning condemned in 43:23 — following "forefathers and predecessors who were confused and ignorant." A practice you cannot trace to sound evidence deserves a hard second look.

**Let knowledge move you.** The three closing rebukes ask for remembrance, then fear of His punishment, then an honest reckoning with how the mind can hold a truth and act against it. Knowing that Allah is Lord is only worth what it changes.

**Take refuge where refuge is real.** He protects, and against Him there is no protector. Qurtubi's note holds in both worlds: none can stop Allah rewarding the virtuous, and none can shield whom He chooses to punish. That single sentence, honestly absorbed, resolves both fear of creation and complacency about the Hereafter.

passages.title: The Prophet's prayers and refuge from devils
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah al-Muʾminūn closes by placing four short supplications on the tongue of the Prophet ﷺ — two about the punishment that may fall on a rejecting people, and two about the enemy no one can see. What binds them into one unit is that each of the four carries the same address, **Rabbi**, "My Lord": after a long sūrah of argument with the deniers, Allah turns His Messenger ﷺ away from debating them and towards asking. Ibn Kathir titles the whole passage in one breath: *the command to call on Allah when calamity strikes, to repel evil with that which is better, and to seek refuge with Allah.*

## Ayat 93–94: a prayer for the day the punishment lands

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is commanding His Prophet ﷺ to make this supplication *when calamity strikes*. The sense of ayah 93 running into ayah 94 is: "if You punish them while I am witnessing that, then do not cause me to be one of them."

Note what is *not* being asked. He is not asking that the punishment be shown to him, nor that it be withheld. The condition is left open — "**if** You show me" — and the request attaches only to where he will be standing when it comes: *do not place me among the wrongdoing people.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up why that request is not redundant. The Qur'an is full of warnings of punishment to the unbelievers; while the punishment is a certainty on the Day of Judgment, it is possible for it to be sent in this world too, even in the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ. And when Allah's wrath descends on a people, it is not confined to the sinners alone — sometimes it afflicts virtuous people as well, who may not be punished in the Hereafter, and may even be compensated with extra rewards for the undeserved suffering they bore in this world. The Qur'an itself warns of this: *"And beware of a punishment which shall not fall on the wrongdoers only"* (8:25). So the prayer of ayah 94 is a prayer to be removed from that company.

**Why teach this to a Prophet at all?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question: this supplication was suggested to the Prophet ﷺ despite his being, in its words, impeccable and infallible. Its answer is that the intention is that he should at all times remember Allah and beseech His mercy — and thereby increase his own reward in the Hereafter. Duʿāʼ here is not an emergency measure for the unsure; it is the posture of the most secure servant there has ever been.

Ibn Kathir sets alongside these ayat a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad and At-Tirmidhi, who graded it Sahih, in which the Prophet ﷺ prayed:

> "If You want to test people, then take me to You [cause me to die] without having to undergo the test."

The same instinct, in the same shape: not "spare them", not "spare me the sight", but *let me not be inside it.*

## Ayah 95: "We are indeed able"

*"And indeed We are able to show you that with which We have threatened them."* Ibn Kathir gives the meaning plainly: if We willed, We could show you the punishment and test that We will send upon them.

There is a tension a careful reader may feel here, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses it. Allah has said, out of regard for His Messenger ﷺ, *"And Allah is not to send punishment upon them while you are in their midst"* (8:33). How then can ayah 95 hold out the possibility of him witnessing it? Some commentators, it reports, answer that what that promise rules out is the punishment of the entire community while he lives among them; the punishment of some selected persons in special circumstances does not negate it. And in fact it happened: the disbelievers of Makkah were punished through famine, and through their defeat at the hands of the Muslims at the Battle of Badr — both in the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ. Ayah 95's emphasis, "We *do* have the power to show you what We threatened them with", was not a hypothetical.

So ayat 93–95 sit together as a single exchange. The servant asks to be kept clear of a people's ruin; the Lord answers that the ruin is entirely within His power to bring.

## Ayah 96: repel evil with what is better

Then, says Ibn Kathir, Allah shows His Prophet ﷺ **the best way to behave when mixing with people**: to treat kindly the one who treats him badly — so as to soften his heart, turn his enmity to friendship, and turn his hatred to love.

That is a striking pivot. The passage has just been speaking of a punishment that could fall at any moment on the very people abusing him. The instruction that follows is not to withdraw from them or curse them, but to answer their worst with something *better*.

Ibn Kathir connects it to the fuller statement of the same principle elsewhere in the Qur'an:

> *"Repel (the evil) with one which is better, then verily he, between whom and you there was enmity, (will become) as though he was a close friend. But none is granted it except those who are patient"* (41:34–35).

He draws two things out of that. First, on *"except those who are patient"* — nobody will be helped or inspired to follow this advice or attain this quality except them; and by "patient" is meant those who patiently bear people's insults and bad treatment, and deal with those people in a good manner while they are on the receiving end of that bad treatment. Notice that the patience is not endured first and rewarded later; it is exercised *while* the abuse continues. Second, on *"and none is granted it except the owner of the great portion"* — Ibn Kathir says that great portion is in this world **and** in the Hereafter. The one who can absorb an insult and return kindness has been handed something valuable, not deprived of something.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens the scope of the command: Allah instructs the Prophet ﷺ to counter evil with good, oppression with justice, and cruelty with mercy — virtues Allah taught him directly, and which are generally observed in settling affairs among the Muslims. It then notes, as its reading, that these instructions were later repealed so far as the infidels and unbelievers were concerned, when Allah permitted the Muslims to embark on jihād; and yet even then the humane limits remained in force. Muslims were forbidden to kill women and children, or the priests who did not engage in battle against them; mutilating the bodies of enemy dead was strictly forbidden.

And here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the link that explains why ayah 97 follows ayah 96 at all: it is for this very reason that the Prophet ﷺ is instructed in the next ayah to seek protection from Shayṭān's evil suggestions — *even on the battlefield*, where he may arouse emotions that push a person to act against ethics. The command to restrain oneself and the prayer for help in restraining oneself arrive together, because the second is what makes the first survivable.

**"We know well what they claim."** The closing words of ayah 96 — rendered by Ibn Kathir as *"We are best-acquainted with the things they utter"* — are the quiet consolation underneath the command. You are not being asked to pretend the slander is not happening. It is heard, precisely, by the One whose hearing matters.

## Ayat 97–98: refuge from what cannot be handled with kindness

Now comes the turn that makes this passage so instructive. Ayah 96 taught a *strategy* for human enemies: disarm them with good treatment. Ayah 97 addresses a different enemy, and Ibn Kathir states exactly why the strategy changes:

> Allah commanded him to seek refuge with Him from the Shayāṭīn, **because no trick could help you against them and you cannot protect yourself by being kind to them.**

A human adversary has a heart that can soften. Shayṭān has no such heart. There is nothing to negotiate with, no goodwill to build, no favour that will buy peace. Against him there is exactly one move, and it is not a technique but a flight: *aʿūdhu bika* — "I seek refuge **in You**." The believer does not out-manoeuvre this enemy; he runs to Allah from him.

**The word *hamazāt*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the key term. *Hamz* — the root behind *hamazāt*, which it renders as "strokes" — means "to push, to press", and is sometimes also used to mean "to make a call from behind". Hold those two senses together and you have an unnervingly accurate picture of how temptation actually works: not a reasoned proposal you can refute, but a shove — a pressure at your back — or a voice calling from behind you, from where you cannot see it, so that you turn without quite knowing why you turned.

Ibn Kathir notes that this seeking of refuge (*istiʿādhah*) was the Prophet's ﷺ own practice — he used to say: *"I seek refuge with Allah, the All-Hearing, All-Seeing, from the accursed Shayāṭīn, from his whisperings, evil suggestions and insinuations."* Three distinct kinds of interference, each named separately. (Ibn Kathir reports this as the Prophet's ﷺ habitual wording without naming a collection here.)

**"Lest they come near me."** Ayah 98 is not a repetition of ayah 97; it asks for something further. Ayah 97 seeks refuge from what the devils *do*; ayah 98 seeks refuge from their *presence*. Ibn Kathir explains *"lest they should come near me"* as meaning: in any issue of my life. Not merely "do not let them succeed", but "do not let them be in the room."

From that he draws a very practical consequence: **we are commanded to mention Allah at the beginning of any undertaking**, in order to ward off the Shayāṭīn — at the time of eating, at the time of intimacy between spouses, when slaughtering animals for food, and so on. Ayah 98 is the theology; saying the name of Allah at the threshold of an act is the daily practice that flows from it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, on the authority of Qurtubi, that according to a hadith in the Sahih of Muslim the Prophet ﷺ said that Shayṭān meddles in all human affairs and tempts people to do evil deeds — and that **this prayer is the best protection** against those attempts. That is why ayah 98 says "in any issue of my life": the interference reaches everywhere, so the refuge must cover everything.

## From the Sunnah: how this prayer was used

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls ayat 97–98 a very comprehensive prayer, often invoked for protection from the guile and mischief of Shayṭān, and reports that the Prophet ﷺ urged the Muslims to recite it frequently for one named purpose: **to avoid sudden bursts of rage**, which are brought about by Shayṭān's promptings and which cause people to lose self-control. Read that against ayah 96 and the whole passage clicks into place: the man commanded to answer evil with good is given the exact prayer that protects the temper which would otherwise make that impossible.

It also relates that this prayer is very effective in repelling other assaults of the Shayāṭīn and the jinn, and gives an incident: Sayyidnā Khālid (may Allah be pleased with him) suffered from insomnia, and the Prophet ﷺ suggested that he recite the following before going to bed:

> "I seek refuge with Allah's Perfect Words from Allah's wrath and His punishment, and from the evils of His slaves, and from the strokes of the Shayāṭīn and from that they come to me."

He did as advised, and was soon cured. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates this without naming a collection.)

Ibn Kathir adds one more supplication of the Prophet ﷺ, recorded by Abu Dawud:

> "O Allah, I seek refuge with You from old age, I seek refuge with You from being crushed or drowned, and I seek refuge with You from being assaulted by the Shayāṭīn at the time of death."

That last clause is the most sobering line in the whole passage. The concern of ayah 98 — *do not let them come near me* — extends to the one moment when a person is least able to defend himself and has the most to lose.

## Living it

Read as a single instruction, these six ayat lay out a complete posture for a believer surrounded by hostility:

**Ask not to be counted with the wrongdoers.** Since a punishment sent on a people need not confine itself to the guilty (8:25, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites), the safety worth praying for is not immunity from hardship but not being *of* them — in company, in character, in verdict.

**Leave the timing to Allah.** Ayah 95 settles the question of power: He does have the power to show it, and He could do so if He willed. Nothing in that is the believer's business to arrange.

**Answer the person in front of you with something better.** Not because the insult was harmless, but because — as Ibn Kathir puts it — good treatment is what softens a heart and turns enmity to friendship. And because, per 41:34–35, only the patient are ever granted this, and being granted it is itself the great portion, in this world and the Hereafter.

**Recognise the enemy you cannot be kind to.** Kindness works on people. Against the Shayāṭīn, Ibn Kathir says plainly, no trick and no kindness will help — only refuge with Allah.

**Say the prayer, and say it often.** *Rabbi aʿūdhu bika min hamazāti-sh-shayāṭīn, wa aʿūdhu bika Rabbi an yaḥḍurūn.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the Prophet's ﷺ urging that the Muslims recite it frequently, so as to be guarded against the sudden rage that Shayṭān's promptings stir up. And note what it finally asks for: something wider than victory over temptation. It asks that the tempter not be present at all.

passages.title: From the barrier of death to the Trumpet and the scales
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** These six ayat follow a single soul from the edge of death, through the waiting that follows it, to the blast of the Trumpet, the gathering where no relative is of any use, the weighing of deeds, and finally the faces of the ruined in the Fire. What binds them into one unit is a single question: *can I go back and do it differently?* Ayah 99 has the dying man begging for exactly that. Ayah 100 answers in one word — *kallā*, "No!" — and everything after it shows what comes instead of a second chance: a barrier, a Trumpet, and a scale.

## Ayah 99 — the plea at the threshold

Ibn Kathir opens by naming who is speaking here: Allah is telling us what happens "when death approaches one of the disbelievers or one of those who have been negligent with the commands of Allah." The plea is *Rabbi arjiʿūn* — "My Lord, send me back" — and the reason given in ayah 100 is *laʿallī aʿmalu ṣāliḥan fīmā taraktu*, "so that I may do good in that which I have left behind."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the psychology precisely: when death approaches an unbeliever and he *senses* the punishment awaiting him on the Day of Judgement, he wishes to return to this world so that by performing good deeds he may escape the punishment he has richly deserved. The request is not born of love for Allah; it is born of sight. He has seen the bill.

Ibn Kathir gathers the places in the Qur'an where this same plea is made: they will ask to go back at three moments, and at none of them is the prayer answered — when death approaches, as here in ayah 99; on the Day of Resurrection when they are gathered for judgement before the Compeller, as in "Or could we be sent back so that we might do deeds other than those deeds which we used to do?" (7:53) and "Our Lord! We have now seen and heard, so send us back" (32:12); and in the agonies of the punishment of Hell, "Our Lord! Bring us out, we shall do righteous good deeds, not what we used to do" (35:37) — which Allah answers, "Did We not give you lives long enough, so that whosoever would receive admonition could receive it? And the warner came to you." The lifetime already given *was* the answer to the request.

**The two deathbeds.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that Ibn Jarir related, on the authority of Ibn Juraij, that the Prophet ﷺ said that when a good Muslim at the point of death perceives the angels of mercy and the luxuries of Paradise spread out before him, and the angels ask whether he wishes to be sent back to the world, his answer is invariably no — he refuses to return to a place full of woes and misery, and desires only to be taken to Allah's presence. When the same question is put to an unbeliever, his answer is *Rabbi arjiʿūn*: send me back. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives this from Ibn Jarir without naming a hadith collection, so it is passed on here exactly as it stands there.) Two people, the same doorway, opposite answers — because what each can see on the other side is different.

## Ayah 100 — "Kallā": the word that shuts the door

Ibn Kathir notes that *kallā* is "a word that is used to rebuke," and its meaning here is: "No, We will not respond to what he asks for and We will not accept it from him." It is not a considered refusal; it is a rebuke that cuts the sentence off.

Then comes the reason: *innahā kalimatun huwa qāʼiluhā* — "It is but a word that he speaks." Ibn Kathir explains that his asking to go back so he can do righteous deeds "is just talk on his part, it would not be accompanied by any action. If he were to go back, he would not do any righteous good deeds, he is merely lying," as Allah says: "But if they were returned, they would certainly revert to that which they were forbidden. And indeed they are liars" (6:28). The repentance of the dying unbeliever is not repentance at all; it is panic wearing repentance's clothes.

**Qatadah's response.** Ibn Kathir quotes Qatadah: "By Allah, he will not wish to go back to his family and tribe, or to accumulate more of the things of this world or satisfy his desires, but he will wish that he could go back to do acts of obedience to Allah. May Allah have mercy on a man who does that which the disbeliever will wish he had done when he sees the punishment of Hell."

You already know what the dying man will wish he had done — and you are still holding the time he is asking for.

## "And in front of them is a barzakh"

*Wa min warāʼihim barzakhun ilā yawmi yubʿathūn.* Abu Salih and others said that *min warāʼihim*, which reads literally as "behind them," means here "before them" — it lies ahead, waiting.

On the word itself, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *barzakh* means "barrier," and implies anything which intervenes between two conditions or two objects; from this it also came to mean the intervening period between death and the Day of Judgement. Ibn Kathir gathers the early definitions:

- **Mujahid:** al-Barzakh is a barrier between this world and the Hereafter.
- **Muhammad bin Kaʿb:** "Al-Barzakh is what is between this world and the Hereafter, neither they are the people of this world, eating and drinking, nor are they with the people of the Hereafter, being rewarded or punished for their deeds."
- **Abu Sakhr:** al-Barzakh refers to the graves — "They are neither in this world nor the Hereafter, and they will stay there until the Day of Resurrection."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion that answers ayah 99 directly: the wish of the dead unbeliever to be returned to this world is fruitless *because he has reached the barzakh, from which no return is possible*, and a second life cannot be given until the Day of Resurrection, when all the dead will rise.

Ibn Kathir adds that in these words there is a threat to those wrongdoers at the time of death — a threat of the **punishment of the barzakh** — comparable to "In front of them there is Hell" (45:10) and "and in front of him will be a great torment" (14:17). "Until the Day when they will be resurrected" means, he says, that such a one will be punished continually until the Day of Resurrection; he cites the hadith wording, "He will continue to be punished in it," meaning in the earth. (Ibn Kathir quotes this without naming a collection, so it is passed on here as he gives it.)

## Ayah 101 — the Trumpet, and the end of family

Ibn Kathir glosses the opening of the ayah simply: Allah is speaking of the moment "the Trumpet is blown for the Resurrection, and the people rise from their graves."

**Which blast?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a detail. The *ṣūr* (Trumpet) will be sounded twice: at the first, the earth, the skies and every living thing between them will perish; at the second, every dead thing comes back to life — "Then it shall be blown again, and lo! They shall stand beholding" (39:68). The scholars differed over which blast ayah 101 refers to. Ibn Jubayr reports that Ibn ʿAbbas took it to be the first; ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd said it is the second, and ʿAta reports that Ibn ʿAbbas supported this view as well — and this second view is the one adopted in Tafsir Mazhari.

**"No kinship among them that Day."** Ibn Kathir explains that lineage will be of no avail — "a father will not ask about his son or care about him," as in "And no friend will ask a friend about his condition, though they shall be made to see one another" (70:10-11). His gloss: no relative will ask about another relative, "even if he can see him and even if he is carrying a heavy burden." Even if he was the dearest of people to him in this world, he will not care about him or take even the slightest part of his burden from him — "That Day shall a man flee from his brother. And from his mother and his father. And from his wife and his children" (80:34-36).

**Ibn Masʿūd's scene of the herald.** Ibn Kathir quotes Ibn Masʿūd: on the Day of Resurrection Allah will gather the first and the last, then a voice will call out, "Whoever is owed something by another, let him come forth and take it" — and a man will rejoice if he is owed something, or had been mistreated, by his own father or child or wife, even if it is little. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same scene from Ibn Masʿūd with a herald appointed by Allah identifying each person by his name and his father's name, and inviting anyone present who has a claim against him to come forward and receive it; that proclamation, it says, will please everyone — a father with a claim against his son, a wife with a claim against her husband, a sister with a claim against her brother. There are "no ties of kinship" because being someone's father buys nothing there, and being owed by your own son is suddenly welcome news.

**But this is not the whole of humanity.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful: this condition applies to the unbelievers, who in their selfishness will abandon their dear and near relatives. For the believers Allah says, "We shall join their seed with them" (52:21) — the children of good Muslims, if they are believers themselves, will be united with their parents. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said that on the Day of Judgement, when everybody is dry with thirst, Muslim children who had died as minors will come out carrying water from Paradise, and when people ask them for it they will reply that the water is for their parents only, whom they are searching for. (The commentary reports this teaching without naming a collection, so it is given here as it stands.) Believers, it concludes, will help one another and will intercede for one another.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān further reports a hadith related by Ibn ʿAsakir on the authority of ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ said that on the Day of Judgement all relationships arising out of a common ancestry or from marriage ties will be severed except in his own case — and notes that scholars have understood this to mean that all the Muslims of his Ummah are part of his family, since he is the father of the Ummah and his wives are its mothers.

**"Nor will they ask of one another."** Elsewhere the Qur'an says of that Day, "And they advance one upon another, asking each other questions" (37:27). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān resolves this with a report from Ibn ʿAbbas (via Mazhari): in the gathering-place there will be different stations, and the conditions in each station will differ. There will be a time when nobody speaks to anybody; later, when the terror that earlier overwhelmed the gathering abates, people will converse with one another. Both ayat are true, at different hours of that Day.

## Ayat 102-103 — the scales

*Fa-man thaqulat mawāzīnuhu* — "as for the one whose scales are heavy." Ibn Kathir gives Ibn ʿAbbas's reading: this is the one whose good deeds outweigh his bad deeds **even by one**. And *al-muflihūn*, "the successful," means those who have attained victory, been saved from Hell and admitted to Paradise. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "These are the ones who have attained what they wanted and been saved from an evil from which there is no escape." Success here is not simply a prize won; it is a catastrophe escaped.

Conversely, "those whose scales are light" means their evil deeds outweigh their good; they "lose themselves" — Ibn Kathir: "they are doomed and have ended up with the worst deal" — and "in Hell will they abide," staying there forever and never leaving.

**Who exactly is being described?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayat 102-103 as a comparison between *perfect* Muslims and the unbelievers, not as a description of every case.
