For perfect Muslims the pan holding evil deeds will be totally empty; for unbelievers the pan holding good deeds will be empty — "We shall not assign to them any weight" (18:105). As for Muslims who have sinned, whose good and evil deeds will both be placed in the two pans, the Qur'an makes no specific mention of them and is in general silent about the punishment and reward of erring Muslims; Mazhari suggests the reason may be that during the period of revelation the Companions were upright men, generally free from major sins, and one who slipped incidentally repented and was forgiven by Allah.

For that middle case Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns to the ayah about those who "mixed a good deed with another that was evil" (9:102), and reports from Ibn ʿAbbas that if such a person's good deeds exceed his bad by a single deed he goes to Paradise, and if his evil deeds exceed his good by a single deed he goes to Hell — **but a believing Muslim is sent there for purification only**, just as gold and iron and other metals are put through heat to remove their impurities, and as soon as he is purged of his sins he is admitted to Paradise. Ibn ʿAbbas is also reported (Ibn Abi Hatim, Mazhari) as saying that the scale will be so precise and finely tuned that it will be tipped by a grain of rye, and that a man whose good and bad deeds are of exactly equal weight will join the People of al-Aʿrāf and spend a while between heaven and hell awaiting a decision, but ultimately he too will go to Paradise. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that this report deals only with believers who have committed sins and makes no mention of unbelievers.

Held together, the passage keeps both its terror and its mercy: the eternity of ayah 103 belongs to those described there, while a sinning believer's stay, on this report, is for purification and ends in Paradise. Neither half cancels the other.

## How will the deeds be weighed?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports three versions, all derived from hadith, and refuses to force them into one:

1. **The people themselves are weighed.** Believers and unbelievers will be weighed bodily in the scale of justice, and the unbeliever will not be able to tilt it however obese and corpulent he may be — attributed to **Bukhari and Muslim**, quoting Abu Hurayrah.
2. **The scrolls of deeds are weighed** — the scrolls on which the deeds are recorded; **Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and Ibn Hayyan** have taken this version from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar.
3. **The deeds themselves are given substance.** A man's deeds, weightless and intangible in this world, are made solid on the Day of Judgement and placed on the scales — **Tabrani** related this from the Prophet ﷺ on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the full wording of all these hadiths is given in Tafsir Mazhari.

Supporting the third version, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a hadith quoted by ʿAbd al-Razzaq, in his chapter on the merits of knowledge, on the authority of Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi: a man's deeds are brought for weighing and, placed in the pan, fail to tilt it; then something resembling clouds is brought and put in the pan of good deeds, which then weighs down. Asked what lent his pan its weight, the man cannot say — and is told it was the learning he used to impart to other people. Dhahabi, in the same chapter, includes a hadith he heard from ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn that the Prophet ﷺ said that on the Day of Judgement the blood of the martyrs will be weighed against the ink of the scholars — with which they wrote books on the science of religion — and the ink will prove the heavier.

Tafsir Mazhari concludes: it is not wholly inconceivable that a man himself and his deeds may be weighed physically, or that he and his record of deeds may be weighed together — and so there is no inconsistency between these three versions.

## Ayah 104 — the faces

*Talfaḥu wujūhahumu n-nār* — "the Fire will burn their faces." Ibn Kathir sets it beside "and fire will cover their faces" (14:50) and "If only those who disbelieved knew the time when they will not be able to ward off the Fire from their faces, nor from their backs" (21:39). In all three the face is named specifically.

*Wa hum fīhā kāliḥūn* is the harder word. ʿAli bin Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it means **"frowning."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies the physical picture: the word is used of a person whose lips do not meet and leave his teeth fully exposed, which looks very ugly; it is said that the upper lip of the one consigned to the Fire will be drawn up and the lower lip drawn down, so that his teeth remain visible at all times. The passage that opened with a mouth pleading "send me back" closes with a mouth that can no longer close.

## Living it

This passage does not ask for a mood; it asks for a use of time.

- **Treat this life as the answer already given.** The plea of ayah 99 is refused because, as ayah 100 says, it is only a word — one who wasted a first lifetime would, on Allah's own testimony, waste a second (6:28). The only granted version of "send me back" is the day you are living now.
- **Do now what the dying will wish they had done.** Qatadah names what the wish is *not* about: not family, not tribe, not wealth, not desires — only acts of obedience to Allah.
- **Settle your debts and your wrongs here.** If the call in Ibn Masʿūd's account invites every claimant to come forward, this side of the Trumpet is the cheap place to pay.
- **Weigh what you do, not only how much.** A single deed decides the tilt, and a grain of rye moves the scale: nothing good is too small to matter, and nothing sinful is small enough to be safe.
- **Teach what you know.** ʿAbd al-Razzaq's report and Dhahabi's report on ink and blood point the same way — knowledge passed on adds weight to the pan.

passages.title: Dialogue with the damned in the Fire
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a courtroom scene inside the Fire: Allah questions the damned, they plead, and He silences them — and then reveals the real charge against them. What holds ayat 105–111 together is that it is a single conversation, the last one they will ever have, and it ends with the mockers and the mocked trading places forever.

## The scene we walk into

The ayah just before our passage (23:104) leaves the damned **كَالِحُونَ** (*kālihūn*), "disfigured therein." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the word is used for a person whose lips do not meet, leaving his teeth fully exposed — a face that looks profoundly ugly. It is said that the upper lip of a person consigned to the Fire will be drawn up and his lower lip drawn down, so that his teeth remain visible at all times.

Hold that image, because it is the face that speaks in ayat 106–107. The mouths that once curled in laughter at the believers are now fixed open in a permanent grimace. And it is with those mouths that they will make their final request.

## Ayah 105 — the question that closes every door

> "Were My revelations not recited to you, and then you used to deny them?"

Ibn Kathir describes this as a rebuke from Allah to the people of the Fire for the disbelief, sins, unlawful deeds and evil actions they committed, because of which they were doomed. The meaning of the question, he says, is: *I sent Messengers to you, and revealed Books, and cleared the confusion for you, so you have no excuse.*

Notice the shape of it. Allah does not open with a list of their crimes. He opens with a question about **information** — did the message reach you? Because the entire logic of divine justice rests on that point. Ibn Kathir cites three places where the Qur'an makes it explicit:

- *"in order that mankind should have no plea against Allah after the Messengers"* (4:165)
- *"And We never punish until We have sent a Messenger"* (17:15)
- *"Every time a group is cast therein, its keeper will ask: 'Did no warner come to you?'"* … through to *"So, away with the dwellers of the blazing Fire!"* (67:8–11)

So the question in ayah 105 is not Allah seeking information. It is the formal reading of the case file in front of the accused, so that the sentence is seen to be just by everyone present — including the condemned themselves.

## Ayah 106 — the excuse that is really a confession

> "Our Lord! Our ill-fate took hold of us, so we became a misguided people."

The word is **شِقۡوَتُنَا** (*shiqwatunā*) — rendered in the tafsir as "our wretchedness," and in the translation above as "our ill-fate." Their claim is that it *overcame* them.

Ibn Kathir reads their words with precision: the meaning is *evidence has been established against us, but we were so doomed that we could not follow it, so we went astray and were not guided.*

Read that carefully and you will see they concede the very thing ayah 105 asked about. **The evidence reached us.** They do not claim ignorance; they cannot. So they reach instead for the only defence left: it was our wretchedness, something larger than us. It is the oldest excuse there is, and it is offered here in the one place where excuses no longer function. Even in the Fire, the instinct is to explain rather than to own — and Allah lets their own words stand as the record of their guilt.

## Ayah 107 — the bargain they offer

> "Our Lord! Take us out of this. Then if we ever return, we will truly be wrongdoers."

Ibn Kathir explains the request: *send us back to the world, and if we go back to what we used to do before, then we will indeed be wrongdoers who deserve punishment.*

This is not a request for forgiveness. It is a request for a second run at life, with their own guilt offered as collateral. And it echoes a plea recorded elsewhere in the Qur'an — Ibn Kathir cites the people who say *"Now we confess our sins, then is there any way to get out?"*, whose exchange ends with *"So the judgment is only with Allah, the Most High, the Most Great!"* (40:11–12). The lesson he draws is stark: there will be no way out, because they used to associate partners in worship with Allah, whereas the believers worshipped Him alone.

Everything the passage is about turns on that one line. The dividing question was never intellectual sophistication or social standing. It was: whom did you worship?

## Ayah 108 — the last word

> "Be despised in there! Do not ever plead with Me."

**ٱخۡسَـُٔواْ** (*ikhsa'ū*) — Ibn Kathir glosses it: *abide therein, humiliated, despised and scorned.* And **وَلَا تُكَلِّمُونِ** (*wa lā tukallimūn*), "and speak not to Me," means, in his words: *do not ask for this again, for I will not respond to you.*

Al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas about this ayah: **"These are the words of Ar-Rahman when silencing them."**

Pause on that phrase from Ibn ʿAbbas, because it carries a weight the English can barely hold. The name he chooses for Allah at this moment is **Ar-Rahman** — the Most Merciful. He does not describe this as the word of some other, harsher attribute. The conversation is closed by the One whose very name is Mercy.

### How long the silence lasts

Ibn Kathir records that Ibn Abi Hatim reported from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr that the people of the Fire will call on Malik — its keeper — for forty years, and he will not answer them. Then he will respond and tell them only that they are to abide therein. "By Allah," ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr said, "their cries will mean nothing to Malik or to the Lord of Malik."

Then they will turn to their Lord and say the words of ayat 106–107. And Allah will not answer them for a span of time equivalent to **twice the duration of this world**. Only then comes the reply: *"Remain you in it with ignominy! And speak you not to Me!"*

"By Allah," the report continues, "the people will not utter a single word after that. They will merely be in the Fire, sighing in a high tone and a low tone — their voices likened to those of donkeys, which start high and end low."

(This is the statement of the Companion ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr as Ibn Kathir transmits it, not a saying of the Prophet ﷺ.)

### The fifth request

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds two pieces to this. Hasan al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) held that these will be the last words the people of the Fire ever speak; Allah's reply, "Do not speak to Me," ends their speech, and afterwards they will not be able to speak as human beings do but will make animal sounds to one another.

And Baihaqi and others quoted Muhammad Ibn Kaʿb as saying that the Qur'an mentions **five requests** made by the people condemned to the Fire. Four of them received a reply. To the fifth, Allah commanded them not to speak to Him at all. These, then, are the last words they will utter, after which speech itself is taken from them. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits this via Mazhari.)

There is something almost unbearable in that structure. Speech is the faculty that made them human — the faculty they used to argue, to deny, and, as we are about to learn, to laugh. It is precisely the faculty that is confiscated.

## Ayat 109–110 — the charge, at last

Now Allah tells them why. Ibn Kathir says: *Then Allah will remind them of their sins in this world and how they used to make fun of His believing servants and close friends.*

> "Indeed, there was a group of My servants who used to pray, 'Our Lord! We believe, so forgive us and have mercy on us, for You are the best of those who show mercy.' But you took them for a laughing stock, so much so that they made you forget My remembrance, while you used to laugh at them."

Three things are worth slowing down over here.

**First, how Allah describes the believers.** He calls them **عِبَادِي** — *"My servants."* Not "the poor ones you despised," not "the ones who were right." He claims them as His own, in front of the people who humiliated them. Ibn Kathir calls them, in his commentary, "His friends and righteous servants." In ayah 109 Allah then quotes their du'a word for word: *Rabbanā āmannā fa-ghfir lanā wa-rḥamnā wa anta khayr ar-rāḥimīn.* Their prayer was preserved. Every syllable of it was heard, remembered, and is now recited back on the Day when it matters. Notice, too, what the prayer contains: no claim of merit, only faith, a request for forgiveness, and a plea for mercy — the exact opposite of the self-justifying speech of ayah 106.

**Second, what the mockery was actually aimed at.** Ibn Kathir explains ayah 110's *"you took them for a laughing stock"* as meaning: *you made fun of them for calling on Me and praying to Me.* And *"you used to laugh at them"* means: at their deeds and their worship. The joke was never really about the believers as people. It was about prayer itself — about the sight of someone begging Allah for mercy. He connects it to a matching scene: *"Verily, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed. And, whenever they passed by them, used to wink one to another"* (83:29–30) — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, they used to slander them in mockery. The wink is the detail that stings: the private signal, the smirk exchanged over someone's head.

**Third, the strangest line in the passage:** *"so much so that they made you forget My remembrance."* Ibn Kathir's explanation is remarkable — it means *your hatred for them made you forget what I would do to you.*

Think about what that describes. The mockery was not idle entertainment. It became an occupation. Sneering at religious people is itself a kind of absorption; it fills the mind, supplies an identity, and quietly relieves you of ever having to face the question yourself. Contempt for the worshippers crowded out any thought of the reckoning. That is why the wording puts the blame back on the mockers: *they* made *you* forget — the believers did nothing but pray; it was, as Ibn Kathir says, the mockers' own hatred that did the damage. The joke cost them everything, and they never noticed they were paying.

## Ayah 111 — the verdict reversed

> "Today I have indeed rewarded them for their perseverance: they are the ones who have triumphed."

Ibn Kathir reads *"I have rewarded them this Day for their patience"* as: for the harm and mockery **that you inflicted on them**. So the very abuse the disbelievers dished out became the raw material of the believers' reward. Every wink, every laugh at their prayer, was quietly being converted into their rank.

And **ٱلۡفَآئِزُونَ** (*al-fā'izūn*) — "the ones who have triumphed." Ibn Kathir explains Allah's words: *I have caused them to attain the victory of joy, safety, Paradise and salvation from the Fire.*

Look at the two halves of the passage side by side. In ayat 106–108, people who once had status and volume are reduced to a plea that is refused, and then to a sound like a donkey's braying. In ayat 109–111, people who had no voice at all — who were the punchline — are quoted verbatim by Allah and declared the winners. The Day of Judgement does not merely punish and reward. It corrects the record.

## Living it

**Take the du'a of ayah 109 and make it yours.** *"Our Lord! We believe, so forgive us and have mercy on us, and You are the best of those who show mercy."* This is the prayer Allah singles out for approval and quotes back on the Last Day. It costs nothing to memorise and carries everything: faith declared, sin admitted, mercy sought from the One who is best at it.

**Watch what mockery does to you, not just to its target.** Ayah 110 is not primarily about the pain of the person laughed at; it is about what habitual contempt does to the one laughing — Ibn Kathir says their hatred made them forget what Allah would do to them. If sneering at the devout has become part of how you talk or how you see the world, the passage says the real damage is landing on you.

**Do not let the mockery of others move you.** Ayah 111 says plainly that the reward is *for their patience* — and Ibn Kathir specifies: patience under the harm and mockery inflicted on them. If holding to prayer, to modesty, to honesty makes you a joke in some room, that is not an obstacle to your reward; the sources say it is precisely what is being rewarded.

**Stop reaching for the excuse of ayah 106.** *"My wretchedness overcame me. That's just how I am."* It did not work in the Fire and it will not work now. Ayah 109 shows what to say instead — *"Our Lord! We believe, so forgive us and have mercy on us"* — and that prayer is still available to you today. The people in ayah 107 asked for exactly one more chance to go back. You are standing in it.

passages.title: A little while on earth, and not created in vain
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat close Sūrah al-Muʾminūn with a short exchange in the Hereafter — Allah asks the people of the Fire how long they actually stayed on earth, they cannot say, and their own answer becomes the evidence against them. Out of that exchange comes the passage's central claim: you were not created for nothing. The unit holds together because one question ("how long?") opens onto one truth ("you were made for a purpose"), which opens onto one response — the glorification of Allah, the rejection of every rival deity, and finally a prayer that the believer is taught to make while there is still time.

## Where the conversation begins

The exchange in ayah 112 is not the first thing said in that scene. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, citing Mazhari, records that Hasan al-Basri held the words of the people cast into Hell in **وَلَا تُكَلِّمُونِ** (23:108) to be their last words, and that Allah's reply to them will be, "Do not speak to Me." After that, Maʿārif adds, they will not be able to speak as human beings speak, but will make animal sounds to one another. Maʿārif also relays, from Baihaqi and others, that Muhammad Ibn Kaʿb said the Qurʾān mentions five requests made by the people condemned to the Fire: four of them received a reply, and to the fifth Allah commanded that they should not speak to Him at all. Those, he said, are the last words they will utter.

So by the time we reach ayah 112, the pleading is over. The question "How many years did you remain on earth?" is not the opening of a negotiation. It is the closing of the file.

## "How many years?" — ayat 112–114

Ibn Kathir reads the question plainly: **كَمْ لَبِثْتُمْ فِي الْأَرْضِ** means *how long did you stay in this world?* And the question is asked with a precise measure attached: **عَدَدَ سِنِينَ**, "the number of years." Give the figure. Count it out.

They cannot. In ayah 113 they answer: **لَبِثْنَا يَوْمًا أَوْ بَعْضَ يَوْمٍ** — "We stayed a day, or part of a day." Even that they will not commit to; they hedge downward mid-sentence, from a day to a fraction of one. Then they defer the whole matter: **فَاسْأَلِ الْعَادِّينَ**, "ask those who keep account" — which Ibn Kathir explains as *those who keep the records*. A lifetime of appointments, deadlines, calendars and anniversaries, and at the end they cannot produce a number and must point to someone else's ledger.

Allah's reply in ayah 114 does not correct them downward or upward. **إِن لَّبِثْتُمْ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا** — "You stayed not but a little." Ibn Kathir's comment is quietly devastating: *it was only a short time, no matter how you look at it.* However you choose to measure that stay, against what stands on the other side it comes out small. Their instinctive answer was right — they simply drew no conclusion from it while there was still a conclusion worth drawing.

That is what the closing phrase presses on: **لَّوْ أَنَّكُمْ كُنتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ**, "if only you had known." Ibn Kathir unpacks it as: *you would not have preferred the transient to the eternal, and treated yourself in this bad way, and earned the wrath of Allah in this short period.* Notice where he locates the harm — in what they did to *themselves*. And notice the sentence is left hanging: "if only you had known" — the answer clause is never supplied. The reader is left to finish it.

Ibn Kathir does finish it, twice, and it is the warmest thing in the passage: *if they had been patient during their short stay in this world, they would have attained victory just like His pious close friends*; **if you had patiently obeyed Allah and worshipped Him as the believers did, you would have attained victory just as they did.** The believers were not given a longer life or an easier one. They were given the same brief stay — and were patient through it. The difference between the two ends of the Hereafter is a matter of ṣabr over a stretch of time that everyone, in the end, calls short.

## "Did you think We created you in play?" — ayah 115

Ayah 115 turns from the length of the life to its point: **أَفَحَسِبْتُمْ أَنَّمَا خَلَقْنَاكُمْ عَبَثًا وَأَنَّكُمْ إِلَيْنَا لَا تُرْجَعُونَ**. The opening is a rhetorical question — *did you really suppose…?* — the kind of question that exposes an assumption a person never actually examined. Almost nobody argues that life is meaningless; plenty of people live as though it were.

The key word is **عَبَثًا**. Ibn Kathir gives two readings, and both are worth holding:

**First:** *did you think that you were created in vain, with no purpose, with nothing required of you and no wisdom on Our part?* On this reading, ʿabath means pointlessness — an act with no aim behind it. Ibn Kathir's wording is careful: to think this of your own existence is to suppose there was *no wisdom on Our part*.

**Second:** it was also said that "in play" means *to play and amuse yourselves, like the animals were created, who have no reward or punishment.* On this reading, ʿabath describes a mode of living rather than a theory about creation — grazing, enjoying, with nothing asked and nothing owed. And Ibn Kathir cuts it off: *but you were created to worship Allah and carry out His commands.* The dignity and the demand arrive together. To be answerable is to matter.

The second half of the ayah names the assumption underneath: **وَأَنَّكُمْ إِلَيْنَا لَا تُرْجَعُونَ** — "and that you would not be brought back to Us," meaning, Ibn Kathir says, *that you would not be brought back to the Hereafter.* He connects it to another ayah that puts the same question even more starkly: **أَيَحْسَبُ الْإِنْسَانُ أَن يُتْرَكَ سُدًى** — "Does man think that he will be left neglected?" (75:36). Left to himself, unattended. The ayah itself joins purpose and return in a single sentence, and Ibn Kathir's parallel keeps them joined: to imagine yourself never brought back is to imagine yourself simply left.

## "So Exalted be Allah, the True King" — ayah 116

Ayah 116 answers the question of 115 by declaring Allah far above the very idea. **فَتَعَالَى اللَّهُ الْمَلِكُ الْحَقُّ** — Ibn Kathir renders the sense as *sanctified be He above the idea that He should create anything in vain, for He is the True King Who is far above doing such a thing.* The ayah does not argue the point; it places Allah above it. Purposeless creation is not merely denied — it is declared unworthy of Him.

Then the passage moves straight from purposeful creation to worship: **لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ** — none has the right to be worshipped but He. If life has a purpose, and that purpose is, in Ibn Kathir's words, to worship Allah and carry out His commands, then the ayah's conclusion follows by itself.

And He is named **رَبُّ الْعَرْشِ الْكَرِيمِ**, Lord of the Noble Throne. Ibn Kathir explains why the Throne in particular is mentioned here: *because it is the highest point of all creation.* As for **الْكَرِيم**, he glosses it as *beautiful in appearance and splendid in form*, and cites its parallel use elsewhere: **أَنبَتْنَا فِيهَا مِن كُلِّ زَوْجٍ كَرِيمٍ**, "every good kind We cause to grow therein" (26:7).

## "No proof for it" — ayah 117

Ayah 117 takes the tawḥīd just declared and states its opposite as a sentence of loss. **وَمَن يَدْعُ مَعَ اللَّهِ إِلَٰهًا آخَرَ لَا بُرْهَانَ لَهُ بِهِ** — whoever calls upon another god alongside Allah, **لَا بُرْهَانَ لَهُ**, which Ibn Kathir explains as *no evidence for what he says*. Ibn Kathir introduces the ayah as a threat: *Allah threatens those who associate anything else with Him and worship anything with Him.* A *burhān* is a proof, the thing that would actually establish a claim — and the ayah states, in passing, that there is none.

Ibn Kathir also points out the grammar, and it is worth pausing on. This is a conditional sentence — "whoever does X…" — and the clause that completes it is **فَإِنَّمَا حِسَابُهُ عِندَ رَبِّهِ**: *then his reckoning is only with his Lord*, meaning, he says, that Allah will call him to account for that. The sentence does not describe the punishment. It hands the matter over. Then the verdict is stated flatly: **إِنَّهُ لَا يُفْلِحُ الْكَافِرُونَ** — *they will not be successful with Him on the Day of Resurrection; they will not prosper or be saved.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān catches the architecture here. The sūrah opened with **قَدْ أَفْلَحَ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ**, "Success is really attained by the believers" (23:1), and closes with **إِنَّهُ لَا يُفْلِحُ الْكَافِرُونَ**, "surely the infidels will not achieve success" (23:117) — the same root, *falāḥ*, opening and sealing the sūrah. This shows, Maʿārif says, that success will come to the believers only, and that the unbelievers will have no share of it.

## The last words are a prayer — ayah 118

After the Fire, the questioning, the exposure of shirk — the sūrah ends not with a threat but with words placed in our mouths: **وَقُل رَّبِّ اغْفِرْ وَارْحَمْ وَأَنتَ خَيْرُ الرَّاحِمِينَ**, "My Lord! Forgive and have mercy, for You are the Best of those who show mercy."

Ibn Kathir says plainly that *here Allah is teaching us to recite this supplication.* He defines its two requests: **forgiveness** (*maghfirah*), in a general sense, means *wiping away sins and concealing them from people*; **mercy** (*raḥmah*) means *guiding a person and helping him to say and do good things.* So the two are not duplicates. One deals with the past — sins erased and covered. The other deals with what comes next — being guided into speech and action that is good. Behind you and ahead of you, in six Arabic words.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, citing Mazhari, notices something in the wording: no object is named. Forgive *what*? Have mercy on *whom*? The omission opens the prayer out — it suggests a general prayer for forgiveness, which would include deliverance from harm and suffering, and a general prayer for mercy, which would include the grant of every wish. Since protection from bodily harm and the acquisition of legitimate gains is the object of all human activity, this prayer covers both these aspects. Nothing is excluded because nothing was specified.

And a question worth asking: why was the Prophet ﷺ, who is impeccable, commanded to say it? Maʿārif answers, citing Qurtubi: *to impress upon his followers the special merit of this prayer.* He says it so that we will.

## The merit of these closing ayat

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān records that the last verses of Sūrah al-Muʾminūn, from 115 to 118, have special merit. Baghawi and Thalabi have related from Sayyidnā Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) that he came across a person who was very ill. He recited these verses into the sick man's ears and he was cured immediately. The Prophet ﷺ asked him what he had whispered in the sick man's ears, and ʿAbdullāh Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) replied that he had recited these verses (115 to 118) in his ears. Thereupon the Prophet ﷺ said: "I swear by Him Who has power over my life that if a person with genuine faith were to recite these verses on a mountain, the mountain itself may move from its place." (Qurtubi and Mazhari)

Read the condition carefully — *a person with genuine faith*. That is the qualification the Prophet ﷺ himself attached to the promise: the recitation is joined to a heart that actually believes what these ayat say — that the stay is short, that the creation is purposeful, that the King is true, that no other deity has a shred of proof, and that mercy is asked of the Best of those who show mercy.

## Living it

**Answer the question now.** Ayah 112 will be asked. The only difference between the two groups is that one of them worked out the answer — "a little while" — before they were asked, and lived accordingly.

**Do not trade the eternal for the transient.** Ibn Kathir names this as the exact mistake behind "if only you had known." Every choice between an immediate pleasure and a lasting reward is that same trade in miniature.

**Be patient through the short stay.** Twice Ibn Kathir says the believers won by patient obedience over the same brief life. Whatever you are enduring, you are enduring it inside a stay that everyone will one day describe as a day, or part of a day.

**Take up the closing prayer.** رَّبِّ اغْفِرْ وَارْحَمْ وَأَنتَ خَيْرُ الرَّاحِمِينَ — *My Lord, forgive and have mercy, for You are the Best of those who show mercy.* Short enough to memorise today, and broad enough, as Maʿārif notes, to cover both protection from harm and the gaining of what is legitimate.
